#8899. How to Start a Workout When You Really Don’t Feel Like It (The Bridge Task Method)

If you can’t get yourself to start a workout after a long day, the problem might not be the workout itself. It’s the gear shift from “couch” to “go.”

A bridge task is a small, neutral action (not fun, not hard, just…meh) that you put in between the two so the jump is smaller.

Below is the 5-step version one of our coaching clients uses with her own students, plus a free worksheet to map your own.

A few weeks ago I was talking with Tabitha, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, about a challenge a lot of people face. ​ Some quick context: Tabitha is an executive function coach. She helps neurodivergent students and their families build the skills and systems that support their academic and personal goals. ​ And she noticed something: ​ The challenge of getting started on a workout is almost identical to the challenge her students face when trying to start homework. ​ This might sound familiar. You get home after a long day, mentally fried, and all you want to do is veg out on the couch. ​ In that state, getting up to cook a healthy dinner or go do a workout can feel really freaking hard.

Switching from a “YEAH!” task (chilling on the couch) to a “NAH!” task (workout/homework), is often harder than the task itself.

If we can make that gear shift less dramatic, it can make a big difference!

Instead of going from YEAH! to NAH!, you insert at least one task that’s just…MEH.

If you’re struggling to start your workout, don’t fight the gear change. Bridge it.

Add a little MEH to the mix and see what happens.

Tabitha put together a free worksheet that walks you through mapping your own task initiation sequence. Your personal YEAH -> MEH -> NAH.

Try it this week, and keep me posted on how it goes. ​ You got this. ​ -Matt

#8898. Does Soreness Mean a Good Workout? No. Here’s What It Actually Tells You

Soreness is not an indicator of a good workout, and not being sore doesn’t mean your workout didn’t count.

That day-after ache (DOMS) mostly tells you that you did something new, not something effective.

Progress is more reliably measured in your training log: more weight, more reps, more control over time, sore or not.

Rachael (a reader and all-around amazing person) sent me a question about this so well-organized it came with multiple choice answers. 😃

I LOVE this question, because almost everyone who’s getting started (or starting again) wonders the same thing:

Quick definition first. That achy, stiff, “why does it hurt to sit on the toilet” feeling that shows up a day or two after a workout has a name: DOMS, or Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness.

It usually peaks somewhere around 24-72 hours after you train.

Severe soreness is NOT an indicator of a good workout.

It’s a sign that you did something new that your body isn’t used to yet:

But it’s also not something to be afraid of, especially if you switch up your routine and are mildly sore for a day or two.

Your body is adapting quickly! And as you adjust to the new exercises, you’ll be less and less sore from it.

So when is soreness helpful, if ever? ​ Soreness can give us a useful signal that we worked a muscle we were trying to target and hadn’t felt before.

But if you’re SUPER sore? Like, can’t get out of bed the next day and have to waddle around like a newborn giraffe sore? That’s a sign the jump was bigger than your body needed.

And the real cost (beyond the discomfort) is that it gets in the way of your next couple of workouts. Either because your technique gets sloppy because everything hurts, or you’re so wrecked that you don’t want to show up at all.

The best way to lower your odds of severe DOMS is to ease into a new program slowly.

Start with fewer sets and lighter weights than you think you need, and build from there. 💪

Yes! You DO need to push yourself over time in order to make progress:

That’s the law of progressive overload, and there’s no getting around it.

Sometimes adding that extra bit will make you sore. Other times, it won’t.

But it’s the underlying principle that matters: are you asking a little more of yourself over time? Not: did it hurt afterward?

So why do we care so much about soreness?

Here’s what I think we’ve fallen into with fitness in general.

We as humans operate really well with feedback. If we touch a hot stove, we get burned and know not to do that again.

We want to know, immediately after doing something, whether it worked or it didn’t.

And with strength training, you don’t feel stronger the next day. It takes time to build up.

So we reach for proxies that close that feedback loop.

It’s exactly like the story of minty toothpaste.

As the story goes, toothpaste manufacturers had a hard time selling their product until they added mint.

Suddenly, there was a tingly clean feeling you could latch onto. “Oh, this IS working.”

The mint doesn’t clean your teeth. But it’s associated with the thing that does, and it gave people something to feel.

It’s not the REASON you’re getting stronger.

But it can be associated with the work you do, especially as a beginner who is new to exercise, so we’ve learned to chase the tingle.

✅ How much weight, how many reps, how many sets are you doing?

✅ Do you feel more stable and controlled with the exercise than you did last month?

Then great! It’s working. Doesn’t matter if you never get sore.

And if you do end up super sore after trying something new, it’s not that you “failed”.

Just take it as a cue to introduce things more gently next time. 😊

So, back to Rachael’s multiple choice question.

C is really close. But I’ll add an fourth option:

D) Soreness tells you what was NEW. Your training log tells you what’s WORKING.

No extra fitness points for being sore. No points off if you do end up sore, either.

All the points gently ramping things up over time, and showing up again next time. 🔥

Is it bad if I’m never sore? No. If your weights, reps, or control are improving over time, your training is working, sore or not.

How long does DOMS last? It usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after the workout and fades over a few days. If you’re regularly wrecked for longer, ease the jumps in your program.

Should I work out while sore? Mild soreness is fine to train through, and easy movement often helps. If you’re severely sore, target a different part of the body, scale down, or take another rest day; what we don’t want to do is have sloppy technique because we’re SO sore we can’t perform the exercise normally.

#8897. Camel Pose Helps Build Balance, Strength, and Flexibility

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Camel Pose first appeared in the September-October 2001 issue of Yoga Journal. You can find more of our Archives here.

When looking at the meanings of the names of yoga asanas, especially those named after animals, you can find clues—sometimes literal and other times only suggestive —about the nature of the pose. With Camel Pose (Ustrasana) it’s a little of both.

What was it about this pose that inspired yogis of ages past to name it after the camel? Only by strenuously stretching the imagination can we find any resemblance to a healthy backbend in the shape of this animal.

Anatomically a camel’s body appears to be an assemblage of odd, unrelated parts, and the hump—the most unique and obvious characteristic—looks almost like an afterthought. Although camel humps may appear to be part of the spine, they are actually sacks of fat used to store partially digested food for long journeys. Through centuries of Asian and African civilization, the camel has also had a reputation for being a stubborn, ill-tempered animal with a serious lack of intelligence. Since it’s doubtful that the ancient yogis aspired to the image of lifting the spine like a camel hump, and a camel’s temperament is not exactly something to emulate in one’s yoga practice, why is this posed called the “camel”?

Traditionally the camel’s presence in the desert, one of the most inhospitable environments on our planet, has been one of the primary forces sustaining human life there. Though a camel’s eyesight is not keen, it relies on some inner compass to navigate its way through the desert. Used primarily as pack animals, camels instinctively know if a load is too heavy to endure over a long journey or if the weight is improperly balanced —and will refuse to move until the load is adjusted. Without a road map, in constantly changing surroundings of drifting sands, camels have the ability to read the signs and find the oases of green where water is present and food at hand.

Looking at the Camel Pose, we can begin to see a parallel. For many beginners, the “environment” in backbends is equally inhospitable. In general, beginning to bend backward is difficult and sometimes frightening, yet backbends are essential to maintaining a healthy spine. Generally we function in a forward-facing, right-side-up world, relying heavily on our eyes for our sense of identity and direction. In Camel, we must learn to cultivate another way of seeing. The shape of the pose places the head and one’s vision behind the body. It is an alien experience; our view of the world is literally turned upside down.

Our normal context for relating to ourselves and the image that sustains us is lost. For the beginner, a common reaction to the fear that comes from this loss of context is to shorten or hold the breath.

In addition, beginners often habitually contract the muscles of the buttocks and abdomen. The neck, if weak, becomes vulnerable as the shoulders grip for protection. When these reactions are present in the body, the movement in this pose does not respond well, especially if the student uses excessive muscular force. The pose feels out of balance, and the more we struggle, the less the pose responds. This only deepens the frustration, and we are likely to shut down or check out.

Basically there are two techniques for entering Camel Pose safely: dropping in from an upright kneeling position or lifting up from a seated position. Once you master these approaches in Camel Pose, a foundation has been laid for approaching the more advanced backbend Wheel Pose (Urdhva Dhanurasana) either by lifting up from the floor or by dropping back from a standing position.

I recommend dropping in from the kneeling position in Camel for your first attempt if your lower back or knees are sensitive. This approach also works with gravity to help you avoid the natural tendencies of the beginner to overdo muscular effort. Begin by kneeling on your mat with your torso upright and the thighs perpendicular to the floor. Place your legs hip-width apart, with the tops of the feet flat on the floor and your arms at your sides. If your lower back is weak, place your hands on your buttocks to give more support to the lumbar spine as you enter the pose. Let your shoulders hang from the sides of your neck and drop your collarbones away from your ears. Initially keep your head upright, with your chin drawn slightly in toward the center of the throat. As you inhale, feel the fullness of your breath feeding the back, rather than the chest.

With each exhalation, let the weight of your chest and abdominal organs sink, as you keep the spine engaged upward from the back of the skull. Visualize the energy of the pose looping down along the front of the body (from the chest down through the hips to the shinbones on the floor) and up along the back of the body (through the spine to the crown of the head). Slowly take your head back; keep the throat soft and the shoulders down and slightly forward, with the shoulder blades broad. Avoid hardening the buttocks or the abdomen. Keep the top of the hips pressing firmly down into the knees, and as you bend the spine backward, let your arms hang from your shoulders with your fingers reaching back to touch the heels.

If the stress is excessive in your lower back, inhale back to an upright position, and after resting for a moment, try the pose again. Once your hands reach your feet, maintain the downward pressure from the top of the hip bones pressing into the knees, continue releasing the chest and abdomen down, and feel the lift from the floor into the thoracic spine.

The head should hang freely, with the neck supported by the width of the trapezius muscle along the top of the shoulders. The breath should remain slow and rhythmic, and with each exhalation, the release of the frontal body will propel the lift in the back body. After three or four cycles of breath, inhale back to an upright position.

Lifting up from the seated position can be more accessible when the neck is weak, but it tends to stress the legs and knees more intensely than the first approach, due to the fact that you are working against gravity. If your knees are weak, take care not to overstress them. And be patient—if your knees and groins are tight, you may not achieve full extension in the pose at first.

From an upright kneeling position, sit between your heels (use a block between your feet if necessary, with the palms of your hands placed on your heels, fingers pointing back. Slowly lean back, straightening your arms, taking your weight onto your hands, and lift your hips upward.

Press the shoulders forward, broaden the shoulder blades, and let the neck rest in the trapezius muscle as you take the head slowly back. As the hips lift upward and more weight is taken onto the lower legs, press the tops of the hip bones (ilia) down into the knees and lift the spine. Be careful to keep the abdomen and buttocks soft and the energy of the chest dropping.

Once you are in the pose, the release of the frontal body will propel the lift in the back body. After three or four cycles of breath, slowly lower your hips on an inhalation and return to the seated position. With Camel Pose, you begin to develop balance and strength in the spine, promoting flexibility in the shoulders and suppleness in the abdomen. By relying less on outer sight for your sense of identity and position in the world, you can cultivate an inner vision that expands into your more authentic, intuitive self.

#8896. The Best Triathlon Suits of 2026, Tested by Real-World Triathletes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Best tri suits of 2026 rated and reviewed based on 10 criteria. (Photo: Triathlete)

Men's 2XU Light Speed React Sleeved Tri Suit

Women's 2XU Light Speed React Sleeved Tri Suit

When you look good, you feel good – and when you feel good, you race great. It’s no surprise, then, that when triathletes gear up for race day, they spend hours looking online for the best tri suit.

Indeed, in our 2025 Triathlete Community Survey, 88% of respondents said aesthetics were at least “somewhat” important, with 38% saying they wouldn’t wear what they felt was an “ugly” kit.

But a great triathlon suit is more than good-looking – ideally, it also needs to fit well, carry your nutrition stash, provide an aero- and hydro-dynamic advantage, and protect the tender bits from chafing.

We’re asking a lot of tri suits these days, but the industry has stepped up to the challenge. Legacy brands like Zoot and Coeur, as well as newcomers Ryzon and Tri-Fit, have made it possible for triathletes to find not only a suit that meets their practical race-day needs but also shows off their own personal style.

With so many options available, we asked the Philly Tri Club and Triathlete contributors to help with real-world testing of the top triathlon suits of 2026. The 150-strong club is all about creating an inclusive training community, and club members in a variety of shapes and sizes put tri suits through the paces, wearing them through workouts and races and making note of what works and what doesn’t in their triathlon kit reviews. Here’s what they had to say about the best triathlon suits of 2026.

In our 2025 Triathlete Community Survey, we asked readers what brands of triathlon apparel they had in their closets. Though more than 20 brands were represented, the top six are familiar names in the industry.

Pockets: 2 back pockets, 2 svelte front pockets, 1 neck ice pocket

The Regna Elite Trisuit offers a custom fit via an app that completes an AI-powered body scan for a fit based on your unique features. For the ultimate test, we tasked Triathlete contributor Jon Dorn and his wife Heather with testing it out. Jon stands at 6’6” and is self-described as very slender. His wife is 5’3” “buxom, and more powerfully built,” according to Jon.

“I’ve finally found a tri suit that doesn’t chafe my ass or distract me as various sensitive parts start smarting,” said Jon.

Heather noted that the suit was a 95% perfect fit, though the midsection was slightly loose. As someone who doesn’t fit into the “one-size-fits-most” size structure, she was still quite pleased. “This is the best my undercarriage has felt in a tri kit in years,” she reported after a four-hour training ride.

Ultimately, the pair found that the price tag is the biggest deterrent and only really justifiable if you’re someone who doesn’t fit into a standard tri kit well.

If you’re looking for a budget triathlon suit for a sprint or Olympic triathlon that won’t chafe, the 2XU Core Tri Suit is a safe bet. It lacks adequate padding and pockets sizable enough to carry enough nutrition for long-course training or racing, but at the $200 price point, it’s a rare find for short-course racing.

It’s light on compression if that’s your preference and when it comes to breathability, the suit was disappointing, so ideally plan to wear it in more forgiving weather, as our tester found that it trapped heat and sweat more than other comparable suits.

Our tester found it hard to criticize anything about this suit because it fit snugly and comfortably. While she doesn’t normally wear sleeved tri suits, she was pleasantly surprised by how thin and breathable the fabric on these sleeves was, to the point that she forgot the sleeves were even there.

The tri suit has ample compression, especially in the core. The one detractor is that this suit only comes in black or black and white, which is a little generic and not as fun as some of the other options on this list. User beware, too: our tester noticed a bit of color leaking when handwashing the suit. Consider wearing the suit for shorter training sessions or wearing a belt with additional fuel, as the two back pockets are medium-sized and diagonally aligned.

Pockets: 3 back pockets, 2 inner front pockets, 1 neck ice pocket

When it comes to tri suits, it’s the little details that make a brand stand out. In this case, Tri-Fit’s attention to pockets – six in total, including one explicitly for holding ice on your neck during hot races – is reason enough to consider the Vortex for a long-course race.

Testers liked the fit, fabric choice, design, pockets, and overall feel, noting that it looks great with small logos, lightweight fabric, and comfortable chamois padding for shorter events. The chest zips up tightly, preventing wind trap, and performed well during rides and runs.

However, there was substantial drag in the water, and the vent holes under the arms caused chafing – vented fabric would be preferable, as would slightly more compression on the legs. In all, however, the Tri Fit feels premium, and with a few minor design tweaks, could quickly become a favorite tri suit.

Pockets: 1 lower-back channel pocket, 1 neck ice pocket

This tri suit performed adequately in the heat, thanks to the use of smart temp technology, which dials up evaporation from the skin to the air as body temperature rises. The super-thin and light chamois also mitigates heat well, especially on long rides, and strategically-placed airflow channels on the shoulders and back help things feel cool and fast on the bike.

However, the top zipper rubbed against the chest, causing discomfort during running and biking. It also chafed at the neckline due to the lack of a zipper cover. Testers liked that it fit well, but disliked that the zipper needed a fabric cover and that the white top was see-through, especially when wet coming out of the swim or sweating on the run (women testers noted their sports bra was visible while wearing the suit in a race).

At $125, Black Bibs brand has created a budget-friendly triathlon suit that stands out in a market full of offerings $300 or more. But “budget” should not be conflated with “cheap” here – the suit fits well, provides exceptional compression, and is a classic style (men’s and women’s one-piece colorways include a solid black as well as a black bottom half with navy, burgundy, or white uppers). Openings for the legs and arms use silicone “power bands” to keep the suit secure throughout a workout or race, and no chafing was reported. The suit also proved extremely durable both on and off the race course, holding up through dozens of laundry cycles without shrinking, pilling, or splitting seams.

The initial impression of the chamois was mediocre, but improved with subsequent use and resolved itself after several rides. Testers reported drag when swimming, with the neckline sagging, and recommended use with a wetsuit. Dislikes included poor moisture wicking, especially in the upper body, and unusually high rear pockets.

Unlike some tri brands, where women’s suits are simply a smaller version of the men’s, Coeur tri suits are designed with a woman’s physique in mind, from the contours of the suit to the women’s specific seamless chamois. Testers also liked the supple fabric and one-piece design with a full front zipper and high-rise short beneath, allowing for breathability and extra roominess in the torso.

This tri suit performed exceptionally well on the swim and run, but some chafing was experienced on the bike – chamois cream is recommended. The arm openings run slightly small, so athletes with muscular arms should size up or opt for the sleeveless version. Luckily, Coeur offers a variety of competitively-priced women’s tri suit configurations in matching colorways: sleeved, sleeveless, sports bra/shorts, aero tops, and tri tops with built-in bras.

Testers liked the sleek, minimalist, and professional appearance of the monochromatic Arise tri suit, as well as its stretchy, comfortable, and “slippery” feel that allowed for movement and flexibility without chafing. It remained comfortable even when wet, ran true to size, didn’t create unnecessary drag, and worked well with other clothing. This tri suit generally performed well across all conditions and disciplines, with no reported poor performance or chafing.

However, a dime-sized hole appeared in the left armpit after two wears, which was surprising and disappointing, given the suit’s $335 price tag. Testers also wished the back pocket was deeper and had multiple compartments.

Pockets: 1 rear pocket, two side pockets, 3 interior pockets

Zoot has been a mainstay of triathlon apparel for more than 40 years, and for good reason – users recognize the balance of form and function present in many of its products. The suits, designed by endurance athletes, for endurance athletes, come in a variety of designs, including flashy patterns and colorways.

The latest offering from Zoot, the Ultra Tri P1, performed well during swims in the ocean, bike rides on a trainer and outside, and runs outside. Testers liked its comfortable and true-to-size fit as well as built-in UPF 35 sun protection fabric.

However, the pockets were not very big, making it difficult to carry proper nutrition during training rides or runs – testers recommended wearing the suit for short-course racing or long-course events only if nutrition on the course is plentiful. The zipper was also annoying and rubbed a bit, requiring multiple adjustments while running.

Overall, however, the suit was rated as “top-notch” for comfort, breathability, and weight.

Looking for more tri suit reviews? Check out our reviews of tri suits from Varlo, Swiss Side, Wyn, Synergy, and more in The Best Tri Suits for 2024.

#8895. How Fast Do You Actually Lose Strength? Slower Than You Think

You lose strength much more slowly than you probably think.

A few days off changes basically nothing, measurable losses take roughly two to four weeks depending on the quality (muscle endurance fades first, maximal strength last).

Muscle memory makes rebuilding faster than building the first time, and maintaining takes a fraction of the training that building did.

Here’s the timeline, and how it can inform your training.

Has this question ever crossed your mind:

This was an awesome question that Charles sent my way. (Thanks Charles! 🙌)

When life gets crazy and you find yourself skipping workouts, there’s a voice that says:

I had that exact thought the first time I had to take significant time away for a back injury.

And heck, just recently my kiddos brought home the “crud” from school and I missed a full week of workouts.

So, let’s look at what actually happens, and what it means for your training.

Short version: a few days off doesn’t impact your maximum strength or muscle size basically at all.

Your muscles may look or feel “flatter”, but that’s because stored water and glycogen decrease, not because you are weaker.

And this “pump” comes back quickly once you start training again. 💪

Here’s a rough timeline of when we start to see the effects of detraining:

Highly trained folks and older adults will notice detraining faster than new or younger lifters (so they’ll sit towards the beginning of these timelines.)

But you don’t lose your progress in any meaningful way after a week or 2 away from the gym. 😊

And if you DO have to spend significant time away for whatever reason, I have good news for you, too:

1) Your nervous system remembers how to do the movement.

The first session or two in the gym after time away may feel a bit clunky, but you’ll quickly regain the technique.

And a big component of strength is neuromuscular coordination (i.e. your brain and muscles firing together more efficiently, which improves rapidly.)

2) The muscle itself seems to hold onto some of the machinery it built, so it rebuilds faster the second time.

A general rule of thumb is about 50% as long as you were away (so if you were away for 12 weeks, it may take ~6 weeks to rebuild your strength.) Take this with a grain of salt as there is a LOT of variation here. This isn’t a hard and fast rule.

(And you don’t want to jump right back in at 100%. Use the 50/50 rule to get yourself going again.)

The point is, it’s generally easier to rebuild than to build the first time.

Building muscle and strength? It takes time and effort.

No one wakes up a day after a workout and has just magically put on 5 pounds of muscle.

That takes only a fraction of the volume.

When you keep intensity the same (i.e. how hard the exercise is), doing 1/3 the number of sets maintains your strength for a loooong time. ​ The point being: doing ANYTHING during a period where you aren’t able to consistently work out is still really really helpful!

When life throws you off track with your fitness goals, you’re not starting back from square zero.

And even a single session each week with a couple challenging sets is enough to hold what you’ve built until things calm down.

There’s that old saying that: “The best time to invest was 20 years ago. The next best time to invest is today.”

I think the same holds true for building up your fitness.

Every session you put in now is strength you get to keep later.

This is exactly why we built our coaching program. Because having a coach makes both of those so much smoother. ​ We take the thinking off your plate so it’s easier to get going.

We direct your limited time and effort toward the stuff that actually moves the needle. ​ AND when life pulls you away (sick kids, a work deadline, etc.) we help you maintain and get right back at it. ​ If that sounds like the kind of help you’ve been looking for, here’s how NF Coaching works. 💪 ​ -Matt

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

Humans featured are exceptional examples and do not guarantee individual success. Your experience and results may vary.

Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class via Alaska Mileage Plan — no fuel surcharges

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Château Léoville Barton in hand, watching the Australian coastline slowly materialize through your window. The cabin is hushed. The seat — Cathay Pacific's renowned Business Class throne on the Airbus A350-1000 — cocoons you in a private pod with a sliding door, direct aisle access, and a mattress pad that makes a five-star hotel bed feel like an afterthought. This is the LAX–HKG–SYD route in Cathay Pacific Business Class. And you booked it for 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles. Now consider what the person three rows up in economy paid in cash for their seat — and what the couple beside you in business paid for theirs. A Cathay Pacific Business Class ticket on this route typically retails between **$5,000 and $12,000**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin pricing on transpacific routes is notoriously aggressive, and Australia amplifies it further because of the sheer distance involved. At 55,000 miles for a one-way business class redemption, you're extracting somewhere between **9.1 and 21.8 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that makes most loyalty program strategists stop and stare. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5–2 CPP for most programs. You are obliterating that benchmark. At the high end of this range, 55,000 miles is doing the work of $12,000 in cash. That is what the FI mindset calls asymmetric value. This is also a premium *experience*, not just a premium number. Cathay Pacific consistently ranks among the world's top airlines for business class. The A350-1000 is their flagship long-haul aircraft, featuring a 1-2-1 configuration with every single seat having direct aisle access. There are no middle seats. There are no awkward climbs over sleeping strangers. There is a full dine-on-demand menu, a curated wine list, noise-canceling headphones, and a ground service team that treats you like a valued guest before you even board. For the FI traveler, this redemption represents something rare: a genuine luxury experience — the kind that recalibrates your sense of what travel can feel like — made nearly free through a well-understood system. The math works. The experience delivers. And once you've done it, you'll understand exactly why the ChooseFI community talks about this one.

Alaska Mileage Plan is one of the most valuable frequent flyer programs in the world despite being a relatively small airline. The secret is their partner award chart: Alaska uses fixed pricing for partner airline awards, meaning costs do not fluctuate with demand the way dynamic programs do. This creates structural pricing inefficiencies — especially on premium cabin routes to Asia and Oceania — that savvy travelers can exploit. Alaska has partnerships with Cathay Pacific, Qantas, Japan Airlines, Emirates, Fiji Airways, and others. The primary way to earn Alaska miles is through the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card (Bank of America), through flying, or via Marriott Bonvoy transfers at a 3:1 ratio.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Here's the insight that transforms this from "interesting" to "actionable": Alaska Airlines Mileage Plan uses a fixed partner award chart, and that chart prices Cathay Pacific Business Class to Australia at 55,000 miles one-way — a number that hasn't kept pace with the explosive cash price inflation of premium cabin fares.

Most major U.S. loyalty programs have migrated to dynamic pricing, where award costs fluctuate with cash fare demand. Alaska hasn't done this for partner awards. Their chart is fixed. That means when Cathay Pacific's cash fares spike to $12,000 during Australian school holidays or peak summer travel, your award cost stays exactly where it was: 55,000 miles. This is the pricing inefficiency at the heart of this redemption, and it's why the ChooseFI community treats Alaska Mileage Plan as one of the most valuable programs in the industry.

Alaska Mileage Plan has only one meaningful transfer partner for most people: Marriott Bonvoy, at a ratio of 3 Bonvoy points to 1 Alaska mile. That's a steep ratio — you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points to generate 55,000 Alaska miles — and transfer times run 1 to 5 days, so plan accordingly. There is no direct credit card transfer path into Alaska Mileage Plan from Chase, Amex, or Citi, which is why the "Easy to Earn" score for this redemption is a 2 out of 5. The miles must be earned directly: through Alaska's co-branded credit card (the Alaska Airlines Visa from Bank of America), through flying Alaska or its partners, or via Marriott transfer.

This is crucial and often overlooked. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on any partner award bookings. This matters enormously for a Cathay Pacific redemption. If you were to book the same Cathay flight through Cathay's own Asia Miles program or through British Airways Avios, you could face fuel surcharges of $400–$900 or more on top of the points cost. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket cost is taxes and fees only — typically in the range of $50–$150 depending on the routing. That's it. A $12,000 experience for 55,000 miles and roughly $100 in fees.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit that is genuinely rare among U.S. programs. On the LAX–HKG–SYD routing, this means you can build a stopover in Hong Kong at no additional points cost. Spend a few days exploring one of the world's most dynamic cities — the markets of Mong Kok, the skyline from Victoria Peak, the dim sum temples of Kowloon — then board your continuing flight to Sydney. Two destinations. One redemption. Same 55,000 miles.

The 55,000-mile rate applies to both Cathay Pacific and Qantas for business class to Australia. Cathay routes you through Hong Kong (HKG); Qantas has its own metal and routing options. If Cathay availability is thin, checking Qantas can open up alternatives without changing your points cost.

Do not start at Alaska's website. Alaska's own search tool for partner availability can be unreliable for Cathay Pacific. Instead, go to ba.com (British Airways' booking site) and run a one-way business class search for your desired route — for example, LAX to SYD or LAX to HKG. British Airways and Cathay Pacific are oneworld partners, and BA's search engine surfaces Cathay award availability with remarkable accuracy. Look for "Reward" seats in the business class (Club World or equivalent) cabin. Any dates showing availability on BA.com are almost certainly bookable through Alaska as well. Screenshot or note the specific dates before moving on.

Alaska opens its award booking window 331 days in advance. If you're targeting peak travel dates — Australian summer (December–February), for example — set a calendar reminder to search and transfer 331 days ahead. Your miles also never expire in Mileage Plan, which gives you flexibility to accumulate without pressure.

Confirm you have at least 55,000 Alaska miles available. If you're converting Marriott Bonvoy points, you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points at the 3:1 ratio. Initiate transfers at least one week before you plan to call, as Marriott-to-Alaska transfers can take 1 to 5 days.

Log into your Marriott Bonvoy account, navigate to "Transfer Points," select Alaska Airlines as the recipient program, and enter your Mileage Plan number. Transfer in increments of 3,000 Bonvoy points (yielding 1,000 Alaska miles). Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 1 — points transfers are generally non-reversible.

This redemption cannot be booked online — Alaska's web portal does not support all partner award bookings, particularly for Cathay Pacific. Call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522. Tell the agent:

Have your Mileage Plan number, passport information, and a credit card for the taxes and fees ready. The call typically takes 20–40 minutes. Agents are generally knowledgeable, but if you encounter confusion, politely ask for a senior agent or call back.

If Cathay availability is limited on your preferred dates, ask the agent to check Qantas availability to Australia at the same 55,000-mile rate. Qantas Business (The Business) has its own award inventory and may have open seats when Cathay is fully allocated.

If you're routing through Hong Kong on Cathay, explicitly ask the agent to add a free stopover at HKG. This is a program benefit, not a favor — Alaska's routing rules allow one free stopover on one-way awards. Specify how many nights you want in Hong Kong before the continuing flight to Sydney.

The best way to find Cathay Pacific Business Class award availability is through the British Airways website (ba.com). Search for one-way flights from your U.S. gateway to Sydney or Melbourne, and look for dates showing Cathay Pacific-operated flights with Business Class availability. British Airways shows oneworld partner availability more reliably than most tools.

If Cathay Pacific shows no availability on your preferred dates, search for Qantas Business Class on the same route. Qantas availability can be found through the Qantas website or through British Airways. The Alaska Mileage Plan price is the same 55,000 miles for either carrier.

Earn miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa card sign-up bonus (typically 60,000 to 75,000 miles), through flying Alaska or partners, or by transferring from Marriott Bonvoy. If transferring from Marriott, allow 1 to 5 business days for the transfer to complete before your booking window closes.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522 and request a partner award booking on Cathay Pacific (or Qantas) Business Class. Provide your desired dates and routing. Ask about adding a free stopover in Hong Kong if routing through HKG. The agent will process the booking and deduct 55,000 miles plus taxes and fees (typically $50 to $150).

After booking through Alaska, manage your seat selection directly through the Cathay Pacific website or app using your booking reference. Select a window or aisle seat in the 1-2-1 configuration — every seat has direct aisle access, so there is no wrong choice. You can also pre-order meals and manage other preferences through Cathay's platform.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner want to celebrate a milestone — a sabbatical, a paid-off mortgage, financial independence itself — with a trip to Sydney. Here's exactly how this redemption plays out.

The Route: Los Angeles (LAX) → Hong Kong (HKG) → Sydney (SYD), on Cathay Pacific Business Class, with a 3-night stopover in Hong Kong.

Cash Price: A quick search on Google Flights confirms what you suspected — this itinerary in business class retails for approximately $8,000 per person during the shoulder season. During the Australian summer or holiday periods, it climbs closer to $11,000–$12,000.

Your Cost: 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles + approximately $85 in taxes and fees. Per person.

CPP Calculation: At $8,000 cash value, your 55,000 miles are worth 14.5 cents per point — more than seven times what you'd get redeeming Alaska miles for domestic economy. At $12,000, you're at 21.8 cents per point, which is among the highest CPP figures available anywhere in the U.S. loyalty ecosystem.

In Hong Kong, Cathay Pacific's The Pier Business Class Lounge awaits during your stopover travel. It's widely regarded as one of the finest airport lounges in the world — noodle bar, live cooking stations, a spa treatment center, and a wine selection that rivals dedicated restaurants.

After three days exploring Hong Kong, you reboard for the six-hour SYD leg, arriving in Sydney ready — genuinely ready, not depleted — to start your adventure.

Total cost for two: 110,000 Alaska miles + roughly $170 in fees. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: extraordinary experiences made nearly free through a system anyone can learn.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days out. Cathay Pacific releases business class award space to partner programs in limited quantities, and the best dates disappear quickly. Set a calendar alert for 331 days before your target travel date and be ready to search — and call — that morning.

The single best technique for this redemption: run your search on ba.com before calling Alaska. BA's search engine is faster, more reliable for Cathay availability, and lets you visually scan a full month of dates. Identify two or three date options before you pick up the phone. This dramatically shortens your call time and reduces the chance of getting an agent who says "I'm not seeing anything."

Don't treat the Hong Kong stopover as a layover — treat it as a destination. Alaska's routing rules explicitly allow a free stopover on one-way awards. Two to four nights in Hong Kong costs you nothing extra in miles. Pair this with a cheap positioning flight or use it as an anchor for a broader Asia itinerary.

This is the most common and most painful mistake. Marriott-to-Alaska transfers are generally not reversible. If you transfer 165,000 Bonvoy points to Alaska and then discover no award space exists on your dates, you're stuck with miles you may not use optimally. Always confirm availability on ba.com before initiating any transfer.

Book two one-way redemptions rather than a round-trip. This gives you full flexibility on return routing — you might come back on Qantas through another city, or extend your trip without penalty.

Since there are no major flexible currency transfer paths into Alaska (no Chase, Amex, or Citi transfers), the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature from Bank of America is your most efficient earning vehicle. The welcome bonus alone can cover a significant portion of this redemption. Pair with everyday spending in categories that earn elevated miles.

If Cathay availability is closed on your dates, Qantas Business Class to Australia prices at the same 55,000 miles. Qantas' "The Business" product on their A380 Sydney routes is exceptional in its own right — and availability patterns differ from Cathay, so checking both genuinely doubles your options.

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI-minded couple or solo traveler who is willing to invest some effort in the booking process in exchange for an extraordinary, nearly free experience. If you've been dreaming about Australia and refuse to pay $8,000–$12,000 for a business class ticket — but you're also not willing to spend 20+ hours crammed in economy for a trip this significant — this is your answer.

Minimum requirements: You need 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per person. For two travelers, that's 110,000 miles. If you're building from zero through the Alaska Visa, factor in 6–12 months of earning runway before booking.

Within a broader FI travel strategy, this redemption pairs well with a Marriott Bonvoy credit card for point accumulation and an Alaska Visa for direct mile earning. It's a medium-complexity move with a very high ceiling on value.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is honest. It's not complicated in concept, but it has two specific friction points that trip up even experienced travel rewards enthusiasts. **Challenge 1: Earning the Miles** Alaska Mileage Plan's isolation from major flexible currency programs (no Chase Ultimate Rewards, no Amex Membership Rewards, no Citi ThankYou transfers directly) means you can't simply funnel points you already have into Alaska. The primary path is the Alaska Airlines Visa (Bank of America) or a Marriott Bonvoy conversion at an unfavorable 3:1 ratio. Plan your earning strategy well in advance. **Tip:** Prioritize the Alaska Visa signup bonus as your foundation, then supplement with Marriott points if needed. **Challenge 2: The Phone Booking Requirement** You cannot book this online. The call-in process intimidates people who've only ever booked travel digitally. **Tip:** Do your homework on ba.com first, have your dates ready, and approach the call as an informed customer — not someone asking for help finding availability. Agents respond well to specific, prepared callers. **Challenge 3: Cathay Award Availability** Cathay Pacific releases partner award space selectively and often in small quantities. Availability rated 3/5. **Tip:** Search exactly at the 331-day booking window, keep Qantas as your backup at the same price point, and be flexible with travel dates by even one or two days — a Tuesday departure often has inventory when Saturday doesn't. The good news: once you've done this once, you'll understand the system deeply enough to replicate it. The ChooseFI community has members who've booked this exact route multiple times. The first time takes effort. After that, it's a process you know cold.

The fastest path is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card from Bank of America, which typically offers a 60,000 to 75,000-mile sign-up bonus. That alone nearly covers the 55,000 miles needed. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy points at 3:1 (165,000 Bonvoy points equals 55,000 Alaska miles) or earn miles through flying Alaska and its partners.

Yes. You would book two separate one-way awards at 55,000 miles each. You could fly Cathay Pacific one direction and Qantas the other, or mix carriers based on availability. Each one-way can include its own free stopover.

Cathay Pacific typically releases Business Class award space 90 to 330 days before departure. The sweet spot for finding availability is usually 90 to 120 days out, when airlines release unsold premium cabin seats. Check frequently, as availability can appear and disappear quickly.

Alaska allows one free stopover on one-way awards. On a routing from the US to Australia via Hong Kong, you can stop in Hong Kong for any number of days at no additional miles cost. Simply tell the agent when booking that you want a stopover in HKG. This effectively gives you two destinations for the price of one redemption.

The Alaska Mileage Plan redemption for Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class to Australia is one of the most extraordinary sweet spots in travel rewards. At 55,000 miles for a seat that costs $5,000 to $12,000 in cash — with zero fuel surcharges and a free stopover in Hong Kong — this redemption delivers 9 to 22 cents per point. It requires more planning and effort than a simple hotel booking, but the payoff is a genuine luxury travel experience that proves the asymmetric value the FI community builds its travel rewards strategy around.

#8893. Why You Keep Falling Off Your Fitness Routine (and the 2-Minute Plan That Fixes It)

Expecting yourself to stick to the same fitness routine, no matter what, is why it fails.

Because the only predictable thing about life is that it’s unpredictable.

A kid gets sick. Sleep falls apart. The to-do list explodes.

You can’t know which one is coming or when, but you can know something is, and you can build your routine to expect it.

That’s the whole trick: take two minutes and decide, in advance, exactly what you’ll do the next time life goes sideways.

Here’s the coaching conversation that shows how it works.

I want to let you in on one of my biggest lessons from the last 15 years of coaching.

Once you know it, it will feel like you can see the future. 👀

On a live Q&A, George (not his real name) told me about a pattern he kept running into.

Then a kiddo would get sick, or some other responsibility would pop up, sleep would fall apart for a bit, and the whole routine would go with it.

And he got this look like “Oooooohhhhhhhh…no. No I haven’t.”

He’d been treating the sick kid as something that happens to the plan.

So we talked through it right there. Here’s what we came up with:

Now, he wasn’t just reacting in the moment, trying to “gut it out.”

He knew exactly what to do and it fit what he needed.

Here’s the thing: these moments don’t come out of the blue. They are predictable.

You’ll have WAY too much on your to-do list.

I don’t know which one, or when exactly, but I do know that it’s inevitable.

Once we accept that the only predictable thing is that life is unpredictable, we can use that to our advantage.

Take two minutes right now and finish this sentence:

First blank: the thing that knocked you off track the last time you were trying to get into a fitness routine.

Second blank: the best version of your plan you can still commit to on one of THOSE days.

Sometimes, life will throw something at you that you REALLY didn’t see coming.

But the more of these you’ve been through, the clearer the crystal ball becomes.

And the better you get at navigating it. 💪

Hit reply and send me your crystal ball plan. I read every one, and I’ll tell you if I’d tweak it.

#8892. Overwhelmed by Fitness Advice? You Need an Action Plan, Not a Perfect Plan

Do you ever feel like you’re stuck at the starting line?​ ​ You want to improve your health and fitness. But there’s so. much. going. on.

Every time you try to make a plan, you get 1,000 opinions on the “perfect” workout. The “perfect” diet. The “perfect” routine.

You’re not sure where to start or what to do.

I hear this story so often that I gave it a name. And a face. 😅

(h/t to Leo, our awesome illustrator who makes these images for us from scratch! 🙌 ) ​ Meet Major Overload.

He’s every fitness voice on the internet at once.

Do this. Never do that. Fasted cardio. Never fasted cardio. Carbs are fine. Carbs are the enemy.

The Major loves it when you have 100 tabs open on your browser, but haven’t done a workout yet.

He wants to keep you plugged in to The Matrix. He feeds off of you staying stuck in planning mode while he drains your batteries.

My client Eric ran into him a few months ago.

He’d spent weeks searching for “best at-home workouts to lose fat”. ​ In his words:

It’s the way I felt when I tasked myself with running Nerd Fitness’s Instagram.

A million different opinions on how to do it. Hours spent researching. And weeks later, I still hadn’t filmed an actual video yet. 😅

I was firmly stuck in analysis paralysis.

Same boss battle as Eric. Different rabbit hole.

What got me unstuck was the same thing that helped Eric.

It wasn’t finding the “perfect” strategy or plan.

1) Follow one plan and block out everything else for now.​ ​ ​2) Commit to taking some small action, most days of the week.

The first one turned Major Overload’s volume down.

I didn’t need every voice. I needed a simple starting point. One that didn’t have a gajillion hoops to jump through.

The second one is where the learning actually happened.

I didn’t have to be perfect. I had to commit to imperfect reps.

I’ve learned more from a couple of weeks of posting than from all the agonizing I did beforehand.

Here’s what I told Eric, and what I’d tell you, too:

Unless you’re Doctor Strange, scrubbing through 14 million possible futures to find the one where everything works out, you can’t know what perfect looks like. Neither can I. Nor anyone on the internet, no matter how loud they get.

Enough structure to get out there and do the thing. Not so convoluted that you never get started.

That’s why we built the Beginner Bodyweight Workout and our Strength Training Templates.

So you stop getting stuck at the starting line, and start putting in the reps.

Moving from planning to action does two things at once.

It breaks the inertia, and it teaches you what fits in YOUR life.

It’s where you learn that, actually, training later in the evening works better for you than trying to force yourself up at 5AM.

It’s how you discover that splitting your workout up into two 15-minute chunks works better for your schedule.

Or that you prefer training with weights to training with bands.

You won’t know those things until you get out there and try.

It’s just as important to learn what DOESN’T work for you as what does.

Three weeks of taking imperfect action will tell you more about what works for you than three months of listening to Major Overload ever could.

Instead of searching for the “perfect” plan, build your action plan.

1 or 2 actions you can take this week, small enough to test and see how they feel.

That’s exactly what we did with Eric. ​ We mapped out his first few action steps. Things that fit his life, and he felt confident doing.

And now? He’s 4-months in and training consistently. Not perfectly. Consistently.

And that’s made all the difference for him. 💪

One more thing about Eric’s story I want to leave you with. He also shared this with me as part of our conversation:

That’s something else I hear all the time. And it’s nothing to be ashamed of!

Sometimes, the bravest thing you can do is to ask for help when you need it.

When you’re stuck at step one, overwhelmed by information and not sure what’s worth your time, that’s exactly where a coach can help.

We build a program around you: your schedule, your equipment, your starting point. And then we help you run it and adjust as you learn. ​ If that sounds like what you’ve been looking for, here’s my invitation:

​Fill out this short form. Someone from our team will reach out to have a real conversation about whether NF Coaching is a good fit for you. ​ And if it’s not a fit? We’ll tell you that too, and point you in the right direction.

Either way, the goal is to get you out of analysis paralysis and moving forward.

TLDR: Build an action plan, not a “perfect” plan. Commit to something simple to start. Learn and build from there. And if you want guidance from a coach who’s been through it all before, here’s how to work with us. 💪

#8891. Your Weekly Horoscope, November 1-7, 2026: Tuning Into Truth

With both Mercury retrograde and Venus retrograde creating aspects with other planets this week, there is an introspective and contemplative vibe, one that is both receptive and restorative. It’s a time to reveal the quiet whispers of truth, the whispers that cannot always be heard underneath the noise of the world. And they reveal what else exists within us, including the deeper longings, the quiet hurts, and the secret wishes. Your weekly horoscope for November 1-7, 2026, explains where to bring your contemplations.

November 4 | Venus retrograde in Libra sextile Jupiter in Leo; Mercury cazimi in Scorpio

Still in her retrograde, Venus in Libra enters a dance with Jupiter in Leo on November 4, 2026, forming a sextile, which is an astrological aspect of ease, openness, opportunity, and inspiration.

Venus retrograde in Libra invites thoughtful consideration around connection, inner harmony, and balance. Jupiter in Leo holds expansion related to authentic self-expression, self-celebration, desire, and creativity. As they meet this week, what results is an easeful flow of energy within and without. Its’s a reminder to remember that medicine can be found in pleasure, creativity, beauty, and self-worth.

This is essentially an aspect relating to how safe we feel in expressing our feelings, how safe we feel in another seeing our feelings for them, and how safe we feel in sharing our feelings. It’s a day for immersing ourselves in beauty, inspiration, and celebration.

As Mercury experiences retrograde in Scorpio, the planet draws near to the Sun on November 4, 2026, in what is known as an inferior cazimi, which is an exact conjunction of a retrograde body with the Sun.

Considered the messenger of our cosmos, Mercury is currently retracing its steps, and when it does so in Scorpio, it explores the unseen outer influences shaping our thinking, perception, narratives, and life experiences. The Sun is also in Scorpio, which invites us into the depths, the underworld, the emotional waters of our inner body.

When these two draw close, mind and body meet. Here feeling and awareness become one. The contents of our unconscious minds, body memories, and psychological patterns begin to speak. They ask for review. They ask for understanding. They ask to be held. They ask to be rewritten into something more truthful.

It’s a day of heightened awareness, enhanced intuition, and inward orientation. There is much moving beneath our own surfaces as these archetypes align, and this conjunction allows us to peer into this movement.

Explore the effects of the Moon, learn what your opposite sign means, and understand how astrology intersects with your everyday life by receiving our astrology email newsletter.

As Venus dances with Jupiter, what are your deeper longings? What connects you to the soft flow of joy and inspiration that sings through our cosmos and earth at all moments? What brings you home to the inner spark of aliveness, a connection to yourself that seems to enliven you when returned to?

While in Scorpio, both Mercury retrograde and the Sun ask for an honest intimacy with yourself. What walls have you built around yourself not just so others cannot reach you, but so that you cannot reach you? Where are you ready to know yourself more truthfully?

As Venus and Jupiter invite us home to exuberance and the freedom of expression, Mercury and the Sun invite us home to the layers of us that we have abandoned in order to reclaim them. Your horoscope explains how these are relevant to you this week. Read for your rising sign.

It’s a week of meeting the fears and hurts within you and holding them with acceptance and compassion. As you learn to trust yourself as a safe space once again, notice where you are ready to lower the walls that once protected you, even if just an inch.

It’s a week for awareness and contemplation. What patterns arise when you meet someone? What fears shape the way you connect with others? What stories influence the way you open or close yourself to love? There is a readiness to release what you no longer require to feel safe.

Welcome to an invitation to remember your worthiness. To disconnect with anything you inherited, absorbed, and learned that says your worth is dependent upon usefulness and achievements or otherwise granted to you by another. The narratives and stories that have you overworking, overgiving, and disconnecting from your own rhythm, pace, vitality, and desires no longer suit you.

Sitting beneath everything this week is the invitation to remember pleasure. To untangle all the patterns, projections, and narratives that say you must earn it or that to be seen in your truth is not safe. To release any ways of navigating life that have you silence and hide yourself. To feel worth and safety originate within yourself.

Can you tell what’s shaping you? There is insight and discernment in the days to come regarding the inherited perspectives and the learned stories that might still drive your existence. discernment. And along with awareness comes alternate ways of seeing, reclaiming, accepting, and loving you. Don’t let them pass you by.

The week ahead acts as a mirror and reveals more of the patterns, narratives, and words that inhabit your mind as well as the underlying fears and longing that shape them. As you gain awareness, insight, and understanding about what has been taking place beneath your everyday consciousness, you begin to unravel whatever is not your truth.

You are in a moment of transition. Old narratives are releasing from your mind; who you must be, what makes you safe. Old emotions are unravelling from your body; projected shame, fears that were never yours to hold. Existing identities are reorganising; where you want to go, who you want to be.

Your identity is moving and self-perception is reshaping itself. Allow what everno longer feels truthful and relevant to fall away and let whatever is longing to step forward begin taking up more space within you. You are changing from the inside out. What new stories want to be told? What old identities no longer fit?

The week draws you into yourself. Beyond noise. Beyond busyness. Where your inner voice can be heard and your emotions can be felt. Where your longings can be met and your fears quieted. Things are rearranging within you. As stories of belonging  unravel, a different self slowly readies itself to emerge.

Can you bring more space to the way you look at your future? Instead of looking ahead for direction, look within. Re-commune with your desires, hopes, fears, and what truly matters to you. Let visions that no longer feel true fall away, even if it’s before something new takes their place.

This week invites you explore your relationship with leadership. Not of others but of yourself and your life. Can you meet each voice that has doubted yourself and hold each with compassion and understanding? Can you consider past mistakes that haunt you and forgive them? Remember, you are still learning. You can still be trusted through that process.

Allow spaciousness to fill your mind wherever outside voices have gotten too close and others’ beliefs and emotions have kept you from your own. In this spaciousness, underneath all else, what are you saying? What are you feeling? What is inspiring you? What perspectives are wanting to emerge?

#8890. Menopause and mental health: The science of the menopausal brain

Reviewed by Brian St. Pierre, MS, RD and Helen Kollias, PhD

On a Friday night, as my husband and I tried to figure out where to eat, a typical conversation would go like this:

Me: Do you want to go to that restaurant?

Me: I can’t think of the name. We’ve eaten there before. It’s that place with the peanut shells on the floor? It’s next to… You know… It’s on that road where we used to take the dog to the vet. Do you know the one I’m talking about??

It was as if certain details got lost in a pile of sludge in the deep recesses of my brain. Then, hours later, the details would escape, and I’d shout into an empty room…

However, what seemed to be happening to me, increasingly in my late 40s and early 50s, felt far from typical.

Not only could I never seem to spit out the names of various restaurants or people or books or movies or so many other things, but my brain was also pooping out during the workday.

I’d sit in front of my computer screen, stare at a document, and will myself to do something constructive with my fingertips. Everything seemed hazy, like those first few moments in the morning when you’re awake enough to turn off the alarm but too sleepy to do basic math.

I had my good moments, usually in the morning, when I attempted to pack eight hours of writing into the two or three hours I possessed mental clarity.

On my worst days, however, I awoke with a haze I never managed to shake. Work was a non-starter. Nor did I have enough bandwidth to read, or do much of anything, really.

Three healthcare professionals recommended antidepressants. I tried one, and felt even worse. I tried another. I tried yet another at a higher dose. Still, I felt like a zombie. Another professional gave me a sleeping pill. It left me feeling even more drugged.

Someone tested my thyroid. There was nothing wrong with it. Nor was I anemic. I tried supplements, mushroom coffee, and just about any product with the word “think” somewhere on its label.

Finally, after nearly two years of seeing a revolving door of doctors, I made an appointment with a gynecologist for my yearly exam. I mentioned vaginal dryness. That information triggered her to ask a string of questions that had nothing to do with my undercarriage. How was my sleep? Mood? Energy levels? Was I experiencing hot flashes? How about brain fog?

“Funny you should mention brain fog,” I said in my usual hazy monotone. “I feel like I’m barely alive.”

By the end of the visit, I understood that I’d likely never had depression.

My gynecologist sent me home with prescriptions for estradiol and progesterone.

Within days, it was as if someone had flipped a switch.

I could think again. I could type words again. I could follow conversations. I could work past noon.

And, for the first time in years, I could sleep more than two hours without waking.
