Instead, like puberty, it’s a life stage—a transitional moment to be precise.

Once you’ve gone 12 consecutive months without a period, you’ve reached menopause. And from that moment onwards, you’re officially “postmenopausal.”

As women approach this transitional moment, hormone levels fluctuate and fall, triggering dozens of symptoms. Weight gain and reduced sex drive get a lot of attention.

However, during and after menopause, roughly 40 percent of women report increased irritability, mood swings, anxiety, fatigue, and trouble concentrating, according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.1 2 As the following image shows, it’s also one of the most vulnerable times in a woman’s life to develop depression,3 particularly if they’ve struggled in the past with it before.

Before starting hormones, I often found myself sobbing for no reason. Other times, the world’s stimuli felt too… stimulating.

Normal everyday sounds—like the buzz of traffic or people at the mall—literally hurt. I was jumpy and irritable and felt anxious about situations that had never bothered me in the past, such as driving over bridges or through construction.

Fluctuating hormone levels likely play a role, as do typical age-related changes in the brain.

In addition, during this stage of life, women often deal with several issues that siphon cognitive capacity faster than a thirsty vampire drains a carotid.

During their 40s and 50s, for example, many women have reached the peak of their careers, with responsibilities that follow them home and keep them up at night. They may also be parenting angst-filled teens, caring for aging parents, adjusting to an empty nest, questioning their marriage, or trying to wrap their bank account around the latest statement from the college bursar or hospital billing department.

However, one of the lesser-known and talked about triggers for cognitive discontent has nothing to do with aging or life stress and everything to do with that hallmark menopausal symptom: the hot flash.

Hot flashes, which happen during the day, and night sweats, which occur at night, fall under the category of vasomotor symptoms. (The word “vasomotor” refers to the constriction or dilation of blood vessels which, in turn, can influence everything from blood pressure to sweating.)

During a hot flash or night sweat, norepinephrine and cortisol levels rise. Blood vessels dilate in an attempt to shed heat. Blood pressure and heart rate increase.

Depending on the severity of the hot flash, your skin might redden as sensations of warmth spread through your face, neck, and chest.

You might sweat, experience heart palpitations, or feel anxious, tired, or faint.4

It’s not entirely clear why hot flashes crop up around menopause.

According to one theory, falling estrogen levels affect the hypothalamus, the area of the brain involved in temperature regulation. The brain’s internal thermostat gets wonky and occasionally thinks your body is too hot or cold (when it’s not).

For many years, experts thought of vasomotor symptoms as mere inconveniences or sources of embarrassment.

(To be honest, so did I. During all of those fruitless visits to various healthcare professionals, it never occurred to me to mention them.)

However, an increasing body of research has revealed that hot flashes may do more than make us uncomfortable or force us to change our sheets in the middle of the night.

They may also affect our blood vessels and brains—and not for the better.5 For this reason, an increasing number of experts now consider vasomotor symptoms to be a treatable medical condition.6 7 8

In one study, researchers asked 226 women to wear monitors that tracked when they were experiencing a hot flash. The women also underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), filled out sleep diaries, and wore smartwatches that recorded how often they woke at night.9

As researchers looked at the brain images obtained from women who experienced the most hot flashes, they noticed an abundance of patchy areas called whole-brain white matter intensities.

These lesions were once thought of as a typical consequence of aging. However, neuroscientists now believe that the presence of whole-brain white matter intensities is predictive of future cognitive decline.

People with an abundance of these brain lesions are twice as likely to get diagnosed with dementia and three times as likely to have a future stroke.10

It’s thought that the increased presence of whole-brain white matter intensities may stem, in part, from changes taking place in the blood vessels that feed the brain.

A three-year study of 492 women supports that theory. It determined that women who experienced frequent hot flashes also tended to experience unhealthy changes in their blood vessels, such as an inability to dilate to accommodate increased blood flow.11

Other research has linked frequent hot flashes with increases in the following:

In addition to directly affecting the blood vessels, frequent hot flashes may also affect the brain by disturbing sleep.17

Interestingly, many women don’t necessarily know that hot flashes are disturbing their sleep.

They may instead—as I did—assume they have insomnia or sleep apnea.

That’s because night sweats aren’t always sweaty.

By the time a surge in cortisol and norepinephrine jolts a woman awake, the hotness of the flash may have dissipated. So, it can feel as if she’s repeatedly waking, over and over and over again, for no discernable reason.

These frequent awakenings may interfere with the brain’s ability to consolidate memories, metabolize toxins, and store all the names, dates, and facts one encounters daily.

It can also lead to lost connectivity in the hippocampus, a part of the brain that’s important for learning and memory.

Sleep loss also means the amygdala, a part of the brain involved in emotion, becomes more reactive, causing people to feel more easily stressed, anxious, irritable, frustrated, or enraged.18 19

All of these brain changes can set in after just days to a week of lost sleep. So, imagine what happens when you’ve been waking over and over again—for years.

To diagnose depression, healthcare professionals use a tool called the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) depression scale. If you check off four of the nine symptoms on the scale, you’re considered depressed.

However, four of the symptoms on the checklist also overlap with the symptoms of menopause-related sleep deprivation:

Check off those four items, and you might be diagnosed with depression, even if what’s really ailing you is the battle with sleep you’ve been waging since you turned 47.

Another problem: On surveys, 80 percent of medical residents admit they feel “barely comfortable” talking about menopause.20 In addition, few residency programs—including ob-gyn residency programs—offer training in it.21

Given the above, it’s no wonder so many healthcare professionals never think to ask about hot flashes or sleep disturbances when people like me show up complaining of fatigue, lack of gumption, and an inability to focus.

In addition, even when it’s clear that vasomotor symptoms are leading to cognitive and emotional symptoms, many healthcare professionals still shy away from prescribing menopausal hormone therapy (also called hormone replacement therapy, or HRT), often telling women that supplemental hormones are “not safe” or “too risky.”

These professionals are practicing what Michigan-based menopause-trained gynecologist Jerrold H. Weinberg, MD, calls “defensive medicine.”

“It’s one of the first reflexes doctors have when they recommend a treatment,” says Dr. Weinberg. “They worry they’re going to get sued.”

These worries are based on research done several decades ago that linked the use of certain types of hormones with a slightly increased risk of developing breast cancer or stroke.22

However, according to more recent research, that small increased risk seems to depend on several other factors, such as age, dose, the type of hormonal preparation, and the duration of hormone use.23 24

As long as you’re younger than 60 and have been postmenopausal for fewer than 10 years, many experts now say the benefits outweigh the risks for women with moderate to severe menopausal symptoms.25

It’s also counterbalanced by health benefits such as reduced risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease or osteoporosis, says Dr. Weinberg, who confirms the health benefits of menopause hormone therapy far outweigh the risks for most women.

Because some antidepressants can lift mood, improve sleep, and reduce hot flashes, some healthcare professionals turn to them instead of menopause hormone therapy. As with any medicine, antidepressants have their own list of side effects. However, for someone practicing defensive medicine, they often seem like a safer bet, says Dr. Weinberg.26 27 28

If you or your client are on what seems like a never-ending quest to find a healthcare professional who understands menopause, use the following advice from Dr. Weinberg and Helen Kollias, PhD, an expert on physiology and molecular biology and science advisor at Precision Nutrition and Girls Gone Strong.

▶ Seek care from a menopause-trained health professional.

Usually, these professionals list this training and interest in their bio. For example, they might list “menopause” as an area of focus.

You can also search this database for practitioners who have earned a certification from the Menopause Society.

Write them down. That way, if you feel foggy or nervous during your appointment, you can lean on your notes.

This information can also help you judge whether MHT or another medicine is working. Based on your symptom data, you and your healthcare professional may decide to switch to a different medicine or change your dose.

▶ Be as specific as you can during your appointment.

Saying something like “I don’t sleep well,” is less likely to get you the right kind of help than saying, “During the past seven days, I’ve only gotten four uninterrupted hours once. I wake, on average, five times a night. On a typical night, my longest stretch of sleep is three hours.”

If you use a smartwatch, come ready to fire up your health app, so your healthcare professional can see the data.

▶ Talk about the pros and cons of treatment.

There’s a concept in medicine known as “shared decision-making.” Part of that process involves frank discussions about the benefits and risks of a given treatment. Then, patients and clinicians work together to make decisions based on those benefits and risks.

Many healthcare networks encourage clinicians to use shared decision-making, as it seems to reduce patient complaints as well as malpractice lawsuits.29 30

For this reason, shared decision-making can help shift a healthcare professional out of the “defensive medicine” mindset.

The lifestyle habits that improve mental and emotional health during menopause aren’t terribly different from the lifestyle habits that improve overall health—for any person, at any stage of life.

Other than avoiding caffeine, alcohol, and spicy or hot foods, there’s no special diet for people with vasomotor symptoms. (And by the way, tofu and other soy products don’t seem to help with vasomotor symptoms as much as once thought30—though they’re still nutritious.)

Healthy behaviors don’t necessarily change during middle age.

Nutrition, physical activity, stress management, sleep, social connectedness, and a sense of purpose matter just as much during the menopausal transition as they do when we’re younger. However, these fundamentals are even more important to dial in as life progresses.

If you answered “no” to some or all of those questions, consider why that is. What’s stopping you? How might you remove barriers or shore up support to make those fundamentals easier?

In addition to helping to blunt age- and hormone-related losses in muscle and bone mass, creatine may also help bolster mood and brain function while reducing mental fatigue.

It also seems to counter some of the negative effects of sleep deprivation. 32 33 Research shows a daily dose of 5 to 7 grams of creatine monohydrate is effective.

In addition to helping you feel alert, sunlight helps to set the internal clock in your brain that makes you sleepy at night and spunky in the morning. Morning and late afternoon light exposure seem particularly potent.

In a study of 103 people, exposure to morning sunlight predicted better sleep quality the following night. When people spent time outdoors in the mornings, they fell asleep more quickly, slept longer, and experienced fewer awakenings the following evening.34

Sunlight may also improve mood and concentration.35

If you’re already worn out, long, intense exercise sessions will likely make you feel worse.

For one, injuries crop up much more easily at middle age than during our 20s and 30s. In addition, it takes longer to recover between sessions.36

String too many overly zealous workouts too close together, and you’ll not only likely start to feel achy but also more irritable, tense, and tired.

However, much like a cold shower, short bursts of exercise may help you to feel alert during the day.

If you’re falling asleep at your desk, encourage yourself to take short movement breaks such as a 5- or 10-minute walk outdoors or a quick set of pushups or squats.

In addition, you may find gentle exercise—such as yoga or stretching—helps you relax before bed. Just don’t make it too intense, or you’ll trigger a release of adrenaline.

Whenever you exercise, tune into how your body feels, especially after a particularly bad night of sleep.

We’re not saying you should never exercise vigorously or try to beat your lifting PRs. However, depending on your sleep and recovery, you might want to pare things back, especially if you’ve traditionally hit the gym hard.

You can still do intense sessions—just balance them out with more moderate sessions, as well as proportionate recovery.

Depending on how you feel, you might decide to go all out, as usual.

However, you might also decide to do a zone 2 training session instead of an intense run. Or, if you’re resistance training, you might still do your planned session, but reduce the number of sets, reps, or volume lifted.

This research-based therapy for insomnia can help you develop skills and mental reframes that encourage sound sleep.

For example, a CBT-I therapist will help you develop the skill of getting up at the same time every day, regardless of how badly you slept (or didn’t sleep) the night before.

(Read more: Three CBT-I skills that can transform how you sleep.)

You may not have the energy (or desire) to do everything you did when you were younger. (When you were 36, your daily checklist defied time and space.)

As a result, you might benefit from looking critically at your current responsibilities to see which ones you can shrink or downsize. For several days, track how you spend your time and bandwidth. Then, analyze your data.

If you’re a coach, use the Wheel of Stress Assessment to help clients identify different dimensions of their life that might be draining their mental and emotional capacity. (When you know specifically where your stress is coming from, you have a better chance of resolving it.)

If it’s demands from other people that prevent you from prioritizing self-care and recovery, you might like to read: How saying “no” can seriously change your life.

You might find you sleep better and experience fewer night sweats if you sleep in a cooler environment.

Try turning down the thermostat a couple of degrees, using a fan, or investing in an electric cooling mattress pad.

When you feel the fog take over your brain, it’s not likely you’ll be doing “your best work” anyway.

So, for a block of time—say, 20 minutes—permit yourself to do nothing. You might:

If you need a quick “refresh,” you can also try a 5-minute mind-body scan.

Get your body into a comfortable position. For example, you might use the yoga “legs up the wall” pose or lie down and place a pillow under your knees.

Then, close your eyes and bring your attention to physical sensations in your body. Start at your head, and work your way down to your toes.

Don’t judge or rush to change anything. Just observe, like a scientist. You can also scan your mind, for example, by noticing thoughts.

When you’ve completed the scan, consider:

You don’t have to “do” anything with the information you uncover, just notice.

The foods that protect the blood vessels around your heart can also protect the blood vessels in your brain.

For example, both the MIND and Mediterranean diets are associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer’s disease and depression.37 38 These eating patterns are rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, olives, beans, fish, and other minimally-processed whole foods.

In addition, nitrate-rich foods like beets and dark, leafy greens may help to dilate blood vessels, temporarily improving memory by helping more blood to reach the brain.39 40

(For more on how our diet can support brain function and emotional regulation, read: Nutrition and mental health: What (and how) to eat)

It’s frustrating when you feel like you can’t do it all.

However, this stage of life presents a hidden opportunity, forcing you to re-evaluate what’s most important.

Before going on hormones, as my ability to type coherent words and phrases diminished, I was forced to ask an important question:

It was more of an existential question than a career-related one, and it allowed me to reassess how I wanted to spend my limited mental resources.

Given that I was self-employed, I didn’t actually need to be working eight hours a day. That was a gift, wasn’t it?

Maybe I also didn’t need to cook dinner six nights out of seven. Maybe the recipes I chose could be simplified, too.

Finally, maybe saying “no” a lot more often and without regret would allow me to continue to say yes to the things that mattered most.

And picking up the phone whenever my kid called from college.

Or meeting a friend for a meandering walk around town.

Thanks to the hormones and life tweaks, I now have energy again. I’m also clear-headed most of the time. However, I still tend to end my work day around 3 p.m.

#8889. How to Hold Yourself Accountable Without Beating Yourself Up

Here’s what that looks like inside real coaching conversations.

When most people picture “accountability,” they picture a drill sergeant.

Someone standing over you going “What were you thinking? Why did you skip that? Do you even want this?“

(And if there’s no drill sergeant handy, we do a pretty good job of beating ourselves up all on our own.)

Here’s the thing: if being hard on yourself worked, it would have worked by now.

Great accountability isn’t built on being a hard-ass.

It’s built on forward momentum and honest feedback.

The drill sergeant questions YOU. Your motivation. How much you want it.

Real accountability helps you try again quickly.

Then helps you see what you’re doing well and what can improve.

A client of mine had a hectic week. Travel, out of their routine, workouts missed.

The drill sergeant move is “why didn’t you do your workouts?!” at the exact moment they were already struggling.

“Hey! I know this has been a hectic week. Let’s do some push-ups together. Do a set next chance you get and shoot me a 👍. I’ll do one too.”

This got a 👍 and a “Thanks for the encouragement! This week has been so hectic my schedule got away from me.”

Then we build off of that by looking ahead to the next few days.

“How’s the rest of this week looking for strength training? I went ahead and put together a few variations in case you’re short on time.”

When you’re already struggling, the question isn’t “hey, why didn’t you do that?”

Then looking ahead to what’s coming up after that.

But forward momentum is only the first part of the equation.

The second step is giving honest feedback on both the wins AND the challenges.

To be a neutral observer. To point out what’s going well, what’s not, and suggest how we can improve it moving forward.

Based on the actual human in front of me: their unique goals, motivations, and whatever flavor of chaos they have going on in their own life (work, family, travel, illness, injury, etc.)

“Hey! I reviewed the strength workout on Friday. Solid work all around here. I can see from your form check video that you’re doing a better job staying balanced across your whole foot on the squat. 💪

I also noticed that the middle of the week has been tougher to get consistent workouts in. You’ve hit 2 out of the last 4 midweek workouts. I know work has been crazy with the project deadline you have coming up, so my guess is you’re getting buried and it makes it hard to get to the gym. Am I on the right track? I have some ideas for how we tackle that next week that I’ll drop down below in a video for you.”

This is the honest part. It didn’t go anywhere!

But instead of berating you for missing a workout, the goal is to look at all the evidence and suggest next steps.

Including if the evidence says that something BIG needs to change. It’s all on the table.

Accountability isn’t punishment for what you didn’t do.

It’s helping you decide what you do next.

If your week went haywire, before you beat yourself up, take this approach:

#8888. Bored With Your Workout? Try a New Level, Not a New Program

This was the first thing a new client said to me.

When we dug into it, here’s the pattern that emerged:

Strength training, then running, then a yoga challenge, then back to lifting with a different app.

Nerd Fitness Coaching was the latest in a long line of fresh starts.

And here’s the thing: all of it was GOOD.

She was moving. She was trying new things. She was having fun (at least at first).

She felt like she kept starting over and never getting anywhere.

And she wanted help figuring out what to do.

Let’s be real: trying something new is exciting.

A new program, a new class, a new challenge. There’s a buzz to it.

And that buzz isn’t bad. Enjoying it is a big part of what keeps people moving.

The catch is that most goals need some repetition.

Getting stronger, running farther, learning a skill. You get better at the things you practice again and again.

So the question isn’t “how do I stop getting bored?”

It’s “how do I keep some of that new-thing fun AND repeat things enough to see progress?” 🧐

When I built her program, I kept its overall shape the same week to week.

But inside it, a few key exercises got a target. Something like:

“Once you can do 12 reps with 25 pounds, we level up.”

The targets were far enough away to stretch her, and close enough that she could hit them in 2 to 6 weeks of focused practice.

When she hit one, we leveled up that exercise: new reps or weight, or a new variation. Everything else stayed put.

There was always a target she was closing in on and a level she’d recently beaten.

But the frame stayed the same. We were still working on the same overall qualities.

And that’s what let her progress stack up instead of resetting every few weeks.

She was able to stay really consistent with her program.

But when she came back, she wasn’t looking for something new.

She was excited to pick up her program and keep progressing.

And sure, sometimes her goals would change.

We spent 6 months training for her first half marathon, then switched gears to focus on building muscle.

If you love bouncing between things and you’re happy doing it, keep bouncing.

This is for when the bouncing starts to feel frustrating.

Before you reach for a new program, try a new level.

✅ Set a target you could reach in 2 to 6 weeks (a rep count or a weight)

✅ When you hit it, level up that one exercise with new reps, a new weight, or a new variation. Leave everything else alone.

I’m excited to see what you come up with. 😃

#8887. Inside the 24-Hour World Record Attempt That Raised Over $500K+ for a Local Food Bank

Ethan Hunger attempts to break the Guinness World Record for the most super-sprint triathlons in 24 hours. (Photo: Grayson Baum/Minus 7, Inc)

Beating the Guinness World Record for the most super-sprint triathlons completed in 24 hours was the goal of my friend Ethan Hunger’s annual community fundraising event. But the record itself was really only a small part of it. The attempt was just one piece of his much bigger, yearlong goal to raise $500,000 for our local food bank – a fundraiser that has been growing through various endurance challenges since 2021.

The idea for his annual “Hunger vs. Hunger” fundraiser was born out of the COVID-related growth of food insecurity in his local area of Bellingham, Washington. What started as a one-year challenge that raised $30,000 has now amassed a total of $1.2 million in donations, and this year’s $500,000 challenge would equate to roughly 7% of the food bank’s annual budget.

The concept and message Ethan shares through these extreme challenges is simple: “No matter how hard a day I create for myself, it will never parallel the struggles of food insecurity.”

For year six, Hunger wanted to go bigger than ever, and a triathlon world record would certainly tick that box while also adding more eyes to the cause. Initially, the record sounded relatively simple when the idea came to light: swim, bike, run, and transition continuously for 24 straight hours – non-stop through the entire night – and beat the previous record of 18 complete triathlons. (Technically, Guinness records the attempt in legs, so he needed 55 completed to surpass the previous record).

However, it quickly became more challenging throughout the buildup. The logistics of putting on a “race” like this at a public park while also adhering to more than 30 pages of Guinness rules began to set in – and that was before considering the largest fundraising goal Hunger had ever attempted.

Here’s how it all unfolded: the behind-the-scenes difficulties of a Guinness World Record, what 24 hours of triathlon actually felt like, how the fundraiser brought it all together, and why he might have stumbled on a revolutionary triathlon idea.

There is a massive difference between saying you broke a world record and having Guinness officially verify it. During the buildup, we found the endless list of verification rules a bit redundant and overly complicated. However, they create a rigorous, no-corner-cutting environment that helps maintain the integrity of the records.

Still, we wished it didn’t cost an estimated $14,000 to send an adjudicator to verify our attempt on-site – which would’ve made everything a lot easier.

Hunger applied for the records six months in advance and was approved. Not everyone gets this approval, as part of the application involves demonstrating that you not only have the experience and skills to attempt something like this, but also the connections and know-how to pull off the necessary verification.

Guinness has a lot of requirements before ratifying an attempt: video, timing, GPS files, logs, photos, and documentation for seemingly everything. So in a feat nothing short of a miracle, we scrambled together seven main cameras to record for 24 hours straight, three additional dedicated cameramen for an upcoming documentary, multiple photographers, timing data, and GPS tracking. But despite all that, one requirement quickly became much more problematic than the others: witnesses.

We discovered late that an individual witness could only cover a four-hour period before needing a four-hour break. We were also further limited in who could qualify, so close friends and family couldn’t simply fill every opening (as we had initially planned).

So, less than a week before a 24-hour event, on top of figuring out nutrition, bikes, course logistics, lights, cameras, batteries, timing, and how the hell any of us planned to stay awake for 24 hours, Ethan now needed to find people willing to stand beside a lake, jump in a safety car for the bike, and on mountain bikes for the run at ridiculous hours of the night and officially confirm that he was, in fact, doing the correct distances.

“If I had to pick one thing that made the event coordination the hardest, it was the witnesses and their four-hour time constraint,” Hunger says.

Somehow, through social media and word of mouth, people volunteered. They came out at midnight, early in the morning, and at all sorts of inconvenient hours. Some of them didn’t know Ethan at all – they simply heard what he was trying to do and wanted to help.

That should have been our first indication of what this event was eventually going to become. The world record might have been Ethan’s, but a lot of people were beginning to feel like they had a small piece of it.

By the end of his record, Hunger had amassed 5.47 miles of swimming, 136.7 miles of biking, and 34.2 miles of running. Yet those numbers are not what he will remember.

I asked him what stands out the most, and his answer goes back to minute one. It paints a picture of the day perfectly:

“The one that lingered for me the longest was likely the starting line. I had been frantically running around for 20 hours trying to get everything set up. I ran over to the start line with my goggles and swim cap, and I looked around with 60 seconds left and finally had the moment sink in of all the incredible people who were there to support me. I saw an older gentleman who I used to volunteer with at the food bank, who I knew had driven 30 minutes to town just to see me start. I saw friends who had flown from around the country. I saw people who currently work at the food bank who came to cheer, and I saw friends who currently rely on the food bank who came to cheer. It was incredibly moving.”

He might have been the one whose name would be attached to the attempt and record, but very quickly it stopped feeling like something he was doing alone. That came partly from the decision to use a real course. From a logistical standpoint, doing the challenge at a pool and track would have been infinitely easier to film, manage, illuminate, and monitor. Every time we left transition on the bike or run course, we disappeared from the main event area, which made everything more complicated.

“There were a ton of moving parts to this, and so many of them were out of my control once the clock started,” Hunger said. “I was able to do my best to get it set up ahead of time and put people in charge of tasks, but then I had to be willing to let it go and hope that it worked out.”

And it did work out: People were joining in on the swim, bike, and run legs throughout almost every reasonable hour (staying behind Ethan to avoid drafting). There was a DJ playing music, food, a campfire, friends sitting around talking, people donating, and strangers coming down simply because they’d heard something ridiculous was happening. Because the distances were short, people could also participate without committing to an enormous endurance challenge of their own. Someone could join one swim, somebody else could do four runs, and others could ride a bunch of the bike legs. Because every leg eventually returned to the same transition area, the group kept coming back together again.

That made the atmosphere completely different from a traditional long-distance triathlon where an athlete might disappear for several hours. If Ethan left on the bike, everyone knew he’d be back in around 25 minutes. If somebody wanted to join the next run, they had a good idea of when it would start.

It helped break the endless cycle of triathlon feeling like such an individual sport and started to feel more like a 24-hour triathlon festival.

We had no idea going in what to expect physically. We’d only practiced this format for about six hours, none of us were truly trained as ultra-triathletes, and sure, we’d completed an Ironman before, but we all safely assumed that somewhere around hour 12 or 15 our bodies would start falling apart.

Weirdly, however, that wasn’t really what happened. Because every individual leg was short and we weren’t moving particularly fast, you’d finish a swim, bike, and run and think, That actually wasn’t too bad. The problem was overcoming the sleep fatigue and the dread of doing specific legs again (and again) with so many hours still ahead.

“My lowest moment was around 3 or 3:30 in the morning,” Ethan says. “I had just finished a triathlon where I was cold the entire time, and I was incredibly sleepy, too. The wind was still causing chop on the lake, and we had headwinds on our bike ride out. I just remember dreading going back in the water because I was already cold, and I knew when I finished the swim, and the wind hit me on the beach, I’d instantly be cold again.”

There were many other smaller obstacles along the way, too. One of which stands out for its irony. Hunger had spent a lot of effort organizing with Outbound Lighting to help illuminate the docks and buoys, to make the night swim one of the coolest parts of the whole experience, yet, in a synchronous moment of shared disbelief, we realized we all had forgotten clear-lens goggles.

On the bike, going from wet to cold to warm meant clothes never quite dried, while chafing, tired hands, wind, darkness, and some sketchy late-night traffic (picture drunk drivers yelling out the window) slowly added up.

Despite that, the hardest part for me might have been the small act of leaving the transition itself: even in the middle of the night, there was a campfire, music, food, and people hanging out, and sitting down beside that fire and prolonging the transition was all too enticing.

Maybe the best way to picture the mental struggle of this challenge is to imagine doing 15 hours of triathlon, getting to 9 a.m. when the sun was finally up, feeling like you’ve survived the hard part – then realizing you still have nine hours left.

For something that had taken 24 hours, the finish felt surprisingly quick. There were lots of people, lots of emotion, and we were all incredibly proud of Ethan. After 22 complete super-sprint triathlons, four more than the previous record, it was finally over.

Then we quickly cleaned everything up and headed to a big party, where Ethan somehow managed to give a speech in front of a few hundred people gathered to celebrate what it was all actually for. The Foodbank.

The number is already over the $500,000 goal, and with still much of the year left, and a documentary release still to come, that should have him far surpassing his expectations.

If you want to donate, you can do so here.

He describes just how much it means to the organization that now helps feed almost 5,000 families weekly in our county:

“My fundraiser is big enough and has been around long enough that the food bank now builds this fundraiser into its annual projection for income. If you combine that with the 2025 federal budget cuts that cost the Bellingham Food Bank around $900,000 and food banks across the country well over $1 billion, the need is there now more than ever.”

There are times when attempting a world record can appear outwardly selfish, done for vanity, to gain attention, or to level up your status. Ethan even received some comments on social media saying so, despite the clear purpose behind the fundraiser. But when you were on-site, you realized there wasn’t much glory in slogging through an attempt like this, and if you dealt with the months of buildup and preparation, you would quickly realize it probably wasn’t worth doing purely for the token of a Guinness stamp.

But doing it for a purpose, and with friends and a community around, made it all worth it. The record gave everyone something ridiculous to rally around; it gave hope, gave purpose, and made every small act feel like it was contributing to something much bigger.

Speaking of bigger, Ethan has already planned next year’s challenge: a 100-mile run around our local track and stadium.

#8885. Why I Lug My Own Props to Yoga Class

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

I had been practicing yoga for years before I discovered the magic of lugging my own mat to class.

Before that, I’d simply borrowed the cheap but convenient studio mats that were available for use. I considered myself too lazy to grapple with a heavy mat as I hauled it from the car to the studio and back again. But following some serious thought about functionality and germ exposure after I ended up with plantar warts (I mean, think about it), I decided it was worth the trouble to practice on my own sturdy mat.

And it was. I found more stability in standing poses from the mat’s refusal to slide or wrinkle on the floor, benefited from its extra grippiness in twists and backbends, and appreciated its additional cushioning in seated poses. It’s no exaggeration to say practicing on my own mat revolutionized my studio experience.

But I didn’t stop there. Following that experience, I began to look askance at other props in the studio—namely, blankets, bolsters, blocks, and straps—which appeared as broken in (or broken down?) as those loaner mats. And, I suspected, just as germy.

So I started bringing my own props—and my own germs—to class. Well, within reason. No sandbags or headstand bench, obviously. But I did load myself up before each class with the basics, including a blanket, strap, and block. If I was heading to a yin or restorative class, I brought my own bolster, too. I’d find my own comfort and marinate in my own sweat, thank you.

I’ve been doing this for 20 years. Beyond basic hygiene, the benefits of using my own props include functionality. Before you say blocks are blocks and blankets are blankets, they come in a dizzying array of shapes and materials, not to mention designs and colors. Do I want a foam block? Wood? Cork? Recycled materials? Purple? Pink? Black? Would my hands rather settle on a support that is rectangular, circular, oval, or square?

And as for a blanket, am I more of a pressed wool “yoga blanket” person or is a pretty “Mexican blanket” more my style? And don’t get me started on bolsters, with nearly infinite options for shapes and styles.

When I curate my DIY yoga props each class, I’m arming myself with props that I’ve worked with before and that strategically suit my body and take me even further into my practice. And because they are set to my preferences, I know them well enough to put them to effective use in a nanosecond.

My strap, for instance, is knotted in strategic locations, including one that makes it easy for me to reel in an errant back leg in my much-practiced Natarajasana (Dancer Pose). When that stays consistent from class to class, it makes it easier for me to find my version of the posture, which in turn means my focus can remain on the demands of the pose rather than fumbling with a strap or figuring out the height to adjust my block.

And although it’s about so much more than looks, it’s also about the looks. I just like having something pretty and functional and familiar surrounding me during my practice. My black mat, purple knotted strap, cork block, and wildly beautiful purple, orange, and teal bolster fit me to a T.

What matters is that by the time I’ve arranged the props around my mat, I’ve built what looks and feels like a cocoon of comfort. I’m no longer practicing in a gym-like room with a bunch of strangers. Rather, it’s as if I’m in my own private studio with my own private equipment among my own private germs. Yoga feels best when it also feels safe.

#8884. Can’t get back into working out? It’s not a motivation problem.

Recently, I asked you: where are you feeling most stuck with your fitness right now?

Hundreds of you wrote back. Thoughtful, honest answers. Thank you.

And one theme jumped out at me IMMEDIATELY.

One reader, let’s call her Supergirl, said it this way:

If you’ve ever had a great run (for a few days or a few years) and then couldn’t find your way back, this one’s for you, too.

I’ve heard this so many times in my coaching career. You were in a really good groove. Something knocked you off. And getting back on track feels incredibly difficult, and you don’t know why.

I’ve experienced this myself! I was in a groove with food logging. It felt easy. Then I took a break, and when I tried to start up again, I couldn’t get it going with any consistency for the life of me.

Here’s my take after nearly two decades of coaching: I doubt this is a motivation thing.

You were cruising at 70 miles an hour. You made a pit stop, and now you’re trying to jump the car straight back to 70. Instantly.

Another reader put it really well in their message to me:

That’s driving with your eyes on the rearview mirror. And it makes anything smaller feel like it doesn’t count.

But smaller is how you get back up to speed.

After multiple false starts with food logging, I realized I was falling into the same trap. And instead of forcing myself to weigh and measure anything, I gave myself a different on-ramp. Protein and veggies at each meal? Check. That allowed me to build back up again and find the groove that worked for me in this current phase of life.

Previous success can feel like a scorecard that you have to grade yourself against.

But what worked before might not work for you right now.

And it’s important to remember that most of us needed an on-ramp the first time, too. That part didn’t change after some time off.

You know what you “should” be doing. Let’s put that aside for now.

Instead, let’s shrink down what our focus is. We don’t have to figure out the whole routine. Not the whole week. Let’s work on today.

Try this thought experiment with me: if you didn’t have any expectations of what this “should” look like, what is one thing that feels doable today?

Maybe it’s performing your warm-up routine. Or doing the first round of exercises in your workout.

Maybe it’s batch cooking some protein tonight, or running to the grocery store to stock up on some easy fruit and veggie options.

Try it out, and see how that feels. Is the resistance still there? If it isn’t, you’ve found the start of your on-ramp. 🙌

And if it still feels hard to start? That’s OK, too. We can choose a different entry point and try again.

If you’re in that camp of “I know what to do. I can’t get myself to start,” give yourself a different, smaller on-ramp.

But it may be exactly what you need right now.

Hit reply and let me know what yours looks like.

#8883. How to stop tracking macros and trust yourself around food

After years of careful macro tracking, Dr. Fundaro finally admitted to herself that the method no longer worked for her. Yet she was afraid to give it up.

If anyone should feel confident in their food choices, it would be Dr. Gabrielle Fundaro. After all, Dr. Fundaro has a PhD in Human Nutrition, a decade-plus of nutrition coaching experience, and six powerlifting competitions under her belt.

Yet, when she was really honest with herself, Dr. Fundaro realized that she felt far from confident around food. For years, she’d used macro counting as a way to stay “on track” with her eating.

After years of macro tracking, Dr. Fundaro was tired of the whole thing. She was tired of making sure her macros were perfectly in balance. She was sick of not being able to just pick whatever she wanted off a menu and enjoy the meal, trusting that her health and physique wouldn’t go sideways as a result.

Yet the idea of not tracking freaked her out. Every time she quit tracking, she worried:

“What if I don’t eat enough protein, and lose all my muscle?”

“What if I have no idea how to fuel myself without tracking macros? And what does that say about me as an expert in the field of nutrition?”

Something that would support her nutritional goals while also giving her a sense of freedom and peace around food.

Calorie counting wouldn’t do it. That was just as restrictive as counting macros—maybe more.

Intuitive eating didn’t seem like a good fit either. Intuitive eating relies heavily on a person’s ability to tune into internal hunger and fullness cues to guide food choices and amounts. After years of relying on external cues (like her macro targets), Dr. Fundaro didn’t feel trusting enough of her own instincts; she wanted more structure.

Meanwhile, at the gym, Dr. Fundaro began lifting based on the Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scale—a framework that helps individuals quantify the amount of effort they’re putting into a given movement or activity. It’s considered a valuable tool to help people train safely and effectively according to their ability and goals. (More on that soon.)

While using the RPE scale in her training, Dr. Fundaro found she was both getting stronger and recovering better. There was something to this combination of structure and intuition that just worked.

And then, it dawned on Dr. Fundaro like the apple hit Sir Isaac Newton on the head:

With that, the RPE-Eating Scale was born.

Dr. Fundaro has since used this alternative method to help herself and her clients regain confidence and self-trust around food; improve nutritional awareness and competence; and free themselves from food tracking.

(Yup, Dr. Fundaro finally trusts her eating choices—no macro tracker in sight.)

In this article, you’ll learn how she did it, plus:

Invented by Gunnar Borg in the 1960’s, Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE) is a scale that’s used to measure an individual’s perceived level of effort or exertion during exercise.

Though Borg’s RPE uses a scale that goes from 6 to 20, many modern scales use a 0 to 10 range (which is the range that Dr. Fundaro adapted for her RPE-Eating scale).

Originally used in physiotherapy settings, the scale is now frequently used in fitness training.

For example, powerlifters might use it to choose how heavy they want to go during a training session. Or, pregnant women might use it to ensure they aren’t over-exerting themselves during a fitness class or strength training session.

Because human experience is highly subjective and individual, the scale allows the exerciser to judge how hard they’re working for themselves. A coach can provide a general guideline, such as “aim for a 7/10 this set,” but it’s up to the client to determine exactly what that means for them.

Dr. Fundaro had used the scale many times with herself, and clients. She always appreciated the sense of autonomy it gave her clients, while still providing some structure.

So, she decided to take the same 1-10 scale and its principles, and apply it to eating.

The goal with RPE-Eating is similar to RPE when training: Develop the skills to determine what is sufficient for you, without having to rely on other external metrics (such as apps or trackers).

If you’ve ever practiced RPE-training, you’ll know it takes some time to get used to. RPE-Eating is the same.

Don’t expect to be in lockstep with all of your body’s internal cues at first, especially if you’ve been ignoring them for a long time.

With this in mind, apply the steps below to practice the RPE-Eating process.

“It’s not about aiming to change your body,” Dr. Fundaro explains. “It’s not about feeling more control over your diet. Nor is it about feeling like you’re eating the ‘optimal’ diet.”

If your priority is maintaining a specific physique (such as staying ultra lean) or changing your body (building muscle or losing fat), this method can be adapted for that, though it isn’t the most efficient one to use.

Instead, RPE-Eating is about sensing into what your body needs and giving yourself appropriate nourishment—while building inner trust and confidence along the way.

“You have to trust that you’ll be able to nourish your body, and that you’ll be okay even though things may change in your body,” says Dr. Fundaro.

Admittedly, this can be challenging to do. It can also be difficult to let go of the expectation that you’ll hit the “right” macros at every meal—which RPE-Eating isn’t specifically designed to do.

However, if your goal is to build more self-trust, RPE-Eating can be a great tool to help you do that.

Before we explore this step, let’s distinguish between two motivators for eating.

First, there’s hunger. Hunger occurs when physical cues in your body (like a general sense of emptiness or rumbling in your stomach, or lightheadedness) tells you that you require energy—known to us mortals as food.

While it’s normal to eat for both hunger and appetite drives, the two can become mixed up. Especially if we have a history of dieting and tracking food.

The RPE-Eating scale helps you tap back into those true physical hunger cues, and learn the difference between hunger and appetite.

To put this in practice, try this before your next meal:

▶ Using the RPE-Eating scale mentioned above, identify your current level of hunger. Record the number on paper or the notes app on your phone.

▶ Then, eat your meal with as much presence as possible. (Note: This in itself takes practice. It can help to limit distractions, such as eating at the table rather than in front of the TV, and focusing on the flavors and textures of the food you’re eating, and how you feel eating it.)

▶ About halfway through the meal, check in again. Based on the scale, how hungry are you now? As before, record the number.

▶ If you’re still hungry, finish your meal. When you’re finished, repeat the same process, writing down where you are on the scale.

▶ Once you’re done, take a minute and tune into what your body feels like. What does it feel like to be full? “Download” that feeling into your mind and internalize it in your body, as if you’re updating your phone with the latest software.

Repeat this for as many meals as you can. Aim to do it for one meal a day for a week or so, or for as long as feels good to you. Don’t worry if you forget: simply repeat the practice when you can.

The more you practice this, the better you’ll become at being attuned with your actual hunger cues. With time, you’ll likely find you develop more trust in your internal compass than what the latest diet tracker says for your needs.

(For more on fully-tuned-in, mindful eating, read: The benefits of slow eating.)

Have you ever come home after a super stressful day and you’ve basically thrown yourself onto a bag of chips or a carton of ice cream?

We might like to imagine ourselves eating every meal mindfully, using the RPE- Eating system to a tee, but life rarely works like that.

Chances are, there are certain situations that trigger you to eat more quickly, mindlessly, and beyond the point of hunger.

Dr. Fundaro’s suggestion? Aim to become more aware of the situations that cause you to overeat in the first place.

To do this, you can practice something we use in PN Coaching: Notice and name.

When you find yourself scarfing down food faster than you can blink, simply try to notice what’s going on.

Can you name a feeling—such as anxiety, or sadness?

Can you identify a situation or moment that happened before you started eating—say, an argument with your teenager, or a nasty email from your boss?

Once you’ve identified the feeling, event, or person that’s triggered you to eat compulsively, see if you can also identify what you might really be needing or desiring.

Eating for comfort is normal. However, if it’s the only coping method we have, it can cause more problems than it solves in the long run.

When you find yourself with an urge to eat mindlessly, consider what non-food coping mechanisms might help you feel better. That could be 10 minutes away from your computer to close your eyes and breathe, a walk outside, or a quick call to a friend to rant—or just talk about something completely unrelated.

Getting to know your non-hunger eating triggers—plus widening your repertoire of self-soothing methods—is just as valuable as getting to know your hunger cues. Over time, this awareness will allow you to eat with more intention.

Even when you’re “adequately fueled” from a physical perspective, you might still feel unsatisfied from an emotional perspective.

That’s because, according to the RPE-Eating framework, eating should fulfill two criteria:

▶ Satiety describes the physical sensation of being full; your calorie or fuel needs are met.

▶ Satisfaction describes a more holistic feeling of being nourished; your calorie needs are met, but your meal also felt pleasurable.

If you ate to satiety only, your calorie needs might be met and your physical hunger quelled, but you might still feel unsatisfied—maybe because chocolate is on your “don’t” list, and even though you’ve eaten everything else in your kitchen that isn’t chocolate, nothing quite “hit the spot.”

In other words, you can eat to satiety at every meal, yet still be “restricting” foods.

You may not be restricting calories per se, but you may have banned entire food groups—baked goods, pizza, or whatever else curls your toes. This can lead to a feeling of constantly needing to police yourself, and doesn’t leave much room for the flexibility and spontaneity that real-life (enjoyable) eating requires.

(Plus, avoiding particular foods tends to work like a pendulum: restrict now; binge later. If you want to learn how to stop those wild swings, read: How to eat junk food: A guide for conflicted humans)

After all, humans don’t just eat for adequate nutrients and energy. We eat for other reasons too: pleasure, novelty, tradition, community, enjoyment.

So, to take your RPE-Eating to the next level, Dr. Fundaro recommends trying it with meals and foods you genuinely enjoy.

If any foods or meals have been “off-limits,” try eating them using the RPE technique. (Macaroni and cheese, anyone?)

Practice using the scale with a variety of meals (including those you may have restricted previously), and notice how you feel over time.

With experience, you’ll get to know what it feels like to adequately fuel yourself with a variety of foods—including those you genuinely enjoy.

RPE-Eating isn’t for everyone, but might be a good fit for you (or your clients) if:

✅ You feel dependent on food tracking, but you don’t want to be.

✅ Every time you stop tracking, the loss of perceived control freaks you out and drives you right back to tracking.

✅ You want to stop tracking, but you want to have some type of system or guidance in place.

✅ You’re currently tracking (or considering tracking) your food intake, and you have elevated risk factors for developing an eating disorder such as high body dissatisfaction; a history of yo-yo dieting; a history of disordered eating patterns; and/or participation in weight class sports.

If you’re a coach looking to use this tool with a client, check out Dr. Fundaro’s resources. Remember this tool may not be for everyone, and how you apply it needs to be flexible.

Note: If you or your client struggles with disordered eating, this tool does not replace working with a health professional who specializes in eating disorders, such as a therapist, doctor, or registered dietician.

According to Dr. Fundaro, the best way to use RPE-Eating is in a weight-neutral setting.

While it could be used for weight modification, she doesn’t recommend treating it as another way to hit your macros or “goal weight.”

“I’m not anti-weight modification,” Dr. Fundaro explains. “I’m pro safe weight modification. I compare weight loss to contact sports. There are inherent risks but they can be mitigated through best practices.”

Dr. Fundaro elaborates: “Since RPE-Eating removes macro-tracking, which can increase risk of disordered eating in some people, and relies on biofeedback and non-hunger triggers, RPE-Eating provides a safety net that macro-tracking alone doesn’t provide.”

But if you do want to use RPE-Eating for intentional weight change, what should you do?

Dr. Fundaro recommends aiming to hover around the ranges that support your goal.

(As a reminder, a 1 to 3 on the RPE-Eating scale is categorized as “inadequate fuel; a 4 to 7 is categorized as “adequate fuel”; and a 8 to 10 is categorized as “excess fuel.”)

▶ If the goal is weight gain, you’ll likely aim to eat within the 7 to 8 range for most of your meals.

▶ If the goal is weight loss, you’ll likely aim to eat within the 4 to 5 range for most of your meals.

A key thing to remember is that you would never use RPE-Eating for extreme weight-modification such as for a bodybuilding competition. “That would be like using physio exercises to prepare for a powerlifting competition.” In other words, it’s not the right tool for the job.

If you’re skeptical and think this is just eating “based on your feelings,” keep in mind that RPE was once laughed at by lifters, too.

These days, RPE and autoregulation are widely accepted in gym culture and have been studied as a valid method for managing and guiding your training. 1

RPE isn’t perfect, but it’s pretty accurate and incredibly convenient. A lot more convenient than, say, using a velocity loss tracker for every set. 2 3

And while it might seem like it’s all feelings-based, the RPE scale is actually built around practicing the skill of interoceptive awareness—the awareness of internal sensations in your body.

The better you get at the skill of interoceptive awareness, the more you’ll be able to use that awareness to make informed decisions about your training.

RPE-Eating is similar: It builds the skill of sensing into your own body, and lets your internal sensations guide your decisions.

Similar to how the bar slowing down on a squat would indicate you’re getting closer to failure, experiencing the absence of hunger at the end of your meal would indicate you’re closer to being full.

Instead of tracking your glucose levels to validate your perceived hunger, you use internal cues that correlate with lowered blood sugar and coincide with hunger.

And, let’s be real: Being mindful of stomach grumbling or general hunger pangs is much more convenient and accessible than tracking glucose readings.

This process will not be perfect. You may undereat or overeat at first. But over time, with practice, you’ll build the core skills of RPE-Eating.

While this tool can be helpful, it’s just a tool. A screwdriver is great, but it isn’t useful when you need a hammer.

RPE-Eating can be great for helping you become more aware of your internal hunger cues and build a better relationship with food along the way.

It can also be more laborious. It requires paying real attention to your feelings (physical and emotional), and reflecting on them.

This can be difficult for anyone—but especially people who aren’t able to sit at the table and have a leisurely meal, like parents with small kids, or people with work schedules that require eating on-the-go.

If this is you, just use RPE-Eating when it does work for you—or simply pick and choose specific steps to use in isolation. For example, maybe you try RPE-Eating on the occasional quiet lunch break. Or, maybe you focus solely on developing your awareness of hunger and fullness cues, without trying to change anything else.

Tracking macros isn’t inherently bad. It can actually be a helpful tool to teach you more about nutrition. But it’s also not something most people want to do for the rest of their lives.

The problem is, if you’ve depended on tracking your food intake, stopping can feel scary.

In these cases, RPE-Eating can be used as a kind of off-ramp to help transition away from rigid and restrictive macro tracking.

(It can also help loosen the compulsion to “always finish your plate.” Though macros tracking and habitual plate-cleaning may sound different, they’re actually similar: both rely on external cues—such as macro targets or what’s served on your plate—to determine when you’re “done.”)

RPE-Eating won’t take away all the scary feelings that may come with changing ingrained ways of eating.

However, it can provide some structure and language to help you, or your clients, eat with less fear, less stress, and a bit more confidence.

“The goal,” says Dr. Fundaro, “is to know that you’re nourishing yourself—and you don’t need a food tracker to do that.”

2. Hackett, Daniel A., Nathan A. Johnson, Mark Halaki, and Chin-Moi Chow. 2012. A Novel Scale to Assess Resistance-Exercise Effort. Journal of Sports Sciences 30 (13): 1405–13.

#8882. Hyatt Luxury — Park Hyatt for 25,000-30,000 Points

Imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt New York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

Here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

The transfer path that makes this accessible is Chase Ultimate Rewards. Chase transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant — meaning you can spot availability, transfer your points, and book within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, also instantly, giving you two powerful earning pipelines into the same program.

This matters enormously for strategy. Chase Ultimate Rewards is arguably the most flexible points currency in travel rewards — earned through cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve — and the fact that it flows directly into Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio without any degradation is a genuine gift. 30,000 Chase UR points become exactly 30,000 Hyatt points. No conversion fees, no waiting period, no surprises.

Another critical mechanism: World of Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award redemptions. With hotel awards this is less of an issue than with airline programs, but it reflects Hyatt's broader philosophy of clean, predictable award pricing. What you see is what you pay — taxes and fees on hotel awards are typically minimal.

Now layer in Globalist status, and the value compounds further. World of Hyatt's top-tier elite status (earned at 60 qualifying nights per year) unlocks complimentary suite upgrades at check-in (space available) and free breakfast for two guests daily. If you're a Globalist checking into the Park Hyatt New York and you receive a suite upgrade, you've just added hundreds of dollars of daily value to an already exceptional redemption — and free breakfast at a Park Hyatt can easily run $60–$90 per person.

The booking window is 395 days out, which matters for high-demand dates. The Park Hyatt Tokyo during cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or the Park Hyatt New York around major events will see award availability evaporate quickly. Understanding that you can search and book nearly 13 months in advance is your single biggest tactical advantage for locking in prime dates.

Finally, it's worth understanding what you're getting at the property level. Park Hyatt is not Hyatt Regency or even Andaz — it's Hyatt's true ultra-luxury tier, with butler service, marble bathrooms, curated art collections, and some of the best city-view room designs in the world. The points-to-experience ratio here is genuinely exceptional.

Before anything else, inventory what you have. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards account and note your balance. You need a minimum of 25,000 points for a Category 7 Park Hyatt night or 40,000 points for a Category 8 property. If you're planning a multi-night stay, multiply accordingly — 30,000 points per night at a Category 7 is a reasonable planning number that covers most Park Hyatt sweet spots.

Decide which property you're targeting. The flagship three for this redemption are:

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search. Enter your destination city and dates. In the rate filter, select "Use Points" to display award availability. The site will show you the points cost per night — if you see the Category rate (25,000 or 40,000), availability exists. Note that peak and off-peak pricing can adjust these numbers slightly, so check a few date combinations.

Search flexibly. If your first-choice dates show no availability, shift by a day or two — award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is released in small blocks and replenished irregularly. Use the calendar view to scan multiple dates at once.

This is critical: do not transfer points until you've confirmed award availability exists on your target dates. Point transfers to Hyatt are irreversible. Once you've found open award space, note the exact dates and room type, then move immediately to Step 4.

If you're using Chase Ultimate Rewards: Log into your Chase account, navigate to "Pay Yourself Back" → "Transfer to Travel Partners" → select World of Hyatt. Enter the amount (in increments matching your need) and confirm. The transfer is instant — your Hyatt account will reflect the points within minutes.

If you're using Bilt Rewards: Navigate to the "Rewards" tab, select "Transfer Points," choose World of Hyatt, and confirm. Also instant.

Return to hyatt.com immediately after the transfer confirms. Search your target dates again, select the award rate, and complete the booking. You'll pay any applicable taxes (typically modest for hotel awards) and your points will be deducted. Print or screenshot your confirmation.

Award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is genuinely limited. If you lose availability between searching and transferring (rare, but possible), call the World of Hyatt member line (1-800-304-9288) — agents sometimes have access to inventory not visible online. Alternatively, set calendar reminders to check again; properties occasionally release additional award space within 30 days of arrival as booking patterns clarify. Remember: the booking window opens 395 days out, so planning ahead dramatically expands your options.

Let's walk through a real booking that illustrates exactly why this redemption has earned its place in the ChooseFI community's hall of fame.

The Setup: Two Nights at the Park Hyatt Tokyo

You're planning a trip to Japan in early April — a shoulder period just after peak cherry blossom season, when the city is still spectacular but the crowds have thinned slightly. You pull up hyatt.com and find award availability at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for two nights at 25,000 points per night.

The Cash Cost: A quick search on the Park Hyatt Tokyo's direct booking page for the same dates shows standard King rooms starting at $1,100/night. For two nights, that's $2,200 in cash — before resort fees or any extras.

The Points Cost: 50,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 × 2 nights), transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards.

The CPP Calculation: $2,200 cash value ÷ 50,000 points = 4.4 cents per point — well above the program's already-impressive baseline and squarely in the sweet spot's 2.7–6.7 cpp range.

What You Actually Experience: The Park Hyatt Tokyo occupies floors 39–52 of the Shinjuku Park Tower skyscraper. Your King Deluxe room on the 42nd floor has floor-to-ceiling windows framing the Tokyo skyline — on a clear morning, Mount Fuji appears in the distance like a postcard. The bathroom features a deep soaking tub, Aesop amenities, and heated floors. Breakfast in the Club on the 41st floor is an exquisite affair — if you hold Globalist status, it's included for both guests, adding roughly $60–$80 per person per day in value.

If you've achieved Globalist status, a complimentary suite upgrade at check-in (space available) could place you in a room with panoramic corner views that would retail for $1,800+ per night.

This is the kind of redemption that makes the FI math click in a visceral way. You earned 50,000 Chase UR points — achievable through a single premium travel card welcome bonus — and converted them into nearly $2,500 of genuine luxury. That's the system working exactly as it should.

The Park Hyatt category properties — especially Tokyo and New York — have notoriously limited award availability. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, and for high-demand dates (cherry blossom season in Japan, summer in Paris, New Year's in New York), competitive award inventory can disappear within days of opening. Set a calendar reminder for 395 days before your target date and be ready to search and transfer the same day.

The 1:1 instant transfer from Chase Ultimate Rewards makes the Chase ecosystem your most efficient pipeline into World of Hyatt. The Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve both transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. Pair either with the Chase Freedom Unlimited or Chase Freedom Flex to funnel everyday spending into the UR ecosystem before converting to Hyatt points when you have a target booking.

Cash prices at Park Hyatt properties fluctuate dramatically — your points cost does not. A room at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme during Paris Fashion Week might run $2,000/night while your award costs the same 25,000 points as a Tuesday in November. The bigger the cash premium on your dates, the higher your effective CPP. Research when local demand spikes and target those windows deliberately.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. This is activity-based expiration — any earning or redemption resets the clock. Don't let a large balance sit dormant. A small hotel stay, a points transfer, or earning through a Hyatt credit card all count as qualifying activity.

This is the cardinal mistake. Chase UR → Hyatt transfers are irreversible. If you transfer 60,000 points and then discover your target dates are unavailable, those points are now stranded in Hyatt — useful for Hyatt redemptions, but no longer flexible. Always confirm award space first, then transfer.

While 40,000 points/night for a Cat 8 property sounds steep, certain Park Hyatt properties in this tier — like the Park Hyatt Maldives Hadahaa — can retail for $2,000+/night, delivering CPP values that rival the best airline redemptions. Don't automatically limit your search to Category 7.

Hyatt does use peak and off-peak pricing tiers that can push Category 7 awards from 25,000 to 30,000 points on high-demand dates. Always check the actual points cost displayed during your specific date search rather than assuming the standard rate applies.

Why this ranks among the best travel rewards redemptions

Park Hyatt is Hyatt's top-tier luxury brand, competing directly with Four Seasons, Ritz-Carlton, and Aman resorts. What makes this a travel rewards sweet spot is the disconnect between cash prices and points cost. While competitors like Marriott Bonvoy may charge 85,000-100,000 points for comparable luxury, Hyatt keeps Park Hyatt redemptions at Category 7-8 (25,000-30,000 points). Combined with the 1:1 transfer ratio from Chase Ultimate Rewards, a single Chase Sapphire Preferred sign-up bonus can fund multiple nights of genuine luxury.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Earn Chase Ultimate Rewards through the Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or business cards like the Ink Preferred. A single sign-up bonus often covers 2-3 Park Hyatt nights. Alternatively, earn directly with the World of Hyatt credit card.

Log into your Chase account and transfer Ultimate Rewards to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio. Transfers are typically instant, so you can transfer right before booking. Only transfer what you need for confirmed availability.

Use the World of Hyatt website or app to search your desired Park Hyatt property and dates. Filter by "Points" to see award availability. Check flexible date ranges to find the best redemption opportunities.

Complete the booking using your Hyatt points. Make sure you are logged into your World of Hyatt account so elite benefits apply. Consider booking a standard room and requesting a suite upgrade at check-in if you have Globalist status.

If you have Globalist status, contact the hotel before arrival to request suite upgrades and confirm breakfast inclusion. Even without top-tier status, joining World of Hyatt (free) earns you base-level benefits and points on incidental spend.

The fastest path is through Chase Ultimate Rewards. Cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve earn Ultimate Rewards that transfer 1:1 to World of Hyatt. A single sign-up bonus of 60,000-75,000 points can cover 2-3 nights at a Park Hyatt. You can also earn directly with the World of Hyatt credit card.

Compared to other luxury hotel chains, Park Hyatt availability is relatively good. Booking 3-6 months in advance for popular properties like Park Hyatt Tokyo or Park Hyatt Maldives improves your chances. Off-peak and shoulder season dates often have wide-open availability.

Yes. Globalist elite status works at all Park Hyatt properties and unlocks suite upgrades (subject to availability), free breakfast, late checkout, and waived resort fees. This dramatically increases the total value of a points stay.

Properties in high-cost destinations like Tokyo, New York, Paris, Sydney, and the Maldives typically deliver the highest cents-per-point value because their cash rates are so expensive. A Park Hyatt Tokyo stay worth $600-$800/night for 25,000 points is a standout redemption.

This redemption is purpose-built for the intentional luxury traveler in the ChooseFI community — someone who has been systematically accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards points and wants to convert that discipline into a genuinely extraordinary hotel experience, not just a free night at a mid-tier property.

The minimum to play: You need at least 25,000 World of Hyatt points for a single night — ideally 50,000–75,000 for a meaningful multi-night stay. This is achievable through a single Chase Sapphire welcome bonus plus modest everyday spending.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating**, and it's worth being specific about where the friction lives — because once you understand it, most of the difficulty evaporates. **The earning is easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards points flow into World of Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, and Chase is one of the most accessible premium rewards ecosystems for new-to-intermediate travel rewards participants. The points pipeline is well-established and reliable. **The transfer and booking mechanics are easy.** The actual process — confirm availability, transfer points, complete booking — is straightforward if you follow the correct sequence. The Hyatt website is functional and the award search is transparent. **The hard part is availability.** Park Hyatt properties are genuinely popular, the award inventory is limited, and the most desirable dates (cherry blossom season, major holidays, Fashion Week) book out fast. This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Plan further ahead than feels natural. If you want Tokyo in April of next year, you should be searching in late March or early April of the current year. 2. **Be flexible by 3–5 days on either side.** Award inventory often opens mid-week when demand is lower. Shifting from a Saturday check-in to a Thursday can unlock availability that doesn't exist on peak nights. 3. **Check repeatedly near the 30-day mark.** Properties occasionally release additional award space as the date approaches. Setting a weekly reminder to re-check your target dates costs nothing. If you're willing to plan ahead and stay flexible on exact dates, moderate difficulty becomes very manageable — and the reward on the other side is worth every bit of the effort.

The Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most compelling redemptions in the entire travel rewards landscape. Booking a genuine ultra-luxury hotel experience for 25,000-30,000 points — points that transfer 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards — delivers 2-4 cents per point in value. Whether it is the iconic Park Hyatt Tokyo, the beachfront Park Hyatt Maldives, or the classic Park Hyatt New York, this sweet spot consistently delivers outsized value. For anyone building a Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, Park Hyatt should be at the top of the aspiration list.
