#8825. Inside Sullivan Middaugh’s Balancing Act Between Off-Road Dominance and LA 2028

There are few races Sullivan Middaugh would like to target more than next year’s XTERRA World Championship in New Mexico. However, if everything goes to plan, there’s only a slim chance he’ll be on the start line to defend his title.

That’s because Middaugh is part of an exciting crop of American men trying to help the Project Podium program live up to its name at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. And with an increasingly crowded triathlon calendar, the timing doesn’t quite work.

The challenge is that the 2027 XTERRA World Championship weekend in Ruidoso falls between the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Hamburg, Germany, and another top-level race in Weihai, China. Both are part of the rebranded T50 Championship series.

Not only could these events prove critical in helping the U.S. secure three men’s spots for Los Angeles – the host nation is already guaranteed two – but Hamburg could also present an opportunity for Middaugh to stake his claim to one of those places.

He can’t afford to let up. It’s still early in the Olympic qualification cycle, but the U.S. currently has eight men in the top 50 of the Olympic rankings, more than any other nation, with Middaugh the fourth-ranked American at 31st overall.

But while the focus will understandably shift toward the work of coach Parker Spencer’s Project Podium squad, which splits its time between Tempe, Arizona, in the winter and Park City, Utah, in the summer, XTERRA will never be entirely out of mind.

After all, it’s the discipline that put the Middaugh family on the triathlon map, and never more so than earlier this month, when Sullivan claimed his first full-distance XTERRA world title, younger brother Porter finished seventh, and father Josiah, at 48 years young, placed sixth.

Three members of the same family, spanning two generations, finishing in the top seven of a World Championship race is a remarkable feat, with few obvious parallels across elite sport.

The achievement was even more special because it had been 11 years since an American man last won the event. That was Josiah, in 2015. Before him, you have to go back another 15 years to Michael Tobin’s victory in 2000.

“No, I haven’t heard anything quite like that,” Sullivan confirms. “And especially having my dad in the race is pretty incredible!”

More than the result itself, it’s the opportunity to continue racing alongside his father that Sullivan appreciates.

“Following in his footsteps is pretty awesome,” he continues. “Every year he says he’s gonna retire, but I don’t know. It’s been pretty awesome to be able to continue to train and race with him. I grew up just following him on the XTERRA circuit and going to races and watching him. I never really thought we’d be racing together.”

Sullivan’s success also made up for his defeat by Reed Legg at the North American Championship earlier this year. Legg’s victory interrupted a Middaugh dynasty that has seen Josiah win 15 U.S. elite national titles and Sullivan dominate the more recent championship era.

And it was made all the sweeter by the XTERRA World Championship’s return to the U.S. after four years in Italy.

“I put it on my calendar and kept it in mind all year,” Sullivan says. “It was a race at altitude, which I grew up at, and so I felt like it was a good opportunity. Grindstone Lake, where we swam, is at 7,000 feet and the course got up to maybe a little bit over 8,000 feet. But at home in Colorado, my house is at like 7,500 feet, and you can only really go up from there. So, the six or seven weeks leading in, I went home and trained with dad because I knew it would be a big advantage if I could be fully acclimatized.”

While Porter, who also trains with Project Podium, finished seventh, Sullivan believes his younger brother might have mounted a stronger challenge had he not been racing at the Under-23 World Championship in Spain.

Sullivan skipped that race to sharpen his mountain biking skills, although it didn’t prevent an early spill on the bike.

“Yeah, I overcooked the corners a little bit on the first couple of turns in the single track section,” he explains. “It wasn’t a bad spill out, but I kinda had to slam on the brake, go off the trail, tip over and get up quick. My bike computer fell off, which wasn’t a big deal, and maybe a blessing in disguise to not worry about power and just focus on effort.”

Sullivan had an almost four-minute lead heading onto the run and extended his advantage with the day’s fastest 10K split, but at no point did he feel comfortable.

“I didn’t really get any splits and thought that no lead was safe on the run. I just tried to give it full gas, focusing on pushing the climbs and rolling the downhills because I knew they’d be coming.”

Among the athletes trying to hunt him down were two very familiar faces – Porter and Josiah – and there was a brief moment of family camaraderie as their paths crossed on the course.

“I just focus on myself for the most part, but it reminds you that they’re also out there battling. I saw them running together, so that was pretty cool because I knew they’d be pushing each other. We were all pumped, gave each other a high five, and that was pretty much it.”

There were plenty more high fives and hugs at the finish, where Sullivan’s mom, sister, and grandparents were also in attendance.

While this was Sullivan’s first full-distance XTERRA world title, he had previously won the Short Track World Championship in Molveno, Italy, in 2024.

In recent years, short-track racing has typically taken place a couple of days before or the day after the main event, although it wasn’t on the schedule in Ruidoso.

“It’s like a three or four-minute swim, maybe a 15-minute bike and a seven-minute run,” Sullivan says, with distances depending on the course layout. “It’s all under 30 minutes for the most part, so more intense and a little bit different, and you can’t make as many mistakes. I think it suits me because I’ve spent a lot of time training for sprint distance draft-legal triathlons. I really enjoy it.”

While XTERRA might be seen as a distraction from road triathlon, Sullivan believes it complements his efforts elsewhere.

“It helps me with my skills for the draft-legal stuff as well. I look to people like Flora Duffy and Hayden Wilde who were able to do well at both, and think they’re an example for me.”

For the next 18 months, the priority will be collecting Olympic qualification points, with the window having opened in May.

Sullivan has already recorded top-10 finishes at World Triathlon Cups in Huatulco, Mexico; Edmonton, Canada; Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; and Asunción, Paraguay. He also competed at the Americas Triathlon Championships in Antofagasta, Chile, finishing 11th. He now heads to Chile for two more World Cup races, in San Pedro de la Paz and Iquique.

While USA Triathlon hasn’t officially released its selection policy for Los Angeles, Sullivan expects the Olympic test event in July 2027 and the World Championship Finals in Hamburg to be key races. He anticipates that a top-eight finish, combined with being the leading American, could be enough to meet the automatic selection criteria.

But first, he needs to secure starts at the biggest races. “Spots keep flipping, so it’s gonna be pretty tough,” he adds. “I’ve been mostly focusing on the World Cup level, which is the step below the World Championship Series, but as my swim develops, I’ll try and focus more on the World Championship Series because that’s the level you need to be at in the Olympics.”

The higher the level, the more critical the swim becomes. “If you’re the best swimmer, you can be in the race up until the run, but if you don’t have a good swim, you may never even be in the race,” he explains. “The swim sets you up for a good day to get in the right bike group, but you also need to be able to run well off a hard bike. That’s something XTERRA helps me with.”

Sullivan admits that bridging the gap in the swim is his biggest immediate challenge, but he also knows he’ll need a blistering run to compete at the very top.

“Especially with Alex Yee and Hayden Wilde, it is just getting faster and faster,” he says. “You need to be an elite runner if you want to be on the podium, and that means hitting sub-14 minutes sometimes in the 5K and sub-29 minutes occasionally on the 10K. Right now, I’m in the low 14s and around 30, maybe a little under depending on the course.”

If he can get there, it will be with the help of Project Podium. Established in 2018, Project Podium is funded by USA Triathlon, corporate sponsors, and private donors, including longtime benefactors Dr. Bill Warren and his wife Lynne. Based at Arizona State University, the program provides promising American male triathletes with coaching, scholarships, and financial support as they pursue Olympic ambitions.

Sullivan, who graduated with a degree in biomedical sciences in August, has enormous respect for coach Spencer, who he says also understands his passion for the trails and why XTERRA should remain part of his program.

“I love mountain biking, and so it’s good for me to be able to kinda go in and out, but I think that as the Olympics get closer I’ll have to take a slight step away from XTERRA, but we’ll see.”

Finally, if Sullivan’s Olympic dream does come to fruition, could there be more than one Middaugh on the U.S. team?

“That’s definitely a big ask, but would be amazing. I don’t know if it’s on the cards for ’28, but maybe for ’32 it could be more plausible. I think we both have the ability to get to that level if we stick with it, and when I see Porter in the race, we don’t really need to say anything. We just understand what we need to do.”

#8823. What Is the SuperHalfs Series? Inside the Popular Half Marathon Challenge

All the information you need, including race dates, registration and course details, and how to prepare for racing abroad.

According to the 2026 Running USA Global Runner Survey or more than 11,000 runners, the half marathon is the most popular race distance. Not only that, but almost half of those runners would be happy to travel more than 500 miles for a good half marathon (and marathon). This might be why the SuperHalfs, a European series of six races through Lisbon, Cardiff, Prague, Berlin, Valencia, and Copenhagen, have become so popular.

These races are not neighborhood events, but international spectacles, and they are difficult to get into. A few of the courses, including Copenhagen (2014), Cardiff (2016), and Valencia (2018), have even hosted the World Athletics Half Marathon Championships. Dubbed “a super series for the ordinary runner,” according to Mark Janik, CEO North America of Sports Tours International, the SuperHalfs are perfect for runners who want to combine racing with travel.

While the early 2027 races are sold out, you can start planning for the autumn 2027 and 2028 races. No rush, though, as you have a lifetime to complete all six races and, once you do, you’ll earn more bling—a seventh medal. If you’re ready to set some international race goals, we have the training plans you need to get to the start lines of these extraordinary competitions.

Date: March 7, 2027 (Sunday)Location: Almada, PortugalNumber of Runners: 35,000Time Limit: 3 hours

A favorite course of many elite runners, racers enjoy views along the River Tagus and journey over the 25 de Abril Bridge, once the longest suspension bridge in Europe and a twin of the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco. This race is the only time when pedestrians can cross, says Sadie Lowell, JetSetting_Runner, who has helped runners plan their international runcations.

Although Lisbon is a hilly city, the course is flat, and typically serves up nice weather, as Portugal’s capital city boasts about 300 days of sunshine most years. It is also famous for record-setting runs including in 20216 Jacob Kiplimo from Uganda broke the world record—again—during this race with a time of 57:20.

The lottery for this race typically opens in June. Follow the race on Instagram for updates!

Date: April 3, 2027 (Saturday)Location: Prague, Czech RepublicNumber of Runners: 17,000Time Limit: 3 hoursREGISTER

Organizers of the Prague Half Marathon, with a theme of “all runners are beautiful,” may have been inspired to create that phrase because the race course itself is considered so lovely. The sights include castles, rivers, bridges, and historic parts of Prague. For the 13.1-mile course, runners will complete a few loops and turnarounds, with the race starting at Bubenské Nábřeží, Holešovice and ending at Jan Palach Square in the Old Town of Prague.

The idea for the SuperHalfs was born in Prague by Czech creator, Carlo Capalbo, and the series is managed by RunCzech. It’s a truly international event: More than half of the runners who participated in 2025 were from other countries.

The lottery for this race typically opens in August. Follow the race on Instagram for updates!

Date: April 4, 2027 (Sunday)Location: Berlin, GermanyNumber of Runners: over 42,000Time Limit: 3:15 hours

This is the largest of the six races, and, throughout the half, you’ll run past many of Berlin’s most iconic landmarks starting with the Victory Column monument in the center of the Tiergarten district. If you’re lucky, you might also spot a glimpse of Checkpoint Charlie as you make your way through the course. The race ends with a celebratory run through the Brandenburg Gate before reaching the finish.

After the race, celebrate your success with delicious German pretzels—the salt is good for rehydration!

This lottery usually opens in April, with results announced in June. Follow the race on Instagram for updates!

Date: September 19, 2027 (Sunday)Location: Copenhagen, DenmarkNumber of Runners: over 45,000Time Limit: 3 hours

Located in the heart of Copenhagen, the course takes runners through the historic inner city as well as the city’s charming and colorful bridge districts. The race prides itself on being a party filled with music from DJs, bands, and choirs. It also features high-energy cheering sections called “Power Zones” designed to energize you through the miles. And if you were lucky enough to snag a bib for 2026, you’ll be in for a treat because Copenhagen is set to host the 2026 World Championships.

The 2027 lottery for this race will likely open in March. Follow the race on Instagram for updates!

Date: October 3, 2027 (Sunday)Location: Cardiff, WalesNumber of Runners: over 28,000Time Limit: 4 hours

One of the smallest cities in the series, Cardiff, the capital of Wales, is 150 miles west of London. On the half-marathon route, runners travel past Cardiff Castle, the Principality Stadium, Civic Centre, and Cardiff Bay—all favorite tourist spots.

The race is known for its cheering sections and you may hear: “Pob Lwc!” or Welsh for “Good Luck!” as you’re running through the course.

While smaller than the other cities that are part of the series, this half marathon began in 2003 with only 1,500 people and now is part of the world stage of running.

The lottery for this race is usually open from through October. Follow the race on Instagram for updates!

Date: October 24, 2027Location: Valencia, SpainNumber of Runners: 25,000Time Limit: 2:45 hours

While you’ll run through the center of this Spanish city, the roads are wide so you don’t have to worry about overcrowding or slowing down. On course, you’ll see the Torres de Serranos, one of the 12 gates that formed part of the ancient city wall built at the end of the 14th century, along with the city’s famous murals, created by local artists.

Valencia is on the east coast of the Iberian Peninsula on the Mediterranean Sea, so the views of the water as you run to the finish are spectacular—and so is the food you get to indulge in afterward. (This is where paella was invented after all!)

You can register for this race just a few weeks after it’s over, typically in early November. Follow the race on Instagram for updates!

Unlike driving to an American city for a half, if you sign up for a SuperHalf race, you do need to handle more details to make sure your travel and race go smoothly.

While all of the races are in major cities with international airports, you can also travel with a company, such as Sports Tours International. They create group schedules that include multi-day hotel stays, race briefings, escorted trips to expos, some walking tours, shakeout runs, and, most importantly, race registration (which can fill up quickly!).

Whether you travel independently or with a group, it’s smart to fly in at least 48 hours before your race, Lowell tells Runner’s World. “This way you will have a buffer to pickup your bib in case of flight delays or cancellations. Many races don’t allow pick up on the morning of the race,” she explains.

You’ll also want to account for jet lag. “If you typically struggle to adjust your sleep cycle, plan to run the race on the last weekend of your trip,” Lowell says. “If you are able to adjust quickly, you can plan for running the race on your first weekend and exploring the rest of the trip.”

Once you’ve arrived, take Lowell’s advice and keep track of your eating and drinking prerace. “It can be easy when you are in a new city to forget about all the carbs you need to consume and all the water you need to drink,” she adds. “I always recommend stopping at a local grocery store and picking up some food to eat the morning of your race.”

While it may not be a selling point, keep in mind that many of these city streets are old—Lisbon was established in 1200 BCE—and weren’t designed for runners. At times, large crowds may run on narrow roads. While the courses are flat and fast, and most of the running is on large boulevards, you may have to be cautious on cobblestone streets. Of course, this is a small price to pay for an athletic adventure in a picturesque location.

Donna Raskin has had a long career as a health and fitness writer and editor of books and magazine articles. A certified run coach who has practiced yoga for many years, she also loves to lift weights, dance, and go for long walks with her hound dog, Dolly.

#8822. How Long to Recover After a Marathon and When to Return to Running

A smart post-26.2 plan for easing soreness, rebuilding mileage, and avoiding a rushed return.

You’ve crossed the finish line, collected your medal, and celebrated a goal that once demanded months of early mornings and long runs. Now comes the less glamorous part of the marathon: recovery.

You might be eager to get back on the road—or perfectly happy to take a break. Either way, the days and weeks after a marathon deserve as much thought as the training that got you to the starting line in the first place.

Here’s how to decide how long to rest, recognize when you’re ready to return, and ease back into training so you can build toward your next goal feeling strong.

Exactly when you return to running after a marathon depends on how the race went, your overall effort during it, and how you feel. Some experts recommend one day of recovery time for every mile raced—so 26 days of rest for marathoners. And some even recommend one day of rest for each kilometer raced, which would mean 42 days of recovery.

Don’t panic, though! The good news is that “rest” does not have to mean no running at all (though it can). It just means taking a break from high-intensity training such as speedwork or other races.

Remember, running a race at a submaximal effort is different than racing it at a high effort. But either way, there’s no exact formula to follow for recovery after a marathon, so the best guide is really tuning in and listening to your body.

At a minimum, take three to seven days completely off from running after a marathon. Sleep in, eat, and enjoy your accomplishment. After that, begin an active recovery program. Active recovery includes light exercise and can include some running, if you are not sore and feel mentally and physically ready to get back to it.

More specifically, “light” exercise means exercising at a low-intensity level, i.e., no more than 60 to 65 percent of your max heart rate for a relatively short duration, like less than 60 minutes. Activity actually helps you recover faster than inactivity because it promotes circulation. And good circulation delivers fresh oxygen and nutrients to muscles and carries away metabolic waste and, therefore, aids healing and recovery.

If you do want to clock miles, focus on recovery runs during this time—keeping the effort light and easy, meaning you should be able to have a conversation the entire time you’re running.

Your body will let you know when it wants to run again, and one message it will send is through soreness. Minimal soreness is a good sign because it means your body is recovering from the challenge, but it may take a few days to kick in.

Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically follows most marathon efforts. The soreness results from microscopic muscle tissue damage, and the severity of it depends on your fitness level and the intensity of the effort relative to the training effort. The degree of soreness indicates the extent of muscle damage, and this will influence the duration of your recovery period.

In other words, the more soreness, the longer the recovery. (A lack of soreness indicates you were well prepared for the demands of your race, so good job with your training.) When the soreness subsides, that’s an indicator that you’re ready for action again.

You could also monitor your resting heart rate (RHR) for an objective assessment of your recovery process or your heart rate variability (HRV), which many fitness trackers take into account when determining your “readiness” to exercise. When your heart returns to its normal pre-marathon resting heart rate, and/or your HRV stabilizes, you are ready to begin running again.

Walking, riding a bike, stretching, or swimming for 30 to 60 minutes at low intensity will promote circulation and assist your recovery. Massage therapy and foam rolling can also help relieve muscle soreness and assist recovery by increasing the body’s circulation.

Avoid a hot bath or the hot tub for 48 hours after the race. Cool water baths with some ice can help minimize soft tissue inflammation, though, during the first 48 hours postrace.

To make it more bearable, fill the tub with water and hop in. Then, slowly add ice to the water to minimize the cold shock factor. You can wear a sweatshirt and sip on a hot drink while you cool down your legs.

After your ice bath, plan on lying down with your feet elevated (legs up on a wall is a good pose for recovery). You can do this regularly during the few weeks after your marathon, too.

When you’re ready to lace up your shoes, return to running with some easy-paced, short runs when muscle soreness has disappeared.

One training option is to follow your taper plan in reverse to rebuild your mileage (this is known as reverse tapering). For example, your first weekday runs would be in the three- to six-mile range. The first long run on the weekend would be around six miles, and the following weekend would clock in at eight to 10 miles. You’d then do a 10- to 14-mile run the weekend after that, depending on your training plan. Future mileage will depend on how you feel and your future running goals.

As you return to running, be aware of your breathing and heart rate while on the move. If your heart rate spikes up, or your breathing sounds like a locomotive, you know you are still recovering from the marathon. These are signs of fatigue, so take it easy until your exercise heart rate and breathing rate also return to their normal ranges.

The recovery period is a good time to decide what you want to do next. Dreaming of your next race and medal is a great way to spend your downtime!

Susan Paul has coached more than 2,000 runners and is an exercise physiologist and program director for the Orlando Track Shack Foundation. For more information, visit www.trackshack.com.

#8820. Jess McClain Took a 2-Year Break From Running—and Came Back Faster Than Ever. Here’s What You Can Learn From Her Impressive Return.

The most important strategy for making a strong comeback.

About six years ago, Jess McClain went out for her scheduled workout—1,000-meter repeats—like any other day. She felt like she was going full send, but was frustrated to see that each rep actually clocked in about 45 seconds slower than her goal time.

The experience was the straw that broke the camel’s back, so to speak, after slowly losing motivation and excitement for competing professionally. “I ended up walking home and I texted my coach that day and said, ‘I think I need to shut this down,’” she recalls. He responded that a week off sounded like a good idea, to which she said: “No, I think I need to shut it down for good.”

Luckily, her professional running break only lasted about two years, during which she met her now-husband, reconnected with old friends, and got married.

In 2022, just after her honeymoon, McClain saw an ad for the Mesa Marathon in Arizona, happening a few days before her 30th birthday, and signed up on a whim. “I actually built a playlist that was two hours and 45 minutes long and I was like, ‘I’d be really stoked if I finished the race before this playlist ended,’” she says.

She finished in 2:32—and won. But the best part? “I was like, ‘damn, that was so fun,’” she says. “I probably still have Mai Tais in my system from my honeymoon and I’m running 2:32 and I ran 45 to 55 miles a week and I felt awesome and I just had so much fun. This is when I knew there’s that competitor still in me.”

That experience was the jump-start she needed to get back to the sport professionally—but with a promise to herself that she would always find joy in the process going forward.

“I think I had a lot of joy running in college, but then I think as a professional, I took it so, so seriously that it was almost like all I had and all I poured myself into,” McClain says. “Taking time away from the sport gave me a lot of perspective and reminded me why I love it.”

Clearly this mindset shift is working for her: Since the Mesa Marathon, McClain has run some of the best races of her life, including placing fourth at the Olympic Marathon Trials ahead of the Paris Games, setting the American course record at this year’s Boston Marathon with a time of 2:20:49, and placing second at this year’s New York City Marathon—the first American woman to podium at the race in eight years—with a time of 2:24:42.

McClain isn’t the only example of an athlete who took time off after feeling burned out, rediscovered the love of the sport, and made an insanely impressive comeback. And you don’t have to be a pro to gain the benefits of running for fun, including leading to your best race performances.

It may sound abstract—and not like your typical training tactic—but here’s why and how adding more joy to your running just might lead to the breakthrough you’re looking to achieve.

Sometimes taking a break is what athletes of all levels need in order to rediscover joy in their sport—and possibly come back stronger than ever. Figure skater Alysa Liu temporarily retired after the 2022 Olympics because of burnout, then came back to win two gold medals at the Milan Cortina Games in 2026 after restarting the sport initially for fun.

Part of the reason taking a break can ultimately have a positive effect on performance could be because the athlete is exercising their autonomy, says Erin Ayala, PhD, a sports psychologist, certified mental performance consultant, and founder of Skadi Sport Psychology.

“When an athlete is able to choose to step away, that helps with motivation because they feel like they’re in charge of their athletic identity,” she says. “And then they’re also usually able to reconnect with what they loved about running because when we take off that pressure, it lights that fire inside of them again where they’re like, ‘oh yeah, this is why I got into it.’”

A break also allows athletes to lean into other parts of their identity, whether that’s as a partner, sibling, parent, cook, or otherwise. “When we only see ourselves as an athlete or a runner, we’re more vulnerable to burnout, depression, anxiety, [and] spirals when running is not going well,” she says.

However, catching the early signs of athletic burnout could help you to prevent it from manifesting and necessitating a long break.

There’s a difference between true athletic burnout and normal training fatigue. Here are a few signs it’s the former, according to Ayala:

Whether you’re burned out or not, making running more joyful can benefit every runner. Looking forward to your runs not only keeps you consistent—a key factor for race-day performance—but can also improve your speed and your endurance.

When Ayala works with clients dealing with burnout, the first thing she does is help them rediscover their why—and it’s something you can do yourself, too, Ayala says. “Think about when you first started doing this, what was driving you, what was getting you excited to get out of bed in the morning or to go for the run?,” she asks.

Greg Laraia, a running coach at Motiv in New York City, says that most people will have five to 10 “whys” if you dig deep enough. A client might say the reason they’re running the marathon is to PR so he’ll ask why they want to PR. “They’re like, ‘Well, because [I want to be] faster than last time,’ and I’m like, ‘Well, why?’ If you can keep asking why and just pull them a little bit deeper than, ‘I want to run fast,’ a lot of times they’ll actually realize either they do really care about this or it’s so superficial that it doesn’t really matter,’” he says. “I think that’s a huge piece of what can help preserve enjoyment, too, and then being able to tap back into that.”

Ayala says that the ways to tap into and preserve fun are often tied to community, self-improvement, or time for yourself.

Again, autonomy is key to helping prevent burnout and there are small ways you can exercise it on the regular. For example, build in more of your favorite kinds of workouts, even if they’re not “ideal” or exactly what’s on your training plan, Ayala says. “If it’s bringing you more joy, it’s totally worth it. Having more agency over [your] training is really important and it is really effective.”

This might look like running your local free 5K in the park or joining your friends for their track workouts.

McClain says that prior to 2020, she was very focused on the outcome. “In practice, I’d get spun up if I was off a few seconds on a rep and then I think that just snowballs into overanalyzing and overthinking racing and worrying about the things I couldn’t control,” she says. “Now I’ve relinquished a lot of that and I just focus on what I can control and I really try to enjoy the whole process. I think that’s lent itself to just feeling a little bit more free while running.”

No one wants to get to a race like the marathon, in which you put in 16 to 20 weeks of training, have it go poorly and look back thinking you didn’t enjoy the build, McClain adds. If you actually enjoyed getting to the start, the finish line in itself is just an extra sweet payoff.

Ayala helps her clients set process goals—where they focus on how they want to execute the race or training instead of just the splits, times, or the paces—for this exact purpose. “That might be showing up on race day with a tutu and sparkles and giving as many high fives as possible or volunteering with an organization,” like Girls of the Run, she says.

Earlier in her career, McClain says she was “bad” at celebrating small wins. “I was just so addicted to setting PRs and hitting my highest mileage week and I think there’s so many things along the way that you can celebrate,” she says. “Don’t take yourself so seriously and have fun along the way and then celebrate all the small milestones and the big ones.”

For McClain, those small wins include celebrating being able to get in 90 grams of carbs per hour on a long run or simply being able to get up on the first alarm during the summer.

These days, McClain says she’s focused on listening to her body and adapting her plan accordingly. “The goal is to get the workout done as it’s written on my plan, but there are a lot of times where I’m pulling audibles and adjusting the pace based on how my body feels on the day,” she says. “I think that’s also made it more fun because my body’s just agreeing with the training and what I’m doing instead of doing three days of high intensity and a ton of mileage.”

In general, McClain focuses on two hard days and about 82 to 85 miles a week, which she says also gives her time for other stuff in her life.

Ayala points out that this flexibility is a great way to work against burnout: “We also know, unfortunately, perfectionists are more vulnerable to burnout,” she says.

“I think it’s good to practice adaptability also because in a marathon, you just never know what’s going to happen and you can feel so different in one mile to the next,” McClain says. “So also practicing how you’re talking to yourself when things get hard, that’s really important to strengthen those muscles in your workouts and your long run.”

Ignoring the data for a short time can help you decompress without reducing training load, Laraia says. That could look like starting your watch but not looking at it until your workout is over (rather than constantly looking at your heart rate, pace, etc.), he says. Or just go out for an hour-long run and don’t even start your device.

“Today, I think we’re surrounded by so much data and information that it’s really easy to get caught up in numbers and stats and either compare them to yourself or you compare to your friends,” Laraia says. And you know what they say about comparison being the thief of joy…

Laraia recommends that his clients jot down their emotional state after workouts and races just as they might keep track of more quantifiable metrics. “How did this long run feel? How did your mind feel? What were you thinking about in the workout or in the race? Those are things that I think are really important because it helps guide where to push them or pull back,” he says. Even without a coach, you can notice patterns in your own notes.

The key is to look for a mismatch in how you felt and how you performed. If your runs are feeling easy but your heart rate is higher, you may be pushing paces you aren’t ready to run.

On the flip side, if a workout felt really hard but your heart rate was lower, that could mean something else is going on (potentially even an early sign of mental burnout) that’s worth paying attention to if it’s repeated (versus just one or two runs).

“Eat more than you think you need—that's my biggest tip,” McClain says. “I feel like the amount that I’ve fueled and eaten on and off the runs in the last two or three years [has] kept me super healthy alongside a few other things, but I think fueling is so important,” she says. “Making sure you’re taking care of your body on the nutrition front is really, really big.”

Think about it: You’re not having fun when you’re hangry, right?

READ OUR COMPLETE GUIDE TO MARATHON FUELING

Now, when McClain travels for races, she builds in time for fun with her husband. “That’s been a huge additive mindset to this whole elite racing thing—you can have a great time,” she says. “You don’t have to be holed up in your hotel room and you can lean into all the fun appearances and the shakeout runs. It’s energy adding instead of energy sucking for me.”

By taking time to enjoy the experience, even if the race doesn’t go exactly as she hoped, McClain still revels in the fact that she enjoyed the trip and the experience.

Some seasons of life necessitate more R&R, and you need to give your body enough time to absorb the stress of training, Ayala points out. She experienced this firsthand on the heels of COVID-19 when a close friend died, and she felt super burned out in general. She took two months off from cycling—the first in almost a decade of consistent training—and ended up setting a new PR within eight weeks of getting back to it.

“I'm really convinced that it was because I just finally listened to my body and took the pressure off and just took a break,” Ayala says. “It led to a huge boost in performance in one of my best seasons afterward, which was pretty cool.”

Sometimes, even a shorter break—like five days—can be enough to circumvent burnout, Laraia says. “It could be as simple as dropping a hard run or taking an extra day off or reducing mileage or just doing an easy run instead of that hard workout.” Whatever break you need to come back with excitement is worth it.

#8819. What Happens When Grief Derails Your Triathlon Training

Rachel Olson wins 2026 Ironman 70.3 São Paulo after struggling to train through the grief of losing her mother in November 2024. (Photo: Romulo Cruz/Ironman)

In late September, Rachel Olson crossed the finish line first at Ironman 70.3 São Paulo, nearly 10 minutes ahead of her nearest competitor. The race, by her own admission, was “not spectacular” for the longtime pro triathlete. But the support that followed was. The crowd embraced her, and athletes and fans who had followed her story cheered a little louder, as though they knew what it took just to get her to the start line.

Because in the months after her mother Janis died in November 2024 of liver disease, Olson could barely bring herself to work out. She did not want to disappear from triathlon. But she’d go to the pool and just sit on the edge and cry. She’d hop on her bike and feel a sudden urge to turn around. Running, always an easy way to manage big emotions, became a chore.

Then her body began to rebel: digestive issues, mysterious inflammation, bone-deep exhaustion, muscles that wouldn’t recover.

“My body was basically screaming at me that something was wrong, like it was constantly fighting something,” said Olson, 35, who lives in Boulder with her fiancé, fellow pro triathlete Andre Lopes. “Your mind is telling you to process, and your body is telling you to slow down.”

For endurance athletes, the instinct after a loss is often to train through the emotional pain. The adage goes that exercise helps with grief: Get outside, move your body, clear your head. Sometimes it does. But for Olson and many others, the very thing that once gave life structure can become one more demand on a body and mind already stretched thin.

“Grief doesn’t just live in the mind. It’s in the chest, in the restlessness, in this low-grade energy that has nowhere obvious to go,” said Kenza Haddock, president and co-founder of Oceanic Counseling Group in Murrells Inlet, South Carolina. “Endurance sport can tip from processing grief into outrunning it, using exhaustion to stay ahead of the feeling rather than move through it. It can just leave you more numb.”

Plenty of endurance athletes have turned grief into a mission. In August 2026, Matthew Hollingham, a 25-year-old doctoral student at Penn State, created an “Arctic Circle to Africa” triathlon in memory of his late fiancée Lovisa Arnesson-Cronhamre, who was killed in a hit-and-run while jogging on campus. Over 61 days and 3,545 miles, he swam in a lake above the Arctic Circle, ran a marathon a day for 37 days, and cycled just over 110 miles a day for 23. He raised more than $40,000 for two charities and kept her memory present.

Others have taken similar routes; at the 2026 London Marathon, Laura Coleman-Day, a 33-year-old mother from Lincolnshire in the U.K., went viral for changing into her wedding dress and running the final miles in it as a dedication to her late husband, Xander.

This kind of public mission can be cathartic, says Hilary Bucell, a psychotherapist and lecturer at Columbia University.

“Engaging in something like triathlon can become a ritualized space where the recognition of the loss is welcomed and at the same time, the sport’s necessity for present moment awareness also helps athletes acknowledge new life experiences continuing now beyond the loss,” she said.

Of course, racing to honor a loved one doesn’t erase grief — it just gives you a place to put it. It can also offer a healthy distraction from the deep ache of a devastating loss.

Some aren’t able to navigate their grief in such a public and profound way. There are those like Olson whose grief hits the body hard enough to derail training. In 2023, Gustav Iden, the 2022 Ironman World Champion, ended his season early to heal and regroup after the death of his mother, revealing “it was very emotional, and it was hard to find joy in training after that.” (He returned to racing about a year later.)

As one of her mother’s main caretakers, Olson spent two years before her death flying to her hometown in Texas for doctor’s appointments. Triathlon took a backseat: She parted ways with her coach and scaled back her training. Even when she did have time to work out, anxiety followed.

“I would think, ‘Am I going to be out on a bike ride and get a phone call saying she’s in the hospital? Are things going to go downhill?’”

After Janis died, that anxiety turned physical. Olson was never diagnosed with one specific issue, but testing showed elevated inflammation markers and low ferritin, requiring an iron infusion.

“Ultimately, I think my body was responding to trauma. It felt like I had an illness,” she said. “Trying to perform in a body that felt completely foreign to me was incredibly difficult. I didn’t understand why my body wasn’t doing what it had done before.”

Research suggests that grief can affect the body as well as the mind. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) lists impaired immune response and increased mortality from heart disease, especially in older, widowed patients, among the physical complications. The effects may vary, as not everyone experiences the same physical response.

Part of the explanation may lie in how the brain processes the loss of a loved one through interconnected systems involved in emotion, threat detection, and the regulation of stress hormones. Grief can flood the body with inflammatory signals. and increase cortisol, the steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands that regulates the body’s response to stress.

“Grief is a neurological event that impacts your ability to learn and remember things, attend to things, and impacts your mood,” said Wilfred van Gorp, a Manhattan-based board-certified neuropsychologist. “Losing someone keeps your amygdala on high alert and elevates cortisol. It impacts you in your body as well as your mind.”

Grief and stress can also disrupt communication between the brain and the gut, which may contribute to everything from irritable bowel syndrome to acid reflux to ulcers, according to research.

For Olson, whose stomach swelled within days of her mother’s death, that brain-gut link was obvious.

“Only two days after [she passed], I woke up, and my stomach was distended about five inches. And then I kind of exploded in inflammation weight,” she shared. “Trying to get that down is not an easy process.”

Still, Olson pushed on. She’d qualified for her first Ironman World Championship slated for about 10 months after Janis died. She wanted to race there to honor her mom. She also didn’t want to lose her identity as a triathlete. Her training “wasn’t even close” to peak levels. In Kona, her stomach rebelled on the bike. After vomiting for three hours, she pulled out soon after starting the run.

“I held onto triathlon so tightly even though my body wasn’t ready. My mind wasn’t ready,” Olson said. “I kept pushing because I wanted it so badly. I attached too much weight to needing training [and racing] to go well and needing something in my life to be OK. Looking back, I realize I didn’t have to be OK.”

After Kona, Olson took a break. She focused on her other jobs as a triathlon coach and as a sales rep, and on envisioning what her wedding to Lopes could look like without her mom.

“I decided I wasn’t going to think about triathlon for a couple of weeks,” she shared. “If I still wanted it afterward, great. If I didn’t, that was OK, too.”

Spoiler: She still loved it. With the fog lifted, Olson saw a different future in the sport, starting with a new coach, Kasper Pedersen, who could build a sustainable load and understand her fragile state.

“I looked for a coach who understands that life happens,” said Olson. “Kasper is great at helping me push my boundaries, but he also knows that I may need to go at my own pace.”

They’re keeping her training volume relatively low as she re-establishes a baseline and repairs her frayed central nervous system.

“I really wanted to make my body and mind think, ‘This is fun. This is helping us,’ rather than setting off alarm bells every time I went out,” Olson shared. “There are still days where I have to take some time off. … Grief really is a roller coaster. But overall, we’ve done a really good job of figuring out what is working.”

Talking about it helps, too, though it doesn’t come easily. Olson describes her grief as a “cloud over her personal life,” and opening up about it has cost her: One friend drifted away, unable to understand what she was going through. Olson wonders if she was simply too much to handle. Still, she finds solace in speaking out, and in being a voice for others who may be grieving alone.

“As athletes, we want to put difficult things in the back of our minds and keep going,” she said. “But I’m glad I can be a voice for other people who are going through the same so they feel less alone than they think they are.”

If her recent win in Brazil is any sign, Olson is rounding a bend toward healing, with an approach to triathlon (and life) that’s less about control and more about leaning into the process, however unpredictable and messy it may be.

“I feel like I’m a different person than I was before [my mom died]. It will always feel like a part of me has been ripped away. But I also know that there’s literally no pain that hurts as bad as what I went through,” she said. “So I’ll keep telling myself, ‘Yes, I can do this thing.’”

#8818. Build Muscle Without Exercise? What Science Says About Using Creatine Without Lifting

Creatine has been around the gym long enough to have survived several generations of invention. And reinvention. And re-re-invention… Let’s just say it’s been a supplement industry staple for decades; it’s cheap, well studied, and, when combined with resistance training, actually useful. Naturally, that wasn’t sexy enough. So, now the Internet has served up a study suggesting you can take creatine, skip the gym, and build muscle anyway. The next sound in my brain after I read it was Ronnie Coleman’s voice in my head sayin’ his famous line: “Everybody wants to be a bodybuilder, but nobody wants to lift no heavy-ass weights.”

But the study is real! Researchers at Texas A&M published it in August in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, and the results have been making the rounds again this fall. I’m very familiar with the ISSN, I’ve presented at one of its conventions. I know several of the members. The organization is legit. And Texas A&M is no joke either.

Researchers recruited 73 sedentary adults between the ages of 45 and 65 for the 12-week study. Of those, 64 completed it. Some chose to follow an exercise-and-diet program. Others didn’t. Within those groups, participants were randomly assigned either ten grams of creatine monohydrate a day or a placebo.

Then this happened. The non-exercisers taking creatine gained about 2.4 pounds of lean tissue on their body-composition scans. The non-exercisers taking a placebo didn’t show the same gain. The creatine group also improved on some strength tests. So, yes, something interesting happened. But is it what we’re afraid it is?

Notice I said “lean tissue,” not two and a half pounds of brand-new muscle. The researchers used DXA scans to measure body composition. Those scans are useful, but they don’t distinguish freshly built muscle protein from all the water sitting inside lean tissue. Creatine increases water stored in muscle, especially when people first start taking it. The study didn’t directly measure changes in body water, so nobody can tell you how much of that apparent gain was actual new muscle.

There’s another detail that tends to disappear somewhere between the scientific journal and the breathless headline. The no-exercise comparison involved just thirteen creatine users and thirteen placebo users. That’s not worthless. It’s also not the population of a medium-sized city. And the researchers randomized the supplement, not the decision to exercise. Participants chose whether to join the training program, so comparisons between exercisers and non-exercisers aren’t the same as a fully randomized test of exercise itself.

The people who did train combined resistance and aerobic exercise three times a week with a calorie-restricted diet. Creatine users in that group gained nearly three pounds of lean tissue and showed greater improvements in several performance measures. That’s interesting, too, although the study can’t tell us that creatine replaces lifting. If anything, the bigger picture still favors the traditional arrangement: take the supplement if you want, but keep showing up and doing the work.

The investigators also reported some promising changes in memory tests, blood lipids, and blood-sugar markers. I’m not dismissing those findings. But they tested a lot of outcomes in a relatively small study, and the authors themselves say the individual cognitive and metabolic results are exploratory. That’s scientist speak for “hmm… now do it again with more people.”

For completeness, the study was funded by a foundation gift. A creatine manufacturer supplied the supplements and paid for one laboratory assay, and the senior researcher disclosed a position on that company’s scientific advisory board. That doesn’t make the results false. It does make disclosure worth reading, which is something every person reporting supplement research ought to do before writing a headline.

None of this changes my opinion of creatine. It’s one of the few products on the shelf with a substantial body of evidence behind it. Ten grams daily was the dose in this experiment; it doesn’t suddenly replace the more familiar 3- to 5-gram maintenance approach used by many lifters. And if you have kidney disease or other medical issues, a conversation with your clinician would be appropriate.

So can creatine help somebody who doesn’t lift? Possibly. This trial suggests it might, and that’s worth investigating. Has anybody proved that a scoop of powder builds meaningful muscle while you sit on your ass? Not from these data. The supplement is interesting precisely because it may do more than we once thought. And what we once thought was pretty damn good. We don’t have to turn it into magic dust to appreciate that.

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate plan.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific issues or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

#8816. ZOLTÁN BÁTHORY OF FIVE FINGER DEATH PUNCH IS COMMITTED TO HIS MUSIC, COMMUNITIES, AND JUDO

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

The members of Five Finger Death Punch have been busy lately. Their 10th studio album, Legacy, was recently released, and they began their 20th Anniversary World Tour in July with the North American leg. Zoltán Báthory is the founder of 5FDP as well as their rhythm guitarist and primary songwriter. When asked his thoughts about celebrating two decades of success, Báthory was proud but more grateful for their legions of fans.

“It was always the people’s band,” he said with a smile. The Las Vegas band has been around so long, they were first getting attention on MySpace. Báthory recalled experts writing in magazines that they wouldn’t be around very long, but staying true to themselves and focusing only on the music has been their key to success.

“We just kept pushing and the people stayed with us.”

Báthory knows their music is not for everybody, but he hears stories all the time from people who have told them that hits such as “Under and Over It” and “Wash it All Away” are on their workout playlists or may have helped them get past a hard time in their lives. Báthory views that as a badge of honor because he himself trains in Flex Lewis’ Dragon Lair gym in Las Vegas and is as much a part of that community as he is the hard rock and heavy metal space.

“I’m proud of that because these are my people.”

5FDP also has a large following in the military and first responder communities. Aside from their many hits, they are known for their support of veterans and firefighters through donations to the Call of Duty Endowment fund, doing other fundraisers through their music, and Báthory has served on boards for groups like the Home Deployment Project.

“When I get a military guy telling me, ‘It’s difficult to be in a war zone. But I got up every day and listened to you guys, and it not just got me ready for the day, it got me through the day.’ That kind of gives us a justification that we’re doing something good. So, it also keeps us going. I love it.”

Báthory’s love for music and working out may only be rivaled by his passion for judo. Growing up in Hungary, judo in his home country was more popular than it is in North America. He first started following the discipline at age 9 and was entering tournaments before becoming a teenager. Báthory felt that taking up judo has done far more for him than improving his skills alone.

“I can say and I can claim that that philosophy of judo was one of the key elements of me becoming successful,” he explained. “It rewires your mind, and you start to think very differently.”

Báthory still makes time to train and actively competes in tournaments to this day. He has also taken up jiujitsu and reports having black belts in both disciplines. But he is not only trying to be better in martial arts but for it as well. Judo is an Olympic sport, and athletes internationally are very committed to excelling in it. The American judo scene is not as prominent as it is in other countries, but Báthory is trying to change that and wants to help those Americans looking to compete in the 2028 Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles, California.

“I’ve worked with USA Judo and IJF (International Judo Federation). It’s one of my missions to make judo more visible in America, for more people to practice it.”

Báthory’s passion and commitment to his mission is more than moral support and advocacy. He has even made a financial commitment to this goal.

“I want the American team to do really well in judo. I’m even financially supporting the judo team. A portion of the tickets of this tour is actually going to USA Judo so they can afford the participation in training camps.”

Even though they have two decades behind them, 5FDP is as popular as ever, and tickets to their shows have already been selling fast. Like any elite band, they have had their shares of growing pains and critics, but the loyal fanbase and joy they get from creating music and performing it continues to fuel their desire.

Báthory has as much love and appreciation for their supporters as they do for the band. That’s because of the communities those fans are in; military, first responders, athletes, martial arts, and others who are looking for something positive to lean on. Báthory proclaimed that 5FDP will continue to make music and do their best to support their fans not only because they support them but because of what they do.

“What is the common denominator between these people? They all help other people.”

You can learn more about 5FDP, their tour, and Legacy by going to their website and subscribing to their YouTube channel.

Follow Báthory on Instagram @zoltanbathory and @zoltanbjj.

#8813. Texas A&M Study Shows Creatine Adding Muscle Mass Gains Without Lifting

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

For better brain cognition through to superior strength and power, creatine is one of those supplements that seems to actually work. Thanks to its cell volumizing and energizing abilities, creatine allows us to lift heavier, recover faster, and focus better under stress. Now, a new study from Texas A&M University is touting that creatine can construct more muscle even without a structured resistance training program.

The study, published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, suggests that creatine could help adults to maintain lean tissue and strength, even without regular exercise. Of course, maintaining adequate levels of muscle mass is particularly important as we age because muscle loss, also known as sarcopenia, can begin as early as 35 years, and typically sees lean mass decline at a rate of 1 to 2 percent, per year, for the average person. In fact, those who fail to engage with regular resistance training could lose as much as 4 to 6 pounds of muscle per decade.

New meta-analyses show this tried and true supp can benefit both men and women—but you still have to...

For 12 weeks, men and women between the ages of 45 and 65 were provided with creatine or a maltodextrin placebo, with each group being split into those who wanted to participate in a supervised, structured exercise program, and those who didn’t want to commit to the organized sessions. As the participants filled out questionnaires during the study, data showed that the structured exercise group racked up more moderate-to-vigorous activity than those who weren’t locked in.

Despite lower levels of activity, those who took two 5g doses of creatine per day, and were not in the structured exercise program, increased their lean tissue by around 2.4 pounds over the 12-week study period. Conversely, those who took the placebo lost almost half a pound. “Creatine Monohydrate supplementation without exercise training and diet intervention increased lean tissue mass, strength, and muscular endurance while promoting favorable changes in selected blood lipids, HbA1c, and selected markers of cognitive function and memory,” read the report.

The results on muscle mass were even more profound in the structured exercise group, however. Creatine users who undertook the supervised sessions gained 2.8 pounds of lean mass on average. Creatine was also shown to preserve muscle even under the conditions of fat loss, because participants in the exercise program were given a modest calorie deficit. After 12 weeks, this group had gained almost three pounds of lean tissue despite dropping fat, while the exercise group that took a placebo showed little change in lean tissue. Still, both the structured and non-structured groups, on creatine, saw a greater reduction in body fat percentage than that seen by exercise or diet alone.

“Creatine Monohydrate supplementation with and without exercise and diet intervention may help middle-aged and older adults maintain muscle mass and strength while favorably affecting selected markers of health and cognitive function,” concluded the study.

#8812. Once Was Enough for the NYC Marathon—Here’s Why I’ll Never Run It Again

Running the race tested my limits, revealed my grit, and brought me full circle with the city that shaped me.

Probably the most excruciating breath I’ve taken in my life was in Lenox Hill Hospital on East 77th Street. It was my first breath on Earth, and my lungs must have wondered what had hit them. Forty-three years later, it seemed fitting that I’d come back to you for another challenge to my lungs and body: my first marathon.

I have lots of memories of you, starting from those early years on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. Then there were holiday visits and sleepovers with my grandmother in Stuyvesant Town, special days in Dad’s office in Washington Heights, Mom’s gallery openings in the Village. There were the fits and starts of my early professional career when I lived in Brooklyn and then Alphabet City, using most of my paycheck for rent, the rest for food. And of course, after I moved away in my late 20s, when I’d see you a couple of times a month for work.

If I’m being honest, you’ve always been a bit of a headache and a challenge. Back when I was just starting out, I couldn’t tolerate your high prices and abrasive attitude, and your tendency to “never sleep.” Which is why I ditched you for a less exhausting life in the country. Even today, I stress out just thinking about seeing you.

But on an unseasonably warm November Sunday, NYC Marathon day, you challenged me more than ever before—and revealed a level of grit I didn’t know was in me.

On the Verrazzano Bridge, I was overcome with emotion at having made it to the starting line. Surrounded by scores of runners from all over the world, with the open waterway below and the iconic skyline in the distance, I felt like a part of something huge and meaningful. It literally brought tears to my eyes.

Running through Brooklyn, I was in a zone. I was able to stay on pace and hit the halfway mark in decent shape, so I forced a smile at the throngs of cheering spectators. I’ve never been one to smile during races, and even your generous Brooklynites couldn’t get me to light up a genuine grin.

Then came the 59th Street Bridge. Long Island City, with its dull stretches of low-slung warehouses, is perhaps one of your most charmless neighborhoods. Nothing against the spectators who did their best in the streets leading up to the bridge, but that endless, gradual incline in the eerie quiet with the wind blowing up off the East River is where I started to unravel.

The screaming wall of people on First Avenue did nothing to energize me. This is where I began to feel like perhaps a marathon is just too long a run to be considered a wise choice.

And, sorry. Even if the Bronx had welcomed me with confetti and a marching band, it wouldn’t have mattered. Once I got to the Willis Avenue Bridge, I regretted not bringing money or a MetroCard so I could duck out and just go home. With every step, my feet, my quads, my knees threatened imminent shutdown. Worse was the shivering that seemed to consume my whole body, like when you lie feverish in bed, begging for the Tylenol to kick in.

Harlem was a fleeting boost, lifting me up ever so briefly at Mile 22 with its gospel choir, its Jamaican ska, its salsa beat. New York, here is where you started to shine and where I started to believe in myself. Your Harlem spectators literally reached out their hands and told me, “You can do this” and “You look strong.” They warmed me with their smiles when my body was wracked with chills. They let me pet their Bernese Mountain Dog, a wagging gift of comfort when all I wanted was to curl up on the sidewalk. They watched me cry tears that were a strange mixture of homesickness, pride, and self-pity. And they saw me smile a genuine smile for the first time all day.

The high was short-lived, but that’s okay. Marathons are not meant to be easy. I had no illusions that I’d skip along Fifth Avenue with my arms in the air. But I was able to hold on to that smile, the one I picked up in Harlem, that was as real as I’ve ever smiled in a race. And friends told me later that I looked strong and was even passing other runners on that stretch just south of 110th Street.

Central Park made my head spin. It was so close to the finish, yet it felt like endless circles. I was ready to be done with you, New York. But you had other plans. After I crossed the finish line (at 4:44, roughly 15 minutes slower than my hoped-for time), you sent me into the arms of a mom-like volunteer named Kate on whose shoulder I blubbered and drooled and snotted until she led me into a medical tent where I collapsed in a shivering heap, and was caught by a dreadlocked medic named Ishmael with gentle eyes who covered me in woolen blankets and placed me next to a heater and fed me hot soup and salt and Gatorade until I could stand up again and hobble back to the hotel and my family and my peaceful life.

And though you raised the stakes in a big way, New York, that day, you made me grateful for the chance to prove to myself that I can do hard things. Even if we don’t see eye to eye, you helped make me who I am. I never believed I could run this distance, that I’d be up to the challenge. But looking back on our history, I’m pretty sure you knew I had it in me all along.

This article originally appeared in the Winter 2025 issue of Runner’s World.

Leah has been editing longform narrative stories for more than 20 years and currently directs features for Bicycling, Runner’s World, and Popular Mechanics. She conceived of and edited “12 Minutes and a Life” by Mitchell S. Jackson for Runner’s World that won both the 2021 Pulitzer Prize and the National Magazine Award for Feature Writing. She lives in eastern Pennsylvania.
