Let's make this concrete. You're planning a two-week Hawaii trip for two people. You've booked your Honolulu arrival flight separately, and now you need to connect the dots between islands: Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) mid-trip, and then Maui (OGG) to Lihue, Kauai (LIH) before heading home.

The cash price check: Pull up hawaiianairlines.com and look at what these tickets retail for. On a typical mid-trip travel day, the HNL→OGG segment is priced at $189 per person. The OGG→LIH hop runs $149 per person. For two travelers, that's $676 in cash — before you've bought a single plate of shave ice.

The points price: Each segment costs 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person in economy. Two passengers, two flights: 30,000 HawaiianMiles total, plus roughly $10–$20 in taxes and fees across both bookings. No fuel surcharges.

The CPP calculation: You're replacing $676 in cash spending with 30,000 miles. That's 2.25 cents per point — well above the 0.8–1.2 cpp you'd expect on typical HawaiianMiles redemptions, and solidly within the 1.3–3.3 cpp sweet spot range for this redemption.

What the experience looks like: Hawaiian's interisland product is no-frills — these are 20-to-40-minute flights on Boeing 717s. You won't get a meal or premium service. But you will get a reliable, on-time carrier, clean aircraft, and the undeniable satisfaction of hopping between two of the most beautiful island destinations on Earth without opening your wallet at the gate.

For the ChooseFI traveler, the win isn't the in-flight experience — it's the mental accounting shift. You budgeted for interisland flights; now that budget goes to a sunset sailing charter or a snorkeling excursion instead. The points paid for the planes. The cash funds the memories.

Do: Transfer Points in the Right Batch Size HawaiianMiles doesn't allow you to transfer partial miles back out, so calculate exactly how many you need before initiating a transfer. For two passengers on two flights, that's 30,000 miles. Transfer exactly that amount — or a small buffer — rather than dumping your entire MR balance into a program you may not use frequently.

Do: Use Amex MR or Bilt as Your Primary Earning Strategy Since HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, your accumulation plan should center on transferable currencies. The Amex Gold Card (4x on dining and groceries) and Amex Platinum (5x on flights) are elite MR earners. Bilt's no-annual-fee card earning on rent is underused by the ChooseFI community for exactly this kind of transfer.

Do: Search for Availability Before You Transfer This is worth repeating as a pro tip because new points travelers make this mistake constantly. Transfer speeds are 1–2 days for Amex MR and Bilt. Don't transfer points and then discover the flight you wanted is sold out. Always confirm availability first, then transfer, then book immediately once miles land.

Avoid: Using Marriott Bonvoy for This Transfer At a 3:1 ratio, you'd spend 22,500 Bonvoy points for a 7,500-mile award. Bonvoy points are worth approximately 0.7–0.9 cpp on their own best redemptions. The math doesn't hold here — save your Bonvoy points for hotel redemptions.

Do: Consider the Merger Context Hawaiian Airlines is in the process of merging with Alaska Airlines, and HawaiianMiles may eventually transition into Alaska Mileage Plan. Pay attention to program announcements. This could change transfer partners, award pricing, or program structure. The current sweet spot exists now — book it while the program operates under its current rules.

Avoid: Waiting for a 'Better' Redemption on These Miles HawaiianMiles are a limited-use currency. They're excellent for interisland and mainland-to-Hawaii flights, but they don't transfer to other airlines and don't unlock international business class sweet spots. If you've got miles in this program, use them for exactly what they're designed for — Hawaiian flights — rather than letting them sit hoping for a better opportunity that may never come.

Do: Book Multiple Segments in a Single Trip If you're doing a true multi-island itinerary, every interisland hop is 7,500 miles. Three islands means two hops — 15,000 miles per person. Plan your island sequence to minimize backtracking, and book all segments at once once your miles transfer.

Make multi-island trips affordable with the right points strategy

Most visitors to Hawaii stick to one island because interisland flights add $100-$400+ per person to the trip cost. By using points for these short hops, you unlock a fundamentally different Hawaii experience — island-hopping from Oahu to Maui to the Big Island to Kauai without the airfare costs stacking up. This is a multiplier strategy: you are not just saving on one flight, you are enabling an entirely different type of trip. Combining a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight with points-funded interisland hops creates a nearly free (in cash) multi-island Hawaiian vacation.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Decide which islands you want to visit and in what order. The most common combinations are Oahu + Maui, Oahu + Big Island, or a three-island itinerary. Map out how many interisland hops you need so you know the total points required.

Check Hawaiian Airlines (7,500 miles each way), Southwest (variable, typically 4,000-8,000 points), and United (5,000-7,500 miles) for each interisland segment. Southwest often offers the best flexibility with no change fees and no blackout dates.

For Hawaiian Airlines, transfer Amex Membership Rewards. For Southwest, earn Rapid Rewards directly or transfer from Chase (transfer to Southwest is currently limited). For United segments, transfer from Chase or use Turkish Miles&Smiles for even lower pricing.

Book each interisland hop as a separate one-way award. This gives you maximum flexibility to mix airlines and optimize pricing per segment. One-way awards have no penalty compared to round trips on these short routes.

Align your interisland hops with your arrival and departure flights. Arrive on one island and depart from a different one (open-jaw booking) to avoid backtracking. For example, arrive Honolulu, hop to Maui, depart Maui to the mainland.

Hawaiian Airlines has the most extensive interisland network and offers the most daily frequencies. Southwest Airlines also operates key interisland routes (Honolulu-Maui, Honolulu-Kona, Honolulu-Lihue). United flies select interisland segments as well. Each airline has different award pricing and transfer partner access.

Hawaiian Airlines interisland awards typically price at 7,500 HawaiianMiles each way. Southwest varies by cash fare but generally costs 4,000-8,000 Rapid Rewards points each way for interisland hops. United interisland segments can be booked for 5,000-7,500 miles using various Star Alliance partner programs.

Yes, especially when booking multiple hops. A family of four making two interisland hops at $150 each way would spend $1,200 in cash. Converting that to points frees up significant cash for accommodations, activities, and dining. The per-point value (1.5-2.5 cents) is reasonable, and the trip flexibility gained is substantial.

A popular strategy is to fly into Honolulu (Oahu), hop to Maui for beaches and Haleakala, then continue to the Big Island (Kona) for volcanoes and snorkeling, and optionally finish on Kauai for dramatic scenery. Each hop is 30-60 minutes. Allow 2-3 days minimum per island.

This redemption was built for families and couples planning a multi-island Hawaii vacation — full stop. If you're visiting multiple islands (which most Hawaii first-timers and repeat visitors do), you're already mentally budgeting for interisland flights. This sweet spot simply redirects that cash budget back into your pocket and replaces it with points.

Families get a 5/5 Family Friendly score here for good reason: availability is wide open, booking is simple, and the economics scale beautifully. Four people, two hops = 60,000 miles to cover potentially $1,200+ in interisland airfare. That's an extraordinary displacement of vacation cash.

Beginners are explicitly welcomed by this redemption's design. There's no partner airline complexity, no fuel surcharge math to calculate, no routing rules to decode. You search on Hawaiian's website, you transfer points, you book. The 5/5 Beginner Friendly and Easy to Book scores reflect that this is genuinely one of the simplest award redemptions you can execute.

Minimum points needed: 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person per segment. For a solo traveler doing two hops, that's 15,000 miles. For a family of four doing two hops, that's 60,000 miles.

This is NOT for: Travelers who don't have an Amex MR or Bilt account and no path to earning HawaiianMiles quickly. It's also not ideal for travelers who only need a single interisland flight — the opportunity cost of setting up the transfer relationship for 7,500 miles may not be worth it unless you're already accumulating MR points for other redemptions.

This redemption earns a **Beginner** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. In a world of waitlists, fuel surcharges, routing rules, and phone-only bookings, Hawaiian interisland awards are refreshingly clean. **What makes it easy:** Award availability is consistently excellent (5/5). The booking portal is functional and user-friendly. There are no fuel surcharges to calculate. Miles never expire, so there's no pressure. You can complete the entire redemption — from transfer initiation to confirmed booking — in about 48 hours. **The one genuine friction point:** Earning HawaiianMiles isn't as straightforward as earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex MR. Hawaiian doesn't have a widely-used co-branded credit card for most people's everyday spend. This means you're dependent on transfer partners, and the Amex MR and Bilt paths are your primary options. If you don't have either, this redemption becomes harder to access. **Tip 1:** Start with an Amex card that earns Membership Rewards — the Amex Gold is the ChooseFI community favorite for everyday earning. Once you're accumulating MR points, you have a direct path to Hawaiian via a 1:1 transfer. **Tip 2:** Always search award availability before transferring. It takes 30 seconds and protects you from the one mistake that could derail an otherwise smooth booking. **Tip 3:** Don't overthink the merger situation. Hawaiian and Alaska remain separate programs today. Book what's in front of you. If you can earn Amex MR points, you can execute this redemption. It's the perfect first award booking for a ChooseFI member who wants to see how the system works without risking complexity.

Interisland awards are the key that unlocks multi-island Hawaii vacations without the stacking airfare costs that keep most travelers on a single island. At 7,500-10,000 miles per hop, the points cost is modest, and the trip transformation is significant. Whether you use Hawaiian Airlines miles, Southwest Rapid Rewards, or United partner programs, the strategy is the same: let points handle the short hops so your cash stays in your pocket for experiences. Combined with a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight, interisland awards make a multi-island Hawaiian vacation one of the most achievable aspirational trips in travel rewards.

#8800. A 24-Year-Old Runner Died After a Medical Emergency in the Final Miles of the NYC Marathon

Rachel Apa was running her first marathon to raise money for Parkinson's research in memory of her grandfather.

Rachel Apa was nearing the end of her first New York City Marathon when she collapsed in Central Park on Sunday, November 1. The 24-year-old had spent months putting in the work needed to conquer 26.2 miles, but never made it across the finish line. Instead, she was taken to Mount Sinai Medical Center, where she died later that night.

Apa, a Bucknell University alum who lived in central Pennsylvania, came to New York to run with Parkinson's Foundation Champions, raising money in memory of her grandfather, who died from the disease in 2022.

According to reporting from The New York Times, the medical emergency happened around 1:30 p.m. close to Mile 24, around 85th Street, right as runners enter the final stretch through Central Park. Several spectators rushed to help and began performing CPR. New York Road Runners medical staff arrived shortly after, and tried to resuscitate her with a defibrillator before paramedics took her to the hospital.

Her parents had been keeping up with Rachel throughout the race as she made her way through the five boroughs, though from different locations. Michelle Apa, her mother, was in New York and watched Rachel run through Queens at Mile 14, while Steve Apa, her father, was back home in Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, following her progress through the marathon's tracking app.

Steve had been texting his daughter throughout the day. According to messages he shared with the Times, Rachel sent an "Ow" text at Mile 18, followed by a double "Ow ow" at Mile 19. She kept moving through the course, although her dad received no replies after that. As she reached Mile 23 on the app, Steve sent another message: "Final stretch." Rachel never responded.

Michelle eventually made her way to Central Park, reportedly arriving just as the ambulance carrying her daughter was leaving, per the Times. Doctors spent hours trying to save Rachel. Steve told the newspaper she was pronounced dead around 9:40 p.m.

"It's unfathomable," he told the newspaper. "Perfect health, perfect shape, 24 years old."

Steve told the Times that his daughter died from rhabdomyolysis, which occurs when damaged muscle tissue breaks down and releases substances into the bloodstream. The condition can cause serious kidney damage and, according to the Cleveland Clinic, can be triggered by extreme physical exertion.

An official cause of death had not been established as of Tuesday, November 3, with CBS New York reporting that the city's medical examiner was still investigating.

Sunday marked the marathon's first runner death following a medical incident since 2024, according to NYRR. The organization released a statement Monday:

"We are deeply saddened by the death of one of our runners following yesterday's race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with the runner's family, friends, and the entire running community."

Before the marathon, Apa explained her decision to run on her fundraising page, sharing how much her grandfather influenced her love of sports and why supporting the Parkinson's Foundation mattered to her.

"He taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement," she wrote.

Apa explained that watching him lose his mobility after his Parkinson's diagnosis had made her want to help others facing the disease. She wanted to use her first marathon to help others affected by it, raising money and awareness in the process “for research, better care, and a cure.”

As of 5 p.m. ET Tuesday, the page had exceeded her $4,000 goal, and reflected more than $28,000 in donations.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

On Episode 307 of The Menace Podcast, host Dennis James was joined by Milos Sarcev and Jose Raymond, and the panel compared the current era of competitive bodybuilders with those of the 90s. How would they stack up?

The 90’s was a decade where size dominated the stage. Often referred to as the “Mass Monster” era, stars like Dorian Yates, Lee Haney, and Ronnie Coleman reigned supreme. But how do current muscle men stack up against these icons of the past? Jose Raymond speculated that there may be a drop in quality in the 2020s, because IFBB Pro Cards are too easily won these days. “If you have to fight for a pro card, for seven to ten years, by the time you get it you’ll be ready,” said the bodybuilder-turned-coach. “And the physique is going to be already matured and marinated.”

Raymond felt that younger bodybuilder’s winning pro cards effects the overall talent pool. “The physique isn’t ready,” he said. “Most of today’s guys would not win a pro card in 1993, 1989.”

Agreeing with Raymond’s take, host Dennis James said that “90% of them, maybe even more than 90%,” would not win a pro card if competing in the ’90s. “You’ve got guys getting a pro card for second place,” added Raymond. “That’s crazy to me.”

To further cement this observation, Milos Sarcev explained that respected and revered bodybuilders of the past like Edgar Fletcher and Matt Mendenhall never even turned pro. “Edgar Fletcher would win pro shows today,” said Raymond. “One hundred percent,” agreed Sarcev.

The Menace further explained that there have been more than 70 athletes qualifying for Olympia categories, from a pool of around 500, although this is being tightened up in many divisions with the requirement to win two shows. So, perhaps restoring quality over quantity is the key to creating the best era.

To see this conversation in full on The Menace Podcast, where the panel also discussed the latest bodybuilding news and results, check it out on the Muscle & Fitness YouTube channel.

#8798. Barbell Grip Guide: How Hand Placement Optimizes Bench, Press, and Squat Form

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Grip sets the table for what comes next because where you place your hands affects wrist position, elbow path, shoulder comfort, stability, and often good form.

Your arm length, shoulder and wrist mobility, and training goal can all influence your grip. Grip is essential for rows, deadlifts, and curl variations, but for presses and squats we often ignore it.

However, paying special attention to it will pay dividends. The goal is to find a grip that makes the lift feel comfortable, strong, and minimizes discomfort.

Here, we’ll break down the best hand positions for the barbell bench press, overhead press, back squat, and front squat, including the grip options for each and how to decide which one fits you best.

We often only think about grip when it fails, but taking the time to set it often makes the difference between a good set and a bad one.

Let’s begin here. Your bench press grip affects wrist position, elbow path, range of motion, shoulder stress, and which muscles work hardest.

Where the Bar Should Sit: Start by placing the bar toward the heels of your palms. This keeps the bar stacked over your forearm and helps prevent wrist hyperextension. Think of your hand, wrist, and forearm as a unit. The better your forearm and wrist stack, the better your bench press.

Grip Width: Begin with your pinky finger wrapped around the barbell ring. This grip is the best starting point for most lifters. At the bottom of the rep, your forearms should be nearly vertical.

A wider grip shortens the range of motion and emphasizes the pecs, but it also moves the shoulder into greater abduction. That can feel strong for some but cranky for others.

A narrower grip increases range of motion and puts more demand on the triceps because the elbows stay closer to the torso and get a deeper stretch. Neither one is better or worse. It depends on comfort and your training goal.

Full Grip vs. False Grip: A full grip, with the thumb wrapped around the bar, gives you the best bar security and should be your default. However, a false grip (without the thumb) may provide more comfort for some lifters, but the tradeoff is less bar security.

How to Know Which Grip Is Best for You: Use the grip and choose the grip width that best balances shoulder comfort, wrist alignment, and stability.

Bar placement and grip width are vital for the barbell overhead press. Maintaining the wrist, forearm, and elbow stack will help you press with power without driving your upper-body joints mad.

Where the Bar Should Sit: The bar should sit toward the heel of the palm, not near the fingers. This places the load over the forearm and helps prevent wrist hyperextension, but some wrist extension in the OH press is normal. The goal is not to force the wrist straight, but to avoid letting the bar roll so far back that it becomes uncomfortable.

Grip Width: For most lifters, a grip just outside shoulder width is a good place to start. If it’s too wide, you shorten the range of motion and may lose leverage. If it’s too narrow, your elbows and shoulders can feel crowded at the bottom. From the front, your forearms should be close to vertical, with the elbows slightly in front of the bar.

Full Grip vs. False Grip: A full grip gives you the most security and should be the default for most lifters. A false grip can feel better for some people because it may reduce wrist bend. The tradeoff, again, is less bar security.

How to Know Which Grip Is Best for You: Use the grip that lets you start with a solid wrist position, keep the forearms vertical, and press without shoulder or elbow irritation.

Grip is secondary to the squat, but your hands secure the bar and help create upper-back tension while your back supports the load.

Use a False Grip: For the back squat, I prefer a false or thumbless grip, with the thumb resting on the same side of the bar as the fingers.

Why? It makes it easier to keep the wrist in line with the forearm instead of letting the wrist bend back under the bar. This helps prevent your hands from taking the load that should be on your back.

Grip Width: A narrower grip can increase upper-back tension by pulling the shoulder blades together and locking the bar in place. But narrower isn’t always better.

If you don’t have the shoulder mobility to reach that position, forcing your hands too close can irritate your wrists, elbows, or shoulders. Moving the hands slightly wider often gives you enough room to keep the wrists aligned while keeping the upper back tight.

How to Know Which Grip Width Is Best for You: Use the narrowest grip you can comfortably maintain while keeping:

If you’re getting wrist or inner-elbow soreness before you squat, widening the hands a little is the better solution.

The front squat gives you more grip options than the back squat because grip is secondary. The goal is to have the bar resting securely across the front of your shoulders while your hands support it.

There are three practical ways to do that.

The best front-squat grip keeps the bar secure, your elbows high, and your torso upright without causing unnecessary discomfort. There’s no need to force-feed one grip when you have options.

Here are the key points to pay attention to with barbell squats and presses.

Does it improve joint alignment? Your wrists, elbows, and shoulders should feel natural and not engaged in a game of Twister.

Does it reduce pain or irritation? A grip that bothers your wrists, elbows, or shoulders is worth changing. Adjust your grip width, switch from a full grip to a false grip, or try a different front-squat setup to fix it.

Are you stronger with it? If one grip gives you better control and lets you get after it without sacrificing technique, then go with that.

Can you maintain the intended range of motion? If your grip shortens your range of motion or forces you into bad lifting positions, it probably needs adjusting.

The key is to make small changes and judge them by how the whole lift feels and performs. A good grip should increase stability and express strength, not add another thing to fight against.

Your grip should make the lift better, not give you another problem to solve.

Paying attention to joint alignment and discomfort before you lift puts you in the best position to succeed. So don’t be afraid to adjust if you’ve been told to grip a certain way; a small grip change can improve comfort, stability, and strength more than most lifters expect.

#8796. XWERKS Motion BCAA Review (2025): A Registered Dietitian’s Honest Thoughts

Written by Perry Nix, MS, RD, LD Last updated on Dec 18, 2023

Your gym bag is probably packed with some of the best supplements for building muscle, including protein powder, creatine, and pre-workout. Crucial for boosting energy and strength during a gym session and reducing muscle soreness afterward, you wouldn’t dare train without them. But imagine a single supplement that combines the benefits of all three.

Enter XWERKS Motion — an innovative supplement formulated to enhance endurance during intense exercise and support a quick post-workout recovery. Sounds too good to be true? We’ll find out in this XWERKS Motion review.

Our team of personal trainers, CrossFit coaches, nutrition experts, and competitive weightlifters shared their feedback on the formulation, price, taste, and solubility of this one-of-a-kind product. As a registered dietitian nutritionist, I’ll do a deep dive into the ingredients and potential health benefits of XWERKS Motion, so you know if it’s worth adding to your supplement stack.

Medical disclaimer: This article is intended for educational and informational purposes only. It is not intended as a substitute for medical advice. For health advice, contact a licensed healthcare provider.

Our Breaking Muscle product testing team has tried nearly 20 of the best BCAA supplements, gaining a thorough understanding of what meets customer standards and what falls short. Here’s how our expert testers rated the following categories after trying XWERKS Motion themselves.

In this XWERKS Motion review, we’ll explore the product’s cost, formula, flavors, taste, and more. We’ll include honest, reliable feedback straight from our Breaking Muscle expert testers, so you’ll know exactly what to expect from this supplement. With transparency in mind, we include the good and not-so-good aspects of XWERKS Motion to give you the full picture.

In comparison, Transparent Labs BCAA Glutamine costs $1.33 per serving, while Jacked Factory BCAA Powder is available at $0.67 per serving at the time of this writing. XWERKS Motion is on the pricier side, earning this category a 3.5 out of 5, but also contains ingredients not found in most other BCAA supplements.

XWERKS Motion is thoughtfully and originally formulated, earning it a 4 out of 5. It is unlike other BCAA supplements in that it contains 25 grams of cluster dextrin carbohydrates, also known as highly branched cyclic dextrin (HBCD). Cluster dextrin passes through the stomach into the intestines rapidly, where it can be absorbed into the bloodstream and taken up into muscle cells to replenish glycogen content and provide a quick energy source. (1)

Human studies suggest that when used before or during a workout, cluster dextrin carbs may decrease perceived exertion and enhance endurance when compared to maltodextrin and glucose, especially when prior carb intake is low. (1) However, those who eat plenty of carbs may not experience any added benefits when supplementing cluster dextrin.

In addition to carbs, each serving offers three grams of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). The product contains the BCAA ratio 2:1:1 of leucine, isoleucine, and valine. BCAAs are essential amino acids (EAAs), meaning you must consume them because the body doesn’t synthesize them on its own. Leucine is often thought of as the king of BCAAs because it activates muscle protein synthesis, which is necessary for muscle growth and recovery. (2)

Other active ingredients include calcium, magnesium, and sodium. During exercise, you lose electrolytes through sweat that need to be replenished. The electrolytes in XWERKS Motion help prevent dehydration and maintain proper muscle function during a workout.

Enhanced with natural flavors, sucralose, and citric acid, this product contains ingredients that add sour and sweet notes.

Sucralose is an artificial sweetener considered safe when consumed in moderation. Unlike table sugar, most research shows sucralose has little to no effects on blood sugar levels or insulin. (3) However, some animal studies suggest it could disrupt healthy gut bacteria and increase inflammation when consumed long-term, but more human studies are needed. (4)

You won’t have any difficulty picking a flavor if you choose to try XWERKS Motion, considering there is only one option available — Raspberry Lemonade. Obviously, if you prefer to stick with one flavor on repeat this won’t be a problem. For those who like to switch things up, the lack of variety may leave you feeling bored, hence the middle-of-the-road rating on flavor.

Luckily, the Raspberry Lemonade flavor delivers. Our expert tester was more than pleased with the taste of the raspberry lemonade supplement, rating it an impressive 5 out of 5. She noticed hints of the tart lemonade with a more robust berry flavor overall. The supplement wasn’t too sweet and had a very refreshing taste to it. Our tester even went as far as to say that she could happily sip on this drink all day.

Another winning category of XWERKS Motion is solubility, which our tester rated a perfect 5 out of 5. She didn’t experience any clumping, grittiness, floaties, or difficulty mixing — a feature you’ll want when drinking it at the gym or on the go. Because the cluster dextrin in this product is highly soluble in water, it dissolves easily and forms a smooth, uniform mixture. Several customer reviews on the XWERKS website rave about the product’s superior solubility, mentioning it “blends so smooth” and is “easy to mix.”

Cluster dextrin is believed to be safe for consumption, with no apparent safety concerns. (5) Our product tester didn’t experience any adverse side effects during her use of this product. As for beneficial effects, she didn’t notice any superhuman strength or noticeable bursts of energy, but she did feel good during longer lifting sessions.

Switching gears, BCAAs are considered safe when consumed in appropriate dosages. It’s best to adhere to the suggested dosage instructions on the product label for optimal safety and effectiveness.

Nevertheless, always consult with your healthcare provider before adding a new dietary supplement to your routine, particularly if you have pre-existing medical conditions or are currently taking prescribed medications. This precaution ensures that the supplement aligns with your individual health needs and won’t pose any risks or interactions.

All of the above considered, XWERKS Motion gets a 4 out of 5 rating for the lack of side effects from its formulation.

Unfortunately, there’s no mention of third-party testing on the XWERKS Motion product page, which is why we gave it a 1 out of 5.

We always encourage consumers to consider supplements that are third-party tested, because it serves as a quality control measure, ensuring that products are safe, effective, and meet certain regulatory requirements. Third-party testing enhances transparency and builds consumer trust by verifying that high-quality products contain what’s on the label and don’t include harmful levels of heavy metals or contaminants.

XWERKS Motion and XTEND Original BCAA powder have both commonalities and differences. To start, both products contain BCAAs and electrolytes to enhance muscle recovery, reduce muscle soreness, and maintain hydration.

However, that’s where their similarities end. While XTEND Original BCAA powder doesn’t contain any carbohydrates, XWERKS Motion contains 25 grams of cluster dextrin carbs for extra energy and prolonged endurance.

XTEND Original BCAA powder also has a much higher BCAA content of seven grams, compared to the three grams in XWERKS Motion. The Original BCAA powder even contains a whopping three and a half grams of leucine, exceeding the recommended two to three grams per day to maximize muscle-gaining capabilities. (2) The same can’t be said for the leucine content of XWERKS Motion.

Customers on the XWERKS website give Motion a 4.4 out of 5-star rating. There are only 35 reviews on the product page. Motion is not available on Amazon at the time of writing.

One happy customer says, “Great taste! No issues with digestion, gives you the fuel needed during most intense workouts.” Another customer says, “It mixes well, I like the flavor, and have no digestive or other issues. Performance-wise I feel great. I feel more energetic during my workouts and that I’m getting more out of them.”

Reviews from customers who were less pleased with the product were written over a year ago, and the formulation and flavors may have changed. One customer says, “I’m not sold on this product. I don’t really notice any difference on the days I take this. Also, it takes a blender to get this stuff mixed! That’s a deal breaker for me.” Other customers complain of the grape flavor, which is no longer available.

XWERKS Motion provides a synergistic blend of cluster dextrin carbs, BCAAs, and electrolytes to support endurance and recovery during and after a workout. Those who enjoy leisurely activity and consume enough carbs to sustain their energy levels may not benefit from this product.

However, it might be worth it for endurance athletes and bodybuilders with high training loads. Taking XWERKS before, during, or after intense physical activity may reduce perceived effort, extend the time to exhaustion, and decrease muscle soreness.

You can consume BCAAs pre, post, or intra-workout depending on your fitness goals. Some prefer to take BCAAs before or during a workout to provide their muscles with amino acids to help prevent muscle protein breakdown. Others like to take BCAAs post-workout to support muscle repair and recovery.

If you eat a whole-food diet high in protein, then you likely consume enough amino acids and may not experience further benefits by supplementing them. If you struggle to eat enough protein, BCAAs may support endurance, helping you train at a higher intensity for longer. Additionally, BCAAs may reduce muscle damage and DOMS post-workout.

BCAAs are a group of three EEAs—leucine, isoleucine, and valine— that must be consumed through the diet. They get their name from their unique molecular structure. While all EAAs are important, BCAAs are thought to play an important role in protein synthesis, muscle recovery, and preventing loss of lean mass.

BCAAs may provide an extended feeling of energy and delay the onset of muscle fatigue, enabling you to work out longer. Moreover, BCAAs might diminish muscle damage, inflammation, and DOMS post-workout. Lastly, BCAAs may aid in preserving lean muscle mass during periods of fat loss, contributing to weight loss efforts.

There are no official recommended daily requirements for BCAAs. The suggested sweet spot for leucine intake is often cited as two to three grams per day to optimize muscle building. (2) Avoid exceeding the recommended serving size on the product label. If you take protein powder or eat a high-protein diet, BCAA supplements likely won’t provide added benefits.

Perry Nix, the owner of The Free RD, is a registered dietitian and freelance nutrition writer. Her passion is breaking down complex nutrition information into bite-sized pieces that are easy to digest and apply. With experience in corporate wellness, public health, and clinical dietetics, Perry has crafted engaging nutrition content for a variety of health-conscious audiences. She resides with her husband and two boys in Texas and enjoys hiking and traveling.

#8795. Here’s How to Train From Now Through the New Year to Maintain Your Hard-Earned Marathon Fitness

A run coach and an exercise physiologist break down the weekly mileage and workouts you need to preserve your speed, strength, and endurance.

You’ve spent months training for your fall marathon, so the thought of losing that hard-earned fitness after race day probably stings. But at the same time, you can’t simply continue logging miles and workouts like you’re in race mode. Trying to stay razor-sharp year-round can lead to injury and burnout; your body needs rest after training for peak fitness.

So, instead, put your marathon fitness on ice. Freeze the adaptations you’ve gained and the endurance you’ve built. Then, you can pick up where you left off on, say, January 1, or whenever it’s time to lock back in for a spring marathon.

If you train right in the weeks between now and the new year, you won’t feel like you’re rebuilding fitness from scratch. Instead, you’ll preserve the key aerobic, muscular, and endurance adaptations you’ve worked so hard to develop.

To do that, we explain the minimum miles you need for maintenance and how speed, strength, and cross-training keep you in prime condition. Expect to return to race training feeling well-rested, confident, and ready to tackle another marathon cycle this spring.

In the first two weeks immediately following your marathon, you’ll want to focus more on rest and easy time-based jogging. Once you’ve recovered, however, you can return to tracking your miles more closely.

The bare minimum mileage you’ll need to maintain will vary from runner to runner, Heather Milton, CSCS, a clinical exercise physiologist and cofounder of Master My Run, tells Runner’s World. Much of it depends on how many miles you regularly put in over the weeks of your marathon training cycle.

“Science does not give us an exact number of what percentage of your marathon volume to decrease to that still allows you to maintain the same amount of aerobic fitness,” Milton explains. From her coaching experience, however, she’s found this number is likely around 50 percent of a runner’s typical weekly mileage.

David Hall, an RRCA- and USATF-certified run coach and founder of Running Coach CT, agrees. When planning his athletes’ schedules for the off-season, he looks at their typical running volume during marathon training and reduces their weekly mileage to no less than half. Every fourth week, however, mileage can drop to as low as 20 percent of their average to help facilitate recovery.

“A runner who was running 60 miles per week during their marathon build could definitely cut that in half,” Milton says. Or, take a runner who averaged around 40 miles per week. This individual could reduce their weekly mileage to 20, add in some cross-training, and expect to maintain much of their progress.

In fact, Milton adds, every runner can benefit from incorporating more of those cross-training sessions in the off-season. “Other forms of exercise can decrease the repetitiveness of the running motion and help you develop more well-rounded fitness, so I do prefer more variety from cross-training in the down-season,” she explains.

At the same time, Milton wants people to do the exercise they enjoy and, of course, runners love running. “I have to be reasonable about what a runner is willing to do and what keeps them healthy while they’re doing it,” she says. If you want to keep running four days per week in the off-season, that’s still workable—with one important caveat: You need to prioritize strength training.

When you’re in the thick of marathon training, running is your main focus. So while you’re still doing strength work during this time, it mostly helps maintain the strength you already have, rather than increase it, Milton explains. The off-season provides an ideal time to really build up and strengthen your muscle mass and bone health as much as possible.

Each week, Milton says to aim for two to three resistance training sessions that focus on heavier weights with a low to moderate number of reps. (You can do more than three weekly sessions as long as you’re not working the same muscle groups two days in a row.) This sets you up for a stronger return to your spring training cycle because it helps improve running economy, your overall neuromuscular health, and your fast-twitch muscle fibers, which help power you through fast bursts of running or hill climbing.

“Plus, when you start training for your next marathon, you’ll be in a stronger position to increase your running volume again because you’ve strengthened all of the areas of your body that were impacted by your previous race, which can help prevent injuries,” Milton adds.

During the off-season, you certainly don’t need to run every day to maintain your fitness. In fact, you can preserve key fitness markers—such as your VO2 max—with as little as three workouts per week.

“The goal is to maintain at least three to four aerobic days per week to maintain your fitness level,” says Milton. You can opt to run as little as once per week, as long as you continue to cross-train on the remaining days, she adds.

Aim for 30 to 60 minutes of whichever aerobic exercise you most enjoy—hit the gym for the elliptical or indoor pool, or get outside for skiing and cycling.

Similarly, the number of running days per week for Hall’s athletes varies, but many have success with three because it allows more time for strength and flexibility work. He also adds a second rest day to the schedules of his runners who typically train six days per week during a marathon block. But in both cases, consistency is crucial—you don’t want to go a week without doing anything. “Do something every other day at a minimum to stay active,” Hall says.

One of your runs each week should be a bit longer than the others, but it doesn’t need to match the lengths of your true marathon long runs. Milton typically recommends a long run between five and 13 miles, depending on the individual’s training volume.

If you don’t want to worry about tracking mileage in the off-season, that’s fine, too. Running for time instead of miles provides the same endurance benefits, Hall says. Around four weeks postmarathon, his athletes will typically start with one-hour long runs. “Then, they’ll go up to 75 minutes, then to 90 minutes, and then maybe up to an hour and 45,” he explains.

Over several weeks, this gradual progression sets his runners up with a solid base to build from when they start their spring marathon training. “But don’t push the pace,” he emphasizes. “These are easy, conversational efforts.”

Whether you run for time or miles, make sure you’re not increasing either too quickly. “Keep the same rules in mind as when you’re building mileage in marathon training,” Milton says. “Aim to increase by no more than 10 percent each week.” Recent research suggests that, to reduce injury risk, you can apply this rule to the distance of any single run, as well.

What does this look like in practice? Let’s say a runner is doing five aerobic sessions per week, which includes about 20 miles of running. Two are cross-training days and the remaining three are running days. They might choose to run three to five miles one day, five to seven miles another day, and then five to 13 miles for their long run. You also don’t need to increase distance as quickly as you would in marathon training, Milton explains.

Over three weeks, she says a runner might balance their mileage as follows:

Week 1: 4 miles, 6 miles, 10 milesWeek 2: 5 miles, 6 miles, 9 milesWeek 3: 3 miles, 7 miles, 11 miles

In the four weeks immediately following your marathon, don’t worry about fast workouts or hitting paces, says Hall. During those first two weeks postrace, he advises his athletes to go for 20- to 30-minute daily walks. In the third and fourth weeks, he reintroduces easy running and a touch of speed.

“The general rule I apply is: no hard running for the number of days that’s equal to the number of miles in the race. So for a marathon, we’re talking about 30 days of walking and conversational effort running—maybe dipping into tempo pace a bit—but certainly nothing above lactate threshold.”

After that time, Hall says runners can start to add back intensity. In fact, he encourages it, suggesting you incorporate either a 20-minute run at threshold pace or an interval session for the same amount of time. He also recommends alternating one mile at your threshold pace, followed by one minute of easy jogging or brisk walking, until you reach 20 minutes.

“Training at lactate threshold pace can make conversational effort feel easier and can help you run faster while still remaining mostly in an aerobic zone,” Hall explains. In other words, your body adapts so running at any pace starts to feel like it requires less work.

Another way to get in some speed during the winter season? Sign up for a holiday race like a Turkey Trot or Jingle Bell Jog, he says. “It can get boring if all you do is train. Racing a 5K keeps the interest alive and lets you put in a hard effort.” Keep in mind, though, you did just run a marathon, so you don’t need to race all out or cross the finish line with a PR.

According to both Hall and Milton, the golden rule that will help you maintain your hard-earned gains is consistency. Once you’ve recovered physically and mentally from 26.2, get back into a routine that keeps you moving. “Doing something is always better than doing nothing,” Hall says—because you can lose 8 percent of your VO2 max in four to six weeks if you pull the plug on activity completely.

Similarly, you’ll want to avoid “stop-and-go” training. “If you’re running two to four days per week, keep running two to four days per week, every week—within reason, because life gets in the way sometimes,” Milton says. But running 30 miles one week, doing nothing for three weeks, and then trying to get back into it can lead to a real struggle, she adds.

As long as you do your best to stay consistent—and don’t stress when the holidays, travel, or other engagements inevitably interfere—you’ll find your fitness quite close to where you left it after your fall marathon. All that’s left for you to do? Thaw it out with a fresh marathon training cycle this spring.

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#8794. Frugal Man Buys $52,000 Car – Why??

As I type this, I’m jumping through the various hoops involved in buying a 2023 Tesla Model Y, a rather expensive, luxury “crossover” that is absolutely loaded to the gills with excess: all wheel drive, faster acceleration than a Lamborghini, enough space for seven people and enough computer gadgetry to function as a small Google data center.

Update: Looking for the ongoing tracker page? It’s here at “The Model Y Experiment“

The total net cost of this thing to me after all the taxes and tax credits* will be about $52,000, which is just a stunning amount higher than the Honda van it is replacing. That old classic cost me $4500 when I bought it off of Craigslist twelve years ago, and it had served me dutifully until just last month, crisscrossing the mountains and deserts of this country and also helping to rebuild a considerable swath of houses in my neighborhood.

I’m supposed to be a frugality-oriented financial blogger, and I’m also known for hating car culture – I think most people use cars about ten times more often than they need to, and most people drive cars they can’t afford. So why the hell am I buying a new one?

From those first three paragraphs, you can see I’m feeling plenty of self-mockery and ridicule over this new purchase. If you’re also a naturally frugal person, you can surely relate to the thoughts and you probably also agree with me that I’m off my rocker.

And indeed, I’m still on-board with frugality and healthy self mockery. After all, it was this overall life philosophy that earned me an early retirement 18 years ago, which provides all of the glorious freedom I enjoy now.

It was also the philosophy that allowed me to procrastinate on buying this expensive car for the last four years, even as countless people both close to me and out on the Internet egged me on and told me I should just loosen up and treat myself.

But there’s a classic slogan that applies to many areas of life, and it is something I like to dig up and ponder every now and then:

How does that piece of wisdom apply to frugal living and enjoying a long life of early retirement?

A quick story from a recent run to the grocery store will explain:

I was standing there in the bakery aisle, hoping to restock with a loaf of Dave’s Killer Bread for the next day’s breakfast with some visiting friends. But since this was in a standard grocery store rather than the Costco where I usually shop, the damned stuff was priced at an eye-watering $6.99 per loaf (instead the $4.50 or so I’m accustomed to paying, and even at the bulk store this stuff is about double the price of normal bread).

“WHO THE HELL DO YOU THINK YOU ARE, TRYING TO SELL BREAD FOR SEVEN BUCKS!!!”

Then I went through a whole mental battle of what I call Grocery Shopping With Your Middle Finger:

“Hmm I wonder if any of the other competing brands are any good?”

“What else is a good substitute for bread for this breakfast?”

And then thankfully, after exhausting all other mental options, I settled on the correct one:

“Because you are never going to wake up in the future and look at your bank account and think, shit, if only I had an extra $2.49 in there I would be a happier person.”

That night, I came home from the store and shared this funny tale with one of my guests. He understood perfectly because he too had earned his own retirement through a lifetime of grinding in tough jobs and disciplined frugality. And despite the fact that he has a net worth several times higher than mine, he admitted that he faces exactly the same mental battles over splurging on himself.

This same friend gives freely to charitable causes, has supported a local school for decades, and is always the first one to pull out the checkbook if a friend has hit hard times or is looking for a trusted business investor.

But he still has trouble bringing himself to take an Uber to the airport instead of riding the bus which takes an hour longer.

We both realized that we were being too cheap with ourselves, and we needed to work on it. And we came up with a set of three ideas that should hopefully work together to help us have more fun with our life savings, while we are still alive:

Principle #1: The Minimum Spending Budget:

Suppose you’ve done well over the years and amassed a pile of productive investments worth about two million dollars. Yes, this is a lot of money for most people, and that is the point: this hypothetical person truly has it made.

But as it turns out, most Mustachians I know with this level of wealth are still living very efficient lives, usually with a spending level of under $40,000 per year. On top of that, they typically live in a mortgage-free house and still have various forms of side income from a small business or two.

The 4% rule tells us that this person should be fairly safe spending up to about $80,000 per year from that cozy nest egg, even if they never earn any other money.

If this person wanted to be ridiculously conservative and set the spending rate at 3%, that still leaves about $60,000 of fun money every single year.. Plus, again, any side income, future inheritances, and social security income only add to the surplus.

Thus, a reasonable minimum spending level for this person might be $60,000 per year.

And in most cases, they know this, but still go right on living on $40k or less and claim they have everything they could ever want.

But if you watch carefully you’ll still catch them firing up the middle finger at things like $6.99 Dave’s bread or the $14.00 Cabernet at the restaurant or driving around in a gas guzzler even when they would prefer to have a proper, modern electric car.

And whenever these people do get extra money, their first instinct is to stash it away on top of the already-too-big pile.  In diagram form, their money flow looks like this:

Note that while this person is great at accumulating money through that big red arrow firing money back into the ‘stash, their “fun stuff” arrow appears quite flaccid and withered.

Principle #2 – the Dedicated Money Wasting Account

Lifelong habits are hard to break, and it’s sometimes hard to “waste” your own hard-earned money on things that seem frivolous, even when you know intellectually that you have way more money than you’ll ever spend.

But have you ever noticed that if you are spending somebody else’s money, preferably an anonymous corporation, it feels different?

For example, when you’re on a business trip and you just show up at the dining table to eat and drink and you never see the bill, you probably don’t fret about the prices, right?

The key is to make your own money feel like somebody else’s, and you can do it like this:

Principle #3 – The Splurge Accountability Buddy

Many of us frugal people tend to stick together. And most of us have different versions of the same problem: we know logically that money is plentiful these days, but our emotions keep us stuck in our old ways of optimizing too much.

But I find that when I team up with local friends who are actually trying to battle these same habits, we can question each other’s decisions, call out cheapness when we see it, and cheer on splurges when we know the other guy would enjoy it.

My super wealthy friend from above has become much better about treating himself (and his family) to quality goods for the home, amazing trips together, and just a general reduction in his stress over being “efficient with money”

My friend and HQ co-owner Carl (Mr. 1500 Days) has finally replaced his beaten-down minivan with a spiffy new Chevrolet Bolt electric car, and is loving that leap into the future.

And of course Mr. Money Mustache, after squeezing one final mountain road trip out of his 23-year-old Honda van, is finally allowing himself to get the Tesla he has been talking about for half a decade.

A recent life change (becoming a co-owner of a fixer-upper vacation rental compound in beautiful Salida Colorado) has reignited the travel fire in my heart and made me realize how much I do love getting out to distant places for visiting, mountain biking, gathering with groups of friends and my favorite activity of all: Carpentourism.

Running the Numbers: how ridiculously expensive is this car?

This is the perfect start to my experiment in spending more. Realistically, a $50,000 car is going to cost me about $10,000 more per year than my old van was burning.  With the biggest costs being these:

Since I personally had a spending deficit of several times more than $10k per year, I figure this is a solid first step. And, since the car’s primary purpose is things like epic camping trips, dream dates, and  long adventures around the country, it will definitely help me spend more on experiences, hotels, and go out to dinner a bit more often as well.

“This Privileged Rich Folk Talk is Making Me Sick, why don’t you give your money away to charity, or to me?”

In general, I agree: the world has problems and the richer you are, the more you should consider giving generously.

But also, to be honest, the whiny people who constantly send complaints like this out to strangers on the Internet really need to get a life. It’s great to encourage philanthropy through positive examples, but completely unproductive to send negativity to shame people you don’t even know for not following your own personal value system. The world has seen more than enough of this.

On top of that, this one-sided thinking can be counterproductive. Both of my friends have given generously throughout their lifetimes. In my own case, I have donated over $500,000 to the best causes I could find during the years I’ve been writing this blog, but I was still refusing to let myself replace that 23-year-old van.

And that overthinking was leading to even more of a scarcity mentality, as I compared my own meager spending to these bigger numbers of my donations, and found myself thinking things like,

“Damn, I’m spending $100 on this dinner date which sounds like a lot, but I also spent ONE THOUSAND TIMES more on donations last year, which sounds like even more. Maybe I am spending too much and need to cut back on EVERYTHING!”And then the fear side of my brain would illogically chime in: “Yeah and you’re going to make us run out of money and be poor forever! waaaah waaaah! Cut back and optimize and conserve!”

Yes – be a super, duper responsible steward of your life savings.

And yes, give generously with all your heart to charity.

But yes, it’s also okay to set aside a portion of the money you’ve earned, for frivolous spending on yourself and those closest to you. You’re not a bad person for having a few nice things.

It’s okay to pay that extra hundred bucks to sit a bit closer to the front of the airplane instead of the back if it helps you enjoy your vacation and spend a joyful half hour walking FREE at your destination while the 49 rows of people behind you fuss infuriatingly with their shit in the overhead bins.

It’s okay to buy the frozen berries at Whole Foods even though they cost eight times more than Costco charges, if it spares you from making a second unpleasant trip through parking lot hell.

And as for me, I am calling it okay to, at last, double flip the Autopilot stalk in my new Tesla and lean back as it it shoots me gracefully through even the highest mountain passes, forever leaving the desperately underpowered wheezing and gear shifting and noise* of the gasoline era behind, forever.

I ended up using an online car salvage service called Peddle*, at the recommendation of a friend. With about five minutes of entering the details of my old Honda, their system offered me $715, and then a towtruck came and took it the next day – and actually gave me the payment in cash, which I found kind of fun. I made a point of using all of that money for splurges like dinners out, in keeping with the theme of this article.

* I later signed this blog up for Peddle’s affiliate program so that link will benefit MMM if you use it.

* A useful tip for more effective splurging:Try to find the truly negative aspects of your life and focus any additional spending on improving those things. But it’s a subtle art so you have to get it right if you want lasting results in happiness.

You don’t want to just reduce hardship or challenge like hiring someone to take care of every aspect of your house, because overcoming daily hardships and having significant accomplishments provides the very core of our life satisfaction.

You also don’t want to just upgrade the things that are already good in your life. For example, a friend of mine is a gourmet coffee expert, and he suggested that I upgrade my setup at home to include on-the-spot roasting, and fancy grinding and brewing equipment. But I already love the good quality coffee I buy off the shelf from Costco, so it would be counterproductive to invest time or money into changing this part of my life.

But when you have something that causes you regular angst and stress, whether it’s a leaky roof that makes you dread rain, or a long commute that makes you dread the daily traffic jam, or a body that is giving you trouble due to not being in the best of shape – those types of things are probably a good target for improvement.

In the case of my car situation, I had a Nissan Leaf which is wonderful to drive, but doesn’t have the range to travel anywhere outside of the Denver metro area. Then I had the van which is a clunky beast to drive, but is otherwise an amazing road tripper because I could bring along whatever and whoever I wanted. But the van was getting increasingly unreliable in several hard-to-fix ways which was making me nervous every time I thought about long distance travel. Which was causing me to avoid certain trips and miss positive lifetime experiences.

In other words, my lack of a reliable long-range car was a small but consistent source of negative stress.

Finally, Vanna gave me the gift of a final hot and smelly transmission failure on a mountain pass on the way home from my new project in Salida. It was just the nudge that I needed. And now I already feel excitement rather than dread at the prospect of all the road trips in the coming decades!

In that case, you might be interested in the Tesla Model 3 RWD, which uses only LFP – Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries (no cobalt and also no nickel). There are a few other advantages to this battery type as well, including even longer lifespan.

In the future, most cars will be using either LFP or Sodium-ion or other new chemistries based on even cheaper, more abundant minerals. But for now, even the cobalt content does not outweigh the benefits of avoiding oil consumption (which as you know also has a long history as a conflict mineral even before you consider the pollution)

Ok, onto the Tesla. We all know you and many others have been very taken by the oversized electric golf carts. I went and drove a bunch of them myself in an effort to first find something I liked and then do the due diligence to justify a purchase. Do I sound like an engineer? Understandable with all the money I spent becoming one. In the end, I drove just about every EV, so I know the plusses and minuses of many of them. I will say that completely outside of the type of car, Elon has the absolute best way to buy a car. Go online, pick what you want, put in your deposit and wait till it’s ready. No listening to “What can I do to get you in a car today?” from some punk kid at a dealership. But in the end, I had to rely on math. What would it cost for ME to drive an EV of my choice. Well, I’d have to modify that to say the most efficient EV because to me the Audi e Tron GT was levels above every other EV I drove in luxury, quality and feeling more like a car with an electric drive system than an electric motor in tupperware. So the catch for me is that I live in a high electric rate area with wonderful total cost per kWh of 45.5 cents. And I’m seeing gas at the cheapo, competing gas stations for $2.89 per gallon on my way to the used tool store. My daily driver is a 2019 Subaru Crosstrek manual that gets 35 mpg in the summer. Note that ICE cars do worse in the winter because we have “winter gas” but also EVs do even more worse in winter temperatures. So in the end, a Tesla Model 3 single motor (the most efficient EV on the planet) calculates out to cost about 2 cents a mile MORE than my pedestrian Subaru that I bought new for $22k. So unless I’m looking to look like Richie Rich with a new Audi Electromobile, I can’t justify the thought of going electric. I’ll back up a second and admit that you people in like Texas who get electricity for 4 cents a kWh should absolutely look at EVs. But I don’t have that luxury. And gas is cheap here. And I like my car quite a lot with it’s utility, all wheel drive so I don’t have to trump up my driveway in the snow (it’s a steep hill that no 2 wheel drive can get up in snow) and I get fun from rowing gears. So my recommendation for anyone considering an EV is to DO THE MATH. the end.

Based on what I’ve read about happiness, humans are generally terrible about figuring out what will make us happy. However, we’re actually very good at identifying things that are making us unhappy; also, unhappiness vs happiness is not a 1:1 comparison (more like 5:1, I believe).

Therefore, eliminating those things that make us unhappy is a logical, sensible and efficient strategy.

For many of us, jobs are the number one cause of dramatic unhappiness, because of the opportunity cost (i.e. time we could be spending on other things we value more), but also stress, commuting, and lack of freedom over our own destiny, etc. So FIRE is the first priority, because that has, by far, the most impact on happiness for most of us. (It’s not the only consideration though, because it takes years to achieve, so the journey matters a lot too).

Once that is achieved, the next steps are going to look very different for everyone, because everyone is different. Many for someone, that’s cutting their own lawn, so they hire someone. For someone else, they hate baking bread, so they buy it pre-made.

Around my house, we refer to it as, “throwing money at the problem”. I detest working on cars, so I always take them to our trusted mechanic. However, I like (or at least don’t mind) carpentry, plumbing, electrical, etc, so I do almost all of that work myself.

MMM identified something that was negatively impacting his level of happiness/life satisfaction, determined the cost to fix it (vs doing other things with that money, because everything is balancing cost/benefit), and decided that the tradeoffs were worth it. It was a decision he researched thoroughly, and although it might not be perfectly logical (although it’s entirely possible it is), he even understood the emotional factors contributing to the decision – we’re humans, not Vulcans! It didn’t impact his life in a negative way financially or otherwise, it doesn’t disproportionately hurt the earth (given the society he lives in), and most importantly, he didn’t make the consumerist mistake of believing that buying the Tesla would make him happy.

That’s the root of the problem for most people, I think – they are constantly fed advertising that convinces them that spending money on something will make them happy. It won’t EVER do that, but using it to remove frustration and pain from your life can definitely improve our level of happiness.

It’s tricky and complicated figuring out that balance at times for sure, but everything is always a balance. Almost nothing in life is binary.

#8793. Anita Herbert Shares Her Upper-Body Smith Machine Workout

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

There’s nothing quite like lifting a barbell loaded with weighted plates when you are looking to dial in your resistance training efforts, but for many people, the idea of balancing a free weight seems daunting, and for others, mobility issues or a lack of experience can become a serious obstacle. It’s good to know then, that buff beauty Anita Herbert has sculpted herself into phenomenal shape by including the Smith machine into her rotation.

“Here are some of my favorite back and shoulder exercises you can add to your next upper body session, using just a Smith machine,” offered the Hungarian in a recent Instagram post for her “Fit Queen Army” on Instagram. This fit female is not only a transformative coach, but she is also an IFBB Pro. “Save this for your next upper body day!” Herbert advised her 150,000-plus followers.

The “FitQueen” showed how to get the most from each machine

Machines, just like free weights, can build muscle by progressive overload, and this session is stacked with plenty of heavy reps. Aim for 8 to 12 on each exercise to put your body into a state of hypertrophy, forcing to adaptations that will build your muscles back stronger.

For her first superset, the Fit Queen begins with the shoulder press, primarily working her anterior deltoid at the front of the shoulder, and also recruiting the upper back, triceps, and core. Next, using a supinated grip, comes the inverted row for taxing the mid-back, lats, and rear delts.

The second superset calls for a pullup that is great for athletes of any level, because you will raise your body from a seated position, and can use the feet for further stabilization. Using a wide grip, pause for a short time at the top of the lift, in order to increase time under tension. This will work the lats, rhomboids, and upper trapezius, but be sure not to shrug, and concentrate on a smooth range of motion. This exercise is followed by the single arm shoulder press, to fix any strength imbalances and fire up those front deltoids once again.

The third and final superset starts with a single-arm row, hitting the lats, traps, and rear delts, while also activating the rotator cuff and forearms. Keep your core braced and focus on engaging the back, while keeping the elbows close to the body. The last move is the upright row for building some serious boulder shoulders. You will also work the triceps and upper back as you improve grip strength all at the same time.

While it is true that the Smith machine stabilizes the weight and reduces the chance of injury, you may be surprised to find that the load can feel heavier on this device.

“It can feel heavier than free weights, especially for upper body exercises because Smith machines have different bar weights, counterbalance systems and resistance,” explained Herbert, who provided further advice to her seriously impressed followers in the comments section. “The fixed bar path also changed how the movement feels, compared to free weights.”
